...how it stands with our work shall be clearly reported: for first, the majority will concern the translation, and thereafter a small portion will concern the annotations <term>Anmerkungen: scholarly notes or commentary provided alongside the main text to explain difficult passages</term>. A soul that is simple <term>einfältig: in this 18th-century context, "simple" refers to a sincere, uncomplicated faith rather than a lack of intelligence</term> and directly seeks a turning point for itself does not need to linger so long on the first part of this preface, but will soon perceive what the basis, the intention, and the use of this translation is, and can be briefly informed of what is necessary in the second part.

### § III.

But whoever considers the translation at first glance to be useless, or might consider it necessary to warn others against it, let them be all the more attentive in this place, so that no one may take or give offense anywhere, but rather recognize the benefit that is present. Never have there been greater disputes regarding new translations of the Holy Scripture than in our time: and for that reason, it will be useful to explain the matter such that even the common man <term>gemeine Mann: the average person or layperson, as opposed to the academic or clerical elite</term> can find his way into it and listen to such an explanation.

### § IV.

The Holy Scripture of the New Testament was originally composed in Greek <note>original: "Griechisch"</note> by the Apostles and their coworkers, but was gradually translated into the languages of those peoples who were brought to Christianity in all parts of the world, as still happens to this day. Therefore, among those who otherwise understand nothing but their German mother tongue <term>Muttersprache: native language</term>, even the simplest person...

<header>Preface. § 4. 5. 6.</header>

distinguish and remember that this or that German New Testament was not written by the Apostles and Evangelists with those exact German words, syllables, and letters, but was translated by the highly gifted <term>hochbegabten: a traditional honorific used here to acknowledge Luther’s intellectual and spiritual talents</term> Doctor Luther, or others, from another language.

### § V.

One may translate a story, a poem, a speech, or a letter—whether of a spiritual or worldly content—from one language into another, who knows how many times: yet no translation, even if each were skillfully done and agreed most precisely with the sense of the original, would coincide with other translations in every word and turn of phrase. For *Blessed is the man* <note>original Latin: "Beatus vir"</note> Luther uses both: *Well for the person* and *Blessed is the man*. *Savior* <note>original Latin: "Salvator"</note> is called *Healer* <term>Heiland: a traditional German term for Savior that carries the root meaning of "making whole" or "healing"</term>, *Rescuer*, or *Redeemer*. *Must* <note>original Latin: "debet"</note> is the same as "shall," "ought," etc. Despite all this, the meaning remains one and the same.

### § VI.

Furthermore, one does not need to be a scholar at all, but only understand a little of a foreign language beyond one’s own mother tongue, to know that in all kinds of writings of spiritual and worldly content, it is very difficult and often impossible to produce a translation that is perfectly identical to the original. This is due to the different natures of languages and the advantages and disadvantages that one has over another. It is even more difficult to achieve this when the text moves from an Eastern <term>morgenländische: literally "morning-land," referring to the languages of the Near East like Hebrew or Greek</term> to a Western <term>abendländische: literally "evening-land," referring to European languages</term> language, and from an ancient into a modern tongue—and, above all, when it concerns the Word of God. § VII.

->### § VII.<-

The main essence <term>Hauptsumma: the "sum total" or the core substance of a matter</term> remains ever the same: even if one had to make do with the clumsiest translation of the New Testament under the sun, and additionally with the most careless transcript of it, he could still distinguish the story of the leper from the story of the paralytic <term>Gichtbrüchigen: literally "one broken by gout," a term historically used for those suffering from paralysis or palsy</term>. Indeed, he would still find the knowledge of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; of the birth, baptism, deeds, and speeches, the suffering and the glory of Jesus Christ; of sin and grace, etc. Thus, with a compliant heart, he could be blessedly edified in faith, in love, and in hope.

->### § VIII.<-

But just as in natural life one seeks not only the barest necessity, but also comfort, cleanliness, adornment, and grace—indeed, pursuing these things in worldly vanity as high as one possibly can—so should it be much more so in spiritual matters. In the translation of human writings, one person can reach and express the meaning of another much more easily, and even if he misses the mark, not much usually depends on it. But in the translation of the words of God, concerning heavenly and eternal things, one should act with a deep respect, with fear and trembling, so that one might not soil anything, withhold <term>unterschlagen: to suppress or embezzle; here meaning to leave out a portion of God's truth</term> anything, or confuse anything. In a speech or a poem, a person does not like to tolerate an incorrect syllable for himself or others; in a painting or a musical piece, an impure stroke or

...others <note>original: *ot...* (continued from previous page: *others*)</note>—just as one considers a bit of clay <note>original: *Ton*</note> in one’s food, a tainted grain, a broken thread in a glove, a nick in a sword or knife, or a cracked window pane in a room to be unacceptable: so too can there be no contemptible trifle when it comes to the words of God. Among the holy men of God, the impression of the things themselves in their hearts and the expression of the words to others matched perfectly; and sometimes much depends on this or that turn of phrase—which might seem entirely indifferent to most—but which can finally be perceived by someone and shared with others for their edification. This does not mean that every reader of the Holy Scriptures must undertake such work; rather, what one person occasionally does in this regard serves many others.

->### § IX.<-

<page-num>IX</page-num>
<header>Preface. § 9.</header>

Reports and traces of this exist in great quantity: and on the contrary, one does not find that throughout all of Christendom at any time anyone ever objected to or took offense at there being more than one single translation into this or that language. In England, Holland, Denmark, Geneva, etc., the translation delivered to the people in print is continually improved from one period to the next, and from one edition to another. Even in the Roman Church—where they have bound themselves so closely to the Vulgate <note>original: *Vulgatam*; the standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> that among all versions there is none for which they have shown such great zeal (having declared it "authentic" at the Council of Trent <term>Council of Trent: a major 16th-century meeting of the Catholic Church that solidified its doctrines against the Reformation</term>)—they nevertheless allow various translations to circulate freely, not only in the Latin language for students and scholars, but also in French and various mother tongues for other readers. One need only consult Jacques Le Long’s *Sacred Library* <note>original: *Bibliothecam sacram*; a comprehensive bibliography of Bible editions published in 1709</note>, where ancient and new translations are described in great number. Before Luther’s time, various German translations of the Holy Scripture were printed, which were indeed very uneven, yet they served the people of that time well enough. However, it was very praiseworthy that Luther made a new translation; and especially since the Reformation, his blessed translation has gained great acceptance. But just as this great instrument <note>original: *Rüstzeug*; literally "equipment" or "tool," here referring to Luther as a chosen vessel of God</note> did not allow himself to be deterred by the German translations common before his time from making a new one, and even refused to bind himself to his own first attempt—

### Preface. § 9.

...[bound] <note>This continues from the previous page, likely meaning Luther was not "bound" to his first draft.</note>, but rather reviewed it further from one time to another, and accepted the suggestions of other capable men in this regard; he also passed away in peace with the recognition that further improvement should take place. Thus, alongside him, after him, and especially in recent times, other industrious people have improved various things here and there in his translation. They have either moved such improvements into the text itself, placed them in the **margin**, or introduced them on other occasions, or even set forth new translations separately, in which they come sometimes closer and sometimes less close to Luther’s words. Luther indeed rightly spoke out with zeal against those who acted unfaithfully in this matter and sullied his work; however, he also looked upon the work of other honest men with favorable and happy eyes. Exactly when he was occupied with translating, he wrote from the "wilderness" <note>original: *Wüsten*; a reference to the Wartburg Castle where Luther lived in hiding and translated the New Testament</note> to Johann Lang, an Augustinian preacher in Erfurt: *In this matter (the translation of the New Testament) I hear that you also are laboring. PROCEED as you have begun. Would that EVERY SINGLE TOWN had its own translator.* <note>original Latin: "In ea re (versione N. T.) et te audio laborare. PERGE ut coepisti, Vtinam OPPIDA SINGVLA interpretem suum haberent."</note>

I desire to give not a better translation, but a different one than Luther’s, and that not without cause. The clarity and purity of the language is, next to the correctness of the meaning, the principal virtue of a translation: and if we did not have Luther’s translation, such a translation as his would be desirable above all others. But since it is now available, it is gratefully pre-sup...

### Preface. § 9.

...[language], and alongside it another translation is good, which does not flow so smoothly, but expresses the genuine Greek source text more carefully. Some, for whom this is helpful, may make use of it for themselves and thus hold two translations together, each of which makes up for the deficiencies of the other. Even if at this hour one had a translation that indisputably contained all the excellences of all modern translators and even those of Luther himself, neither we nor our immediate descendants should give up Luther’s version. It should rightly be left in possession for general and public use, and in particular, the well-known core passages, as he rendered them into German, should be retained. Furthermore, in the Bibles printed under his name, one should change nothing and add nothing that did not originate from Luther. For the many souls who have been saved since the Reformation, Luther has been of service to them either through his translation or through other translations, sermons, and writings prompted by him. This precious instrument <term>instrument (Rüstzeug): Literally "tools" or "equipment," used here to describe Luther as a divinely chosen vessel or tool for the faith.</term> reigns with his gift in the best part of Western Christendom, especially from his first appearance—from the end of the 1260 days of the woman in the wilderness, until the woman has endured her three and a half times in her place in the wilderness. <note>These are chronological references to the Book of Revelation (12:6 and 12:14). The author is using biblical prophecy to frame the historical era of the Reformation.</note> The rest should be left to enlightened posterity.

If there were as yet no newer German translation after Luther, one might rather say that we should stay with Luther alone; but now that there are so many newer ones, this very fact is an advantage for [Luthe-]

<page-num>XII</page-num>
### Preface. § 9.

**Luther’s Version.** Friend and foe alike can remain calm in this matter: the latter, because so many other translations do Luther’s work all the less harm, and instead always hinder and wear each other out; the former, because these translations provide exactly the benefit that Augustine, long ago, attributed to the comparison of many Latin translations—some of which were more precise, others more free. Even the latest among these translations cannot be compared with Luther’s, nor can it become dangerous to Luther’s version, as long as it concerns only the New Testament and not also the Old, and as long as it is not printed entirely on its own, but is accompanied by intervening interpretations. The German translation of the Holy Scripture by Luther is an excellent, heroic work. Muthmann, in particular, has shown this in great detail in his preface to the *German Original-Bible*. <note>Muthmann likely refers to Johann Muthmann (1685–1747), a theologian who defended the linguistic power of Luther's work. The "Original-Bible" refers to a scholarly edition of the time.</note> It is an easy thing to translate the New Testament into German. The Old Testament, however, presented the greatest difficulties.

Yet, it is not intended that all Protestant Germans should be bound to Luther’s translation alone. There are many Protestant nations outside of Germany that either have more than one translation or improve their standard translation from time to time. See: Rumpeus’s commentary on the books of the New Testament in general, pages 344–443. <note>original: "Vid. Rumpei comm. ad libros N. T. in genere"</note> Thus, among the Protestants in Germany, one may allow other German translations to stand alongside Luther’s. Indeed, while the Vulgate <term>Vulgate: The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible which became the official Catholic version.</term> was declared free of all errors at the Council of Trent, we, on the other hand, recognize that there are errors in Luther’s work. When Augustus, Duke of Lüneburg, <note>Augustus the Younger (1579–1666), a learned prince and famous book collector who authored his own biblical studies.</note> was considering a new German translation, it might have been for Luther’s...

<meta>catchword: Bi= (likely beginning of "Bibel" or "Bibliothek")</meta>

<summary>The author argues that while Luther's translation is a "heroic work," it is not perfect, and Protestants should be open to comparing it with other translations, much as St. Augustine encouraged comparing Latin versions.</summary>
<keywords>Martin Luther, Bible translation, Saint Augustine, Johann Muthmann, Council of Trent, Vulgate, Augustus Duke of Lüneburg, Protestantism</keywords>

At this point, it is not possible to detail the entire doctrine of the correct manner of translating with all its rules: yet I wish to indicate several of them which I have deemed particularly necessary to observe, and to explain them in the proper way.

1. A translation must be based on a *precisely revised original text*.
There is something here that must primarily be disclosed. If an unbelieving Greek read the Hebrew-Greek <note>original: "Hebräisch-Griechische"; referring to the Hellenistic Greek of the New Testament which is heavily influenced by Hebrew idioms and thought patterns</note> in the **New Testament**, he could not declare it free of barbarisms <note>original: "Barbarismis"; a term used by linguists to describe words or expressions that are considered "foreign" or "unpolished" in a specific language</note> and solecisms <note>original: "Soloecismis"; perceived grammatical errors or deviations from standard classical rules</note> compared to his native pure-Greek dialect. But whoever recognizes it as **God’s Word** should abstain from immodest thoughts and speech, considering that just as the heavens are higher than the earth, so too is God’s language. Despite all His condescension <term>Condescendence: In theology, this refers to God "lowering" Himself or His language to a human level so that finite beings can understand Him.</term> regarding the human instruments He uses, His language remains higher than all human linguistic arts.

Sometimes, the idioms of the **New Testament**—even in cases where one would not expect it—finally find their equivalents in pagan <note>original: "heidnischen"; referring here to secular or classical Greek authors like Plato or Homer</note> writings through the diligence of those who examine everything. This is not to be completely disregarded; however, such idioms are sparingly sown among the pagans, while in the **New Testament** they are common. Therefore, these must rather be explained through a comparison of the texts with one another, and with the Hebrew **Old Testament** along with its Greek translation <note>The Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament used by the early Church</note> which was very well known among the Hebrews in Greek lands. 

Now, regarding individual words: the Apostles did not have much choice whether they said a money-box <note>original: γλωσσοκομεῖον or γλωσσόκομον</note>, to recline at table <note>original: ἀνάκειμαι or κατάκειμαι</note>, or beyond <note>original: ἐπέκεινα or ὑπερέκεινα</note>. Thus, much appears in the **New Testament** which does not please the Atticists <term>Atticists: Greek stylists who insisted on the "pure" dialect of ancient Athens and looked down upon the common Greek (Koine) used in the New Testament.</term>, because such variations did not hinder understanding; indeed, for common people, it was actually more helpful. But where the distinction in expression affects the meaning itself, there their accuracy—because according to Divine purpose they had to give a clear tone—is quite incomparable. It is also no violation of precision to express ancient things using terms common and known in our own times, even if there is no perfect equality between them. For example: "to recline" <note>Greek: ἀνάκειμαι, ἀνακλίνομαι, ἀναπίπτω, etc.</note> actually means "I lie down to eat," because that is how the ancients did it; whereas we "sit down to table." Therefore, I retain the latter phrasing, following Luther's example. In truth, the two postures are not far apart. A bottle <note>Greek: Ἀσκὸς / *askos*</note> is a **wineskin**—not just the kind of tube through which one lets wine run into a barrel, but also a sack made of leather or hides in which wine and other drinks are carried and stored. Similarly, in the context of a bed, one calls that which is filled with feathers and covered with a casing a **ticking** <note>German: *Schlauch*; the author is comparing the biblical "skin" to the feather-filled "casing" of a mattress common in his time.</note>.

A "penny" <note>Greek: Δηνάριον / *dēnarion*; Latin: *denarius*</note> is worth ten small coins <note>Latin: *asses*; Greek: ἀσσάρια</note> or **kreutzers** <note>A common silver coin in the author's time.</note>, and is not inconveniently called a **ten-ner** <note>German: *Zehner*; a coin worth ten units.</note>.

A **farthing** <note>original Greek: κοδράντης / kodrantes; Latin: *quadrans*</note> is the fourth part of a kreuzer, a penny; a **mite** <note>Greek: λεπτόν / lepton</note> is half of a penny, a small coin <note>German: *Heller*</note>. A **drachma** <note>Greek: Δραχμή</note> is the same as a **denarius** <note>Latin: *denarius*</note>; therefore a **didrachm** <note>Greek: δίδραχμον</note> is a **silver coin** <note>German: *Kopfstück*</note>; a **stater** <note>Greek: στατὴρ</note> is of the same value. A **mina** <note>Greek/Latin: μνᾶ / *mina*</note> is equal to one **mark** <note>A traditional unit of weight for precious metals.</note>.

There are concerns regarding the word **repentance** <note>Greek: μετάνοια / *metanoia*</note>. According to Greek etymology, it means a **change of mind**; however, the Greek word is used in place of the Hebrew <term>Nicham: A Hebrew term suggesting deep regret or a change of will and purpose, rather than just a shift in intellectual opinion.</term>, which signifies a feeling of regret and a change of the **will** rather than just the **mind**; and thus this latter meaning should take precedence. Meanwhile, the short, simple German word **penance** or **repentance** <note>German: *Busse*</note> is exactly that.

One might object: "repentance" <note>German: *Busse*</note> is the same as **punishment**. Answer: If one wishes to go that far, one should go even further. Even to "punish" <note>German: *strafen*</note> actually means to **convict** or **convince**. (Genesis 20:16; John 16:8). For this is why one punishes a transgressor: so that he may look within himself and be convinced of his guilt. Now, when a soul is convinced of its deviation and allows itself to be convinced, that is precisely the **remorseful change of mind**, through which it certainly judges, avenges, and punishes the sin.

Furthermore, to "atone" <note>German: *büssen*</note> actually means to **supplement**, **remedy**, or **fulfill**, as in "filling gaps" or "satisfying a desire" (Nehemiah 4:7; Psalm 78:30). (Hence, punishment is also called "penance" <note>German: *Busse*</note> because a lawmaker restores himself through the transgressor, so that the lack of obedience may be compensated). And through this remorseful change of mind, the gaps, fractures, and tears of the heart—as well as the new desire and longing for salvation—are atoned for, supplemented, and fulfilled. If someone only finds within themselves that which the word "repentance" requires, then

3. A translation must not be darker, but also not clearer; not weaker, but also not more forceful; not harsher, but also not more elegant than the original.

Otherwise, either something is taken away from the divine meaning of an Apostle, or something is added through the human sense of the translator. This latter is even more precarious than the former. In all things, that which is simpler and purer is better.

For example: Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, Hebrews 10:38. It says: **The just shall live by faith.** In the Greek, this phrase, **by faith**, can be connected with what precedes it or with what follows it, so that it can be understood as "righteousness from faith" or "living from faith" <note>This refers to a grammatical ambiguity in the Greek text of Romans 1:17 (*ho de dikaios ek pisteos zesetai*), where "by faith" could modify "the just man" or "shall live."</note>: and that which is so ambiguous in the original, a faithful translator should diligently translate as ambiguous as well, and not forestall the readers, but leave the choice free,

4. A translation must not be "un-German" to our ears, but it also must not be *too* "good German." <note>The author warns against over-polishing the language so much that the specific character of the original Greek and Hebrew is lost.</note>

<page-num>XX</page-num>
### Preface. § 10.

...he will certainly be remorseful and of a different mind. I do not wish to find fault with anyone who translates *repentance* <note>original: μετάνοια (*metanoia*)</note> into German as "change of mind," but I am simply providing the reasons why I, for my part, retain the word **Repentance** <note>original: *Buße*; a term that carries connotations of both internal regret and outward acts of penance.</note>. Even those who in ancient times used "Repentance" for *metanoia* did not mean a punishment; otherwise, they would not have translated *penitence* <note>original: *poenitentiam*</note> (which they divided into *contrition*, *confession*, and *satisfaction* <note>original: *Contritionem*, *Confessionem*, *et Satisfactionem*; these are the three traditional parts of the Sacrament of Penance in Catholic theology: sorrow for sin, verbal confession, and works of reparation.</note>) in such a way, but only *satisfaction*. Today, we are so accustomed to the word "Repentance" that anyone who might be moved by the phrase "change of mind" is moved just as much, or even more, by the word "Repentance."

3. A translation must not be darker, but also not clearer; not weaker, but also not more violent; not harder, but also not more elegant than the original.

Otherwise, either something is taken away from the divine meaning of an Apostle, or something is added through the human sense of the translator. The latter is even more precarious than the former. In all things, that which is minimal and pure is better.

For example: Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, and Hebrews 10:38 state: **The righteous shall live by faith.** In the Greek, this phrase, *by faith*, can be connected to what precedes it or what follows it, so that it can be understood either as "righteousness from faith" or "living from faith." Since the original is so ambiguous, a faithful translator should diligently render it into German as equally ambiguous, and not anticipate the readers' decision, but rather leave the choice free,

This admittedly sounds somewhat forced: but the loss of elegance is compensated by the power of the words which, in the original text, do not rhyme by mere chance. And whoever looks at the matter itself will not take offense, but rather, once he is accustomed to this manner, will find much grace.

<page-num>XXV</page-num>
<header>Preface. § 10.</header>

**Robber** <note>original: λῃστής</note>; **Murderer** <note>original: φονεύς</note>.
**To bathe** <note>original: λούειν</note>; **To wash** <note>original: νίπτειν</note>. John 13:10.
**Candle** or **Lamp** <note>original: λύχνος</note>; **Light** <note>original: φῶς</note>.
**Dead** <note>original: νεκρός</note>; **Deceased** <note>original: τεθνηκώς</note>.
**New** or **Young** <note>original: νέος</note>; **Fresh** <note>original: πρόσφατος</note>.
**Child** <note>original: νήπιος, τέκνον</note>; **Son** <note>original: υἱός</note>. Gal. 4:1, 6 etc.
**Worse** [in character] <note>original: πονηρότερος</note>; **Worse** [in condition] <note>original: χείρων</note>.
**To keep** <note>original: τηρεῖν</note>; **To guard** <note>original: φυλάσσειν</note>. John 17:12.

Thus, in John 21:15 ff., I have translated *agapan* <note>original: ἀγαπᾶν</note> twice as **to love**, and *philein* <note>original: φιλεῖν</note> five times as **to have affection for**; likewise *boskein* <note>original: βόσκειν</note> as **to feed**, and *poimainein* <note>original: ποιμαίνειν</note> as **to shepherd**. I did this not because I saw a significant or equal difference in the Greek and German <note>The author admits that the German words "lieben" and "lieb haben" are nearly identical, just as the Greek words can be, but he wants to remain linguistically precise.</note>, but merely to indicate that two different words were used in the original text. The word *philadelphia* <note>original: φιλαδελφία</note> I have rendered as **brotherly love**, as it is explained in 1 Thess. 4:9 and 1 Pet. 2:17. However, in two places, to distinguish it from "love" in general, I have used **brotherly favor** <note>original: brüderliche Huld</note>, specifically in Rom. 12:9–10 and 2 Pet. 1:7, just as the names Gotthold and Gottlieb, or Christhold and Christlieb, essentially carry the same meaning. 

There is a greater distinction between *aito* <note>original: αἰτῶ</note>, **I ask**, and *eroto* <note>original: ἐρωτῶ</note>, **I request** (John 14:13, 16). For the Son of God never uses the former word when speaking of Himself, but rather the latter, as it is a more dignified term <note>The author suggests that *eroto* implies a request between equals or a more formal petition, highlighting Jesus's unique relationship with the Father.</note>.

Where the Greeks have very distinct words and we Germans do not, we must manage as best we can. For example, the word **Devil** <note>original: Teufel</note> properly corresponds to *diabolos* <note>original: διάβολος</note> and signifies that wicked enemy of God and all goodness. However, it has also been customary from ancient times to use the same word for *daimon* <note>original: δαίμων</note> or *daimonion* <note>original: δαιμόνιον</note>, which generally refers to one or more spirits in various degrees of malice. <page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>Preface. § 10.</header>

However, it is not necessary to treat these separately. For they flow of their own accord from the <term>original text</term> <note>original: Grundtext; the source language of the Bible, such as Hebrew or Greek</note> into the translation, provided that the translation follows both the two previously mentioned rules and those that now follow.

8. A translation must remain with the order of the words, as much as the <term>mother tongue</term> <note>the language into which one is translating</note> permits.

**John 13:15** says, according to the Greek: that, *as I have done to you, so also you should do.* In this instance, the action of the Lord precedes the action of the disciples. In such cases, and many others, the order of the words is very natural and deliberate. One should especially consider the **17th Chapter of John**. There are many common phrases, such as *heaven and earth*, *mother and brothers*, *hands and feet*, *flesh and blood*, etc., and in such a standard word order, no special meaning should be sought. But where the order is reversed against custom—so that it says: *the earth and the heaven*, *the brothers and the mother*, *feet and hands*, *blood and flesh*—then there is something significant behind it. In the same way, it is common for it to say *Jesus Christ*, because *Jesus* is the name and *Christ* is the <term>surname</term> <note>or title, meaning "Anointed One"</note>; and from this natural order of words, nothing further can be made. But when, on the other hand, it sometimes says *Christ Jesus*, then regard is being paid to the promises of the <note>original: "Messia"</note> Messiah or the Christ, and to the faith of the ancients.

<page-num>XXIX</page-num>
<header>Preface. § 10.</header>

Occasionally, in a single passage, the order of the words is deliberately swapped:

**Luke 11:36** <note>original: Luc. XI. 36.</note> says: **entirely bright**, and, **bright entirely**, where in the first clause the phrase "entirely" stands first, and in the second clause the word "bright" stands first. The leading word in both clauses must be raised with an <term>accent</term> <note>a vocal stress or emphasis</note> in pronunciation, because in the first clause the "entirely" is contrasted with the dark part, and in the second, the "bright" quality is specifically being considered.

Similarly, the Savior speaks in **John 14:1** <note>original: Joh. XIV. 1.</note> to his disciples: **Believe in God, and in me believe.** In the first clause, the word "believe" stands at the beginning, and in the second, the word "me" comes first. To the Old Testament faith in God, the New Testament faith in Jesus Christ was now also to come to the disciples in full measure.

In the same place, **verses 2 and 3**, it says: **a place for you**, and then, **for you a place**. First the "place" comes first, then the "you" comes first in the word order, with an emphasis and a vocal <term>accent</term>. Speaking in a worldly way, one might say: the castle is already built; now it must be fully furnished so that you can move in.

In passing, we make this observation regarding these passages where the accent was mentioned: how much is required of a person even just to correctly read a single chapter or a text from the Bible aloud in a public congregation.

What has been reported here regarding true <term>emphasis</term> <note>original: Emphasi; the specific weight or importance given to a word</note>, and particularly regarding the order of words, might be viewed by some as a useless and far-fetched

<page-num>XXX</page-num>
<header>Preface. § 10.</header>

[...to] laugh at and destroy such subtlety. But I am not ashamed: I am also not the first to bring this up <note>original: "auf die Bahn bringt," meaning to introduce or champion an idea</note>. Many wise people, especially among the ancients, have recognized it, and it does not rely on just one or two passages alone, but is grounded in the nature of human speech itself. Therefore, it can be deduced through a constant analogy throughout the entire New Testament, so much so that one could write a substantial commentary <note>original: "Commentarium"</note> just on the order of words. Indeed, in the courtly style <note>original: "Stilo curiæ," referring to the formal, often rigid language used in legal or diplomatic circles</note>, the rank and sequence of words is sometimes observed so precisely that the natural sentence structure is set aside. At the very least, it is certain that one should stick to the original order of the words in the translation: afterwards, a reader has the choice to look for deeper meaning in such an order or not. This point will likely be the primary reason if anything in my translation seems strange to the reader.

9. A translation should represent the articles, pronouns, particles, numbers, tenses, middle verbs <note>original: "articulos, pronomina, particulas, numeros, tempora, verba media"; these are specific technical terms for Greek grammar</note>, and other elements, sometimes with a sensible freedom and sometimes with the utmost precision.

The speeches of the people whom the Savior <note>Heiland</note> and his apostles had around and before them—whether they were friends or enemies—are by no means as significant as what is spoken by God, Christ, the Holy Spirit, an angel, John the Baptist, an apostle, a prophet, or an evangelist. Furthermore, depending on the content, there is sometimes more and sometimes less importance placed on the accuracy <note>original: "Accuratesse"</note> of the translation versus its clarity <note>original: "Deutlichkeit"</note>.

<page-num>XXXI</page-num>
<header>Preface. § 10.</header>

Whether the Article <note>original: "Articulus"; the grammatical category for words like 'the' or 'a'</note>—the <note>original: "ὁ, ἡ, τὸ"</note>—as well as "a" or "an" is included or not, is often not as trivial a matter as many might think. One should examine the passages where it appears, such as Matthew 1:23, 5:35, 6:6, 8:12, Mark 4:38, John 1:21, 34, 10:11; and those where it does not appear, such as John 5:27, 13:2, 18:15, 1 John 4:16, Revelation 13:11, 18. Thus, in the beginnings of Matthew, Mark, Revelation, and many of the Apostolic letters, I have followed the Greek and simultaneously our own custom; for on the title pages of books, one does not say, for example: "this is the Church Postil <note>original: "Kirchenpostille"; a traditional collection of sermons or commentaries</note> of Luther," but simply, "Church Postil," etc. Similarly, one does not write "Eberhard, a Duke," but simply "Eberhard, Duke." Strictly speaking, the Son of Man <note>original: "ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου"</note> means "the Son of the Human," but when one wishes to give this title—which the Savior uses so frequently in the Gospels—more briefly, it is more convenient [to say] the Human-Son <note>original: "Menschen-Sohn"</note>, to the Human-Son, the Human-Son, rather than "the Son of the Human," so that the Article <note>the word "the"</note> belongs to the noun, "Son," and the compound word, "Human-Son," may be regarded as a single name.

Among the Greeks, verbs <note>original: "Verba"</note> very often stand without the *I, you, he, we, you, they*, and when they do add these pronouns <note>original: "pronomina"</note>, it carries an emphasis <note>original: "Nachdruck"</note> which we Germans cannot indicate in the same way, because we always include these pronouns with our verbs. In speech, one can indicate this emphasis with vocal stress, and in writing or printing with a capital letter; we also use this to distinguish the numeral <note>original: "numerale"</note> "One" <note>original: "Ein, unus"</note> from the article "a" <note>original: "ein"</note>, and so on.

With the particles <note>Small, uninflected words that indicate grammatical relationships</note> *and* <note>original Greek: "καὶ"</note> and *but* or *and* <note>original Greek: "δὲ"</note>, the narratives of the Evangelists <note>The Gospel writers</note> begin very often; and in the Gospel of John, they also very frequently begin with *therefore* <note>original Greek: "οὖν"</note>. The use of *and* <note>original Greek: "καὶ"</note> and *also/and* <note>original Greek: "τὲ"</note> often creates a *polysyndeton* <note>A stylistic device using several conjunctions in close succession to create emphasis or rhythm</note>. The German language, however, does not make use of such small words so frequently. Similarly, the Greeks also place *for* <note>original Greek: "γὰρ"</note> where the text moves from the premise to the discussion <note>original Latin: "a propositione ad tractationem"</note>, as seen in Matthew 1:18, Luke 9:44, Romans 1:18, and 1 Thessalonians 5:3. We Germans usually omit the word "for" in such cases, or use "namely" in its place. Otherwise, I have paid close attention to the <term>conjunctions</term> <note>connecting words like 'and', 'but', 'because'</note>. For they often signify a great deal, as do sometimes the <term>prepositions</term> <note>words like 'in', 'at', 'from'</note>, which I have endeavored to translate into German not simply according to the dictionary <note>original Latin: "Vocabulario"</note>, but according to their inherent power.

The Greeks often use the word *all* or *every* <note>original Greek: "πᾶς"; original Latin: "omnis"</note> in the singular number, which we imitate in German as best as can be done. Conversely, they often use neuter adjectives and nouns in the plural where German has only the singular, yet with the same concept as the former. For instance, *crowd* <note>original Greek: "ὄχλος"</note> means a heap of people; *crowds* <note>original Greek: "ὄχλοι"</note> means the heaps. This plural form appears often in the Evangelists regarding the multitude of people who came to Jesus. "The people," in the singular, means exactly that in German. The Greeks say *heavens* <note>original Greek: "οὐρανοὶ"</note> in the plural, just as the Hebrews use the dual form <note>A grammatical number denoting exactly two</note>; hence *the kingdom of the heavens* <note>original Greek: "ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν"</note>, the kingdom of those heavens, or the Kingdom of Heaven. However, they also use *heaven* <note>original Greek: "οὐρανὸς"</note> in the singular, like the Romans <note>referring to the Latin "caelum"</note>. Luther <note>original: "Lutherus"</note> also occasionally imitated the plural; we, however, follow the original text <note>original: "Grundtext"</note> consistently in this regard,

Luke 24:35 and Acts 7:13, *he made himself known* <note>original Greek: "ἐγνώσθη, ἀνεγνωρίσθη"</note>.

### § XIV.

It is an established matter among those who teach or practice the science of interpretation <note>The author is referring to the academic study of hermeneutics—the theory and methodology of interpreting texts, especially the Bible.</note> that a translation must be accompanied by <term>scholiis|scholias; explanatory notes or comments on a text</term> or short annotations to fulfill the goal of reflecting the original as closely as possible. I provide such notes here as well, placed beneath the text. Much has already been mentioned above regarding the rules in general, and much will now be explained in the annotations—and this most especially in those places where the translation might perhaps most surprise the reader.

In the annotations themselves, the primary focus is on growth in the grace and knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ. Yet I provide very few explicit practical applications <term>Nutzanwendungen|Theological lessons or moral instructions intended to be "used" by the reader for personal spiritual growth</term>; not out of coldness, but out of modesty. For Scripture carries its own applications within itself. When the Lord says: "Strive for it," no one can say anything more powerful. When the Apostle says: "Rejoice," no one can offer anything more awakening. Therefore, if you wish to have many practical applications, take for example one section and go through it entirely—the text as well as the annotations below—with the intent of looking for: 1) the doctrine, which is then looked at again for 2) the refutation of error, 3) exhortation, 4) warning, and 5) comfort. In this way, you will have application enough.

### § XVI.

Should the preface to a German New Testament not have been more <term>edifying|German: "erbaulicher." In this context, it refers to the Pietist tradition of writing that aims to provide spiritual nourishment and emotional connection rather than just academic information.</term>? Many will think so—even those who always desire something "strong and aggressive" (which they alone consider edifying) and yet do not actually build themselves up. My answer is this: this is a preface not to the New Testament itself, but specifically to the translation. 

A servant in a hall who properly <term>trims|German: "schneuzet." Literally to "snuff" or trim the charred part of a candle wick so it doesn't smoke and the flame burns brighter.</term> the candle provided by the master of the house on the table, so that it burns brightly, performs a far better and more pleasant service for those present than if he were to light his own special little candle from that one. Now, Holy Scripture is a light that in itself possesses perfect clarity at one time as at another; however, through the fault of men, such clarity is often hindered in various ways. He who removes such hindrances performs a more important service for the lovers of Scripture than many of them themselves appreciate. 

It is enough for a faithful worker that he serves them, even if they do not notice the difference between the previous and the current radiance of the light. This is my aim with the present translation of the New Testament; and in this preface, it was necessary to show how one should approach the translation and notes, just as one was also compelled to focus primarily on that purpose in the appendix. But whoever <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "ber" suggests the next word is "lieber" (rather).</note>

### Note.

The <term>New Testament|original: "Neue Testament," which in this context refers both to the books of the Bible and the "New Covenant" established by Christ.</term> is actually the great <term>institution|original: "Anstalt," referring to God's divine arrangement, decree, or dispensation.</term> itself, through which God—by the death of His Son—brought about the forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation for the human race, and thus truly fulfilled the promise given previously. Therefore, all the holy books in which such a great matter is described are called the New Testament, because they give us news of this New Testament. Just as a <term>sovereign|original: "Herrschaft"</term> gives their servants their <term>statutes|original: "Stat," referring to formal ordinances or standing orders.</term> not only verbally but also in writing, so too has the great God—both before and after the coming of His Son in the flesh—communicated to His people, at first verbally and then also in writing, that which was necessary for them as a saving report of His holy and gracious will and of their required duties. The scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments consist of three kinds of content. For in the Old <note>The text breaks off here; the "three kinds of content" likely refer to history, laws/doctrines, and prophecies, a common distinction in 18th-century biblical scholarship.</note>

A complete report! An invaluable benefit!

# The Gospel,
## as described by Matthew.

---

### Note.

There is but one single <term>Gospel|original: "Evangelium"</term> or message regarding the <term>life and conduct|original: "Wandel," referring to his earthly journey and behavior</term> of the Son of God on earth, and of that which he did and taught. However, there are four holy men—namely two Apostles, John and Matthew, and two other <term>capable witnesses|original: "tüchtige Zeugen"</term>, namely Mark and Luke—who composed it in writing. I have brought their four books together into one in the *Harmony* <note>A "Gospel Harmony" is a common theological project where the four different accounts of Jesus's life are blended into a single chronological narrative to show their consistency.</note>; but now we shall take up each one individually.

### Annotations.

**Ch. I, 1-17. The Genealogy of Jesus Christ.**

Matthew composed the history of Jesus Christ for the benefit of the Jews in such a way that he simultaneously demonstrates how the prophecies of the Old Testament <note>original: "A. T." (Altes Testament)</note> were fulfilled in him, and that he is therefore the true promised Messiah. For this reason, he so often states: *In order that it might be fulfilled.*

The genealogy belongs especially to the proof that Jesus is Christ. Now, Joseph was initially held to be the biological father of the Lord Jesus, and therefore Joseph’s descent from Abraham and David had to be set forth: and this is what Matthew does. Luke provided the actual descent later, showing how Jesus, the son of Mary, the daughter of Eli, descended from David through Nathan: but in such a way that he also mentioned Joseph, because it was customary among the Jews for genealogies to report only the fathers and not the mothers.

O, if only Abraham, if David and other believers had already possessed this beginning of Matthew’s Gospel—this passage which we pass over so lightly <note>original: "so ring hinfahren"</note>—how highly they would have prized it!

**V. 1 David - Abraham)** To Abraham was promised Christ and the blessing in him (which is the salvation indicated by the name Jesus), and to David was promised Christ with his Kingdom.

This is the summary repetition of the Old Testament <note>original: "A. T." (Altes Testament)</note>, namely that Christ is a son of David and a son of Abraham; and that Jesus is Christ is the summary presentation of the New Testament <note>original: "N. T." (Neues Testament)</note>. Thus, the sum of Holy Scripture is contained in this little verse.

2 **And his brothers)** The Messiah concerned the 12 tribes of Israel above all other nations.

8 **Joram begat Uzziah)** There were Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah in between. Matthew passes over these before others because Joash was the only one of the royal seed remaining in his time; thus, the genealogical register had no branching point <note>original: "Wegscheide"</note> here but simply continued onward.

11 **Brothers)** Cousins, father’s brothers, one of whom, Zedekiah, only reigned after Jechoniah.

13 **Abiud)** This person is called Hodaviah in 1 Chronicles 3:24. The name is the same. Between him and Zerubbabel there were several generations, just as there was Pedaiah between the latter and Shealtiel.

So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the Babylonian captivity <note>The period in the 6th century BCE when the Jews were forcibly relocated to Babylon.</note> are fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian captivity until Christ are fourteen generations.

<margin>18</margin>
Now the birth of Christ happened in this way: when his mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.

<margin>19</margin>
Joseph, however, her husband,

---

**16 Of whom)** Mary is quite properly the mother of Jesus—indeed, more so than any other woman is the mother of her child. For what a child usually receives from father and mother together, Jesus received from his mother alone, through the coming of the Holy Spirit (verse 18; Luke 1:35).

**Who is called Christ)** "Christ" in Greek <note>original: "Christus"</note> and "Messiah" in Hebrew <note>original: "Messias"</note> both mean "Anointed One," which is to say, a King. Jesus is the personal name of our Lord; Christ is a title, referring to his office. The ancients waited for the Christ before Jesus was born; once Jesus was born, it was testified that he was the Christ. This proof later spread further, and it then became a common naming convention: Jesus Christ.

**17 Fourteen)** The entire genealogical record from Abraham to Christ is divided into three rows. In the first row, there were actually fourteen generations; in the second and third rows, an equal number is achieved through the wise omission of several generations. In this way, chronology <note>The science of arranging events in order of time.</note> is provided alongside the genealogy. From Abraham until the Babylonian captivity, there are twice fourteen members, and more precisely, twice fourteen generations <note>original: "Mannsalter," referring to the span of a man's life or a generation.</note>. Fourteen members—and more precisely, fourteen generations—are from then until Christ. The first row begins with Abraham. David is the last in the first row and the first in the second. The third row has no prominent beginning, but the goal is Christ himself. For this reason, it says with emphasis, *until Christ*, and not simply *until Jesus*. This person, Jesus Christ, arrived at exactly the time he was meant to come.

*Notes on the text:*

**4 Locusts:** See Leviticus 11:22, where various types of locusts are mentioned as being permissible to eat.

**7 coming:** They came not merely to watch, but to be baptized themselves. See verse 11.

**8 fruit:** The person is the tree; the fruit is the act of repentance.

**9 do not think:** People, and especially those who rely on their own religious works for holiness, seek every excuse to avoid true repentance while still claiming a right to God.
**God:** He can fulfill what He promised to Abraham without being bound to you specifically.

**11 Stronger:** Every person experiences the strength of Christ, either in a blessed way or in a terrifying way.

---

Chapter 5, 1-12. In this and in the two following chapters is contained the so-called Sermon on the Mount, and the summary of what Christ presented to the people.

### The first part deals with blessedness.

1 **Disciples**) not only the twelve <note>The text suggests a wider circle of followers beyond the primary Apostles</note>.
2 **Them**) partly the disciples, v. 11, 13, and partly also the people, v. 17.
3 **Blessed**) The first word of this speech indicates its entire purpose. Here a great blessedness is presented by the <term>Lord<note>Original German "HErrn" is capitalized to denote the Divine name or title</note></term>. Hebrews 2:3.
**Poor**) those who have nothing of their own, but enjoy the kindness of others <note>In a spiritual sense, this refers to those who recognize their own spiritual poverty before God</note>.
**Kingdom of heaven**) With this, this section is begun and concluded, v. 10.
4 **They**) Here the opposite is implied: Those who do not mourn will not be comforted.
5 **The earth**) Although they are often displaced, everything must nonetheless turn out for their good.
6 **Righteousness**) The entire speech deals with righteousness <note>German "Gerechtigkeit" encompasses both personal morality and social justice</note>.
**Satisfied**) precisely with righteousness.
10 **For righteousness' sake**) and thus for Christ’s sake, v. 11.

# V.

<margin>18</margin> ...to abolish it, but to fulfill it. ¹ For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single i <note>original: "ein einiges i" — referring to the jot or the Greek letter iota, the smallest letter of the alphabet</note> or a single tiny stroke shall pass from the law, until all of it comes to pass. ¹ Whoever then <margin>19</margin> shall break even one of these least commandments and shall teach people so, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever shall do and teach them, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. <margin>20</margin> ¹ For I say to you, unless your righteousness is more complete than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. <margin>21</margin> ¹ You have heard that it was said to the ancients: you shall not murder; but whoever murders shall be liable to judgment. <margin>22</margin> ¹ But I say to you, that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment...

***

**17 To fulfill**) This is the aim of Christ’s coming. He gave no new law. He fulfilled it himself through his obedience; and he taught how it is to be fulfilled by those who belong to him.

**19 Abolish**) through one's own actions.
**least :: least**) As you treat God’s commandments, so will God deal with you.
**Teach**) As one acts, so one also teaches, even in the smaller commandments. No false teacher makes his error too obvious: he will still call some evil things "evil" and some good things "good."
**In the kingdom of heaven**) This refers to him being spoken of there, without him actually entering it, as seen in verse 20. When people ask about him, the citizens of the kingdom of heaven will say, "He is insignificant; he counts for nothing."

**20 For**) The righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was considered the best and highest standard at that time.
> Holy are you, O God, and holy is your law. Preserve me, that I may not offend against it in small or great matters, nor forfeit the kingdom of heaven.

**21 To the ancients**) This refers not to the time of Moses, but to the times of the scribes and Pharisees. They adorned their innovations with the name of antiquity <note>the author suggests the Pharisees claimed their traditional interpretations were ancient to give them more authority</note>, as very often happens in religious disputes or in the case of bad habits.

<margin>V.</margin>
...will be [liable]: But whoever says to his brother, "You Raca" <note>original: "du Raka" — an Aramaic term of contempt meaning "empty-head" or "worthless person"</note>, he shall be liable to the council: but whoever says, "You fool," he shall be liable to the burning fires of hell <note>original: "heissen Feuerhölle" — referring to Gehenna</note>. <margin>23</margin> Therefore, when you bring your gift to the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you, <margin>24</margin> leave your gift there before the altar and go, first be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer your gift. <margin>25</margin> Be quick to agree with your adversary while you are on the way with him, so that the adversary does not hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. <margin>26</margin> Truly I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last penny <note>original: "Pfennig" — used here to represent the smallest denomination of currency</note>.

---

...already liable to hell. Everything that strives against gentle love rises up against life, and is therefore murderous.

> O God, you who take pleasure in love: Teach me to act according to your pleasure.

**You Raca)** Means empty, without real wits. It was a formula used to reproach someone for their thoughtlessness.

**Liable to the council)** That is: even worse than being liable to the [local] court. The council, or the *Synedrium* <note>original: "Synedrium" — the Sanhedrin, the highest judicial and religious assembly in ancient Jerusalem</note>, was much more distinguished than, say, a city court.

**You fool)** This signifies one who has an incurable lack of understanding. Oh, how common this insult is! We should rebuke precisely these ordinary sinful speeches, which people consider minor, following the example of Christ. See also verse 34.

**Liable to hellfire)** even more than the previous two.

**23 Altar)** The meaning is not that one should wait until that moment to seek reconciliation, but rather it indicates that all worship by an unreconciled person is in vain.

**Leave it there)** even if it might seem strange to other people.

**25 On the way)** toward the judge.

**26** How much better it is to be rid of the debt through forgiveness than to suffer for it.

**The last penny)** One of the deceptive maxims of the old man <note>The "old man" is a common theological term for human nature before spiritual rebirth</note> is when one says in false security: "God does not take it so strictly." Yes, He takes it most strictly, where no...

### V.

18 ...not to abolish them, but to fulfill. | For amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single 'i' <note>original: "i" — referring to the Greek letter iota, the smallest letter of the alphabet</note> or a single tiny stroke <note>original: "Strichlein" — referring to a tittle, a small decorative mark in Hebrew script</note> will pass
19 from the law, until it all comes to pass. | Whoever then shall dissolve even one of these least commandments and shall teach the people so, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: But whoever shall do and teach them, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
20 | For I say to you, unless your righteousness is more complete than that of the scribes and Pharisees, then you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. |
21 You have heard that it was said to the ancients: you shall not murder; but whoever murders shall be liable to
22 judgment. | But I say to you, that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment...

17 **To fulfill)** This is the aim of Christ’s coming. He gave no new law. He fulfilled it Himself through His obedience: and He taught how it is to be fulfilled by those who belong to Him.

19 **Dissolve)** with one's actions.
**least == least)** As you deal with God's commandments, so God will deal with you.
**Teach)** As one acts, so one also teaches, even in the smaller commandments. No false teacher is entirely coarse: he will still call something bad "bad," and something good "good."

### Chapter 5, 33-37. Swearing.

34 **Not at all)** The scribes <note>The religious legal experts of the day</note> forbade only false oaths, but Christ also forbids true oaths—yet not all: otherwise the Law, in which true and lawful swearing by the name of the LORD is commanded, would be abolished. Rather, he forbids swearing by heaven, *etc.*
<margin>Psalm 48:3.</margin> 35 **Of the great King)**
36 **You cannot)** Because nothing is in your power, neither great nor small, you also cannot pledge anything through swearing.
37 **Yes yes)** Where the matter itself is a "yes," there the speech should say "yes": and the same for "no."
> O God, you are in heaven, and I am on earth. Therefore teach me to be sparing in my speech.

### Chapter 5, 38-42. Eye for an eye.

38 **Eye for an eye)** This is commanded to the authorities <note>referring to the legal principle of proportionate punishment administered by a judge</note>, and heathen wit has strayed too far from it: But the scribes applied it to personal revenge.
39 **But)** Spiritual wisdom teaches the children of God how they are to observe these commandments, according to the letter, more or less, as different occasions require. Christ's words are not words of the natural human life, but words of eternal life. What appears foolish to the world is viewed differently in eternal life.

### Matt. 7, 7-12. Prayer. Content of the Law and the Prophets.

<margin>7</margin> **Ask: seek: knock)** O how needy, lost, and cast-out people we are, that we require asking, seeking, and knocking! Why then have you not come further? As often as such a promise comes before you, make use of it: ask, seek, knock.

### Chapter 8, 23-27. Wind and Sea.

**23 His disciples)** On all occasions, this was an excellent instruction for them; much more so than if they had been comfortably listening at a certain place, on certain days and hours.

**26 Speaks)** ...without the slightest unrest.

**Fearful)** Faith drives out fear. In the entire life and conduct of Jesus Christ, not the slightest trace of fear toward any creature is to be found, despite everything that happened to him.

**Ye of little faith)** He could have said here, "You inconsiderate ones," because they disturbed his rest. However, he does not regard what concerns himself, but only what concerns the disciples.

> Lord Jesus, release me from tiresome unbelief and from painful fear through the experience of your power, which stills everything.

**31 Allow)** Thus, it is the evil spirits who have inflicted the damage upon the people here. Jesus, the Lord over all, permitted it to them for holy reasons.

1 **His twelve disciples)** Here Matthew assumes the election of the apostles had already taken place before the Sermon on the Mount.

2 **the first)** In truth, Simon was superior to the others: although this has nothing to do with the See of Rome <note>The author is making a Protestant theological point, acknowledging Peter's leadership while denying it justifies the authority of the Papacy</note>.

**and)** The Apostles are listed here in pairs, just as they were sent out at that time. Matthew had not long before been brought from the tax booth to the apostolic office (oh, the swift work of grace!), and for that reason, he calls himself "the tax collector" here. In humility, he also places himself after his companion Thomas, whereas in Luke’s account, it is written "Matthew and Thomas."

->**Chap. 10, 5-42. How the Apostles should conduct themselves during their mission.**<-

In the meantime, while Jesus himself preached, he first sent out the Twelve, and afterward the Seventy, to preach.

5 **City)** Because Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee, the disciples could not avoid the roads and villages of the Samaritans while traveling through. Therefore, they are only forbidden from entering the *cities* of the Samaritans for this specific time.

7 **the)** Repentance <note>original: "Busse"</note> was included in this message. Mark 6:12.

**10 Bag)** in which one carried food.

**Nor a staff)** A staff is permitted in Mark 6:8. Whoever had one was allowed to take it along: whoever had none was not to trouble themselves over it <note>The author is harmonizing a perceived contradiction between Matthew (who says take no staff) and Mark (who says take nothing *except* a staff)</note>.

**13 Let your)** This is spoken as a command: Let your peace come upon the house. Let your peace return to you again. **Return)** You must not let yourselves be grieved. What others do not want will become an even greater blessing to you yourselves.

**15 More tolerable)** How intolerable it will be for those who not only reject a single message of peace, but persistently disdain it.

**16 wise = without guile)** Take care that no one harms you, and that you offend no one. Many a person treats others as if they were just like themselves. Know this: many are worse than you; others perhaps even better.

# XII. Matthew.

[blasphe]my will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven people. <margin>32</margin> ^1 And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him: but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this present age <note>original: "Weltzeit," referring to the current era or eon of the world.</note>, nor in the <margin>33</margin> future one. ^1 Either make the tree good, and its fruit good: or make the tree rotten <note>original: "faul," which can mean lazy, but here refers to spoiled or decayed fruit.</note>, and its fruit rotten: for by the fruit one knows <margin>34</margin> the tree. ^1 You brood of vipers, how can you speak good things, since you are evil? For out of the abundance of the <margin>35</margin> heart the mouth speaks. ^1 The good man brings
<meta>catchword: out</meta>

---

31 **will be forgiven)** upon apology <note>original: "auf Abbitte," implying a formal request for pardon or a public retraction of one's words.</note>.
**Des Geistes Lästerung (Blasphemy of the Spirit))** That is the blasphemy against the Spirit. Christ possessed this Spirit without measure. There are many sins committed against the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51, 1 Thess. 4:8) which are not also a blasphemy of the same. Only of blasphemy is it said that it will not be forgiven.
32 **And whoever)** The speech immediately preceding is repeated even more explicitly.
**wider den Sohn des Menschen (against the Son of Man))** Jesus Christ is very often called the "Son of Man" in the speeches he gave about himself: and Stephen also called him this when he saw him (Acts 7:55). Otherwise, however, no other witness of Jesus Christ used this title. Thus, this designation belongs to the Lord insofar as he is visible. Therefore, they were speeches against the Son of Man when people spoke disparagingly of him because of his origin from Nazareth, because of his humble appearance, etc. But they were speeches against the Holy Spirit when the people blasphemed his miracles <note>original: "Wunderwerke"</note> wrought through the Holy Spirit and attributed them to a dark power. Through both kinds of speech, people could especially incur guilt at that time when Christ walked among them. What, however, is the status of those people today who blaspheme the good effects of the Holy Spirit in his instruments <note>original: "Werkzeugen," referring to the believers or ministers through whom the Spirit works.</note>? Christians have the Spirit as their portion, and yet have their failings alongside it. Whoever blasphemes one of them looks largely at their failings and becomes the less aware of the good, and he does not thereby blaspheme the Spirit in others: yet he hardly avoids heavy guilt. Christ Jesus had the Spirit without any measure and in all purity. Therefore, the blasphemies against him are much more severe.

### Severe Judgment.

40 **Three)** These three days and three nights were quite literal, from Thursday morning until the end of the night that followed the Sabbath. ## XII. Matthew.

[Blasphemy] will be forgiven to men, but the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven to men. <margin>32</margin> And whoever will speak a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him: but whoever will speak against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this present world-age, nor in the one to come. <margin>33</margin> Either make the tree good, and its fruit good: or make the tree rotten, and its fruit rotten: for by the fruit one knows the tree. <margin>34</margin> You brood of vipers, how can you speak good things, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. <margin>35</margin> The good man brings out of <meta>catchword: out of</meta>

---

31 **be forgiven)** upon repentance <note>original: "auf Abbitte," suggesting that forgiveness is granted when one seeks reconciliation or apologizes.</note>.
**The blasphemy of the Spirit)** This refers to blasphemy directed against the Spirit. Christ possessed the Spirit without measure. Many sins are committed against the Holy Spirit (as seen in Acts 7:51 and 1 Thessalonians 4:8) that are not necessarily "blasphemy" of the Spirit. It is only of blasphemy that it is said it will not be forgiven.
**32 And whoever)** The discourse immediately preceding this is repeated even more emphatically.
**against the Son of Man)** Jesus Christ is very often called the "Son of Man" in the speeches he made about himself; Stephen also used this name when he saw him (Acts 7:55). Otherwise, however, none of the other witnesses of Jesus Christ used this title. Thus, this designation applies to the Lord insofar as he is visible <note>The author suggests "Son of Man" emphasizes Jesus's humble, earthly appearance which people might easily misjudge.</note>. Therefore, there were words spoken against the Son of Man when people spoke disparagingly of him because of his origin from Nazareth, because of his lowly appearance, etc. However, there were words against the Holy Spirit when people blasphemed the miracles he performed through the Holy Spirit and attributed them to a dark power <note>referring to the Pharisees' earlier claim that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebub.</note>. Through both types of speech, people could make themselves particularly guilty during the time when Christ walked among them. But what is the case for people today who blaspheme the good works of the Holy Spirit in His instruments <note>meaning fellow believers or ministers</note>? Christians possess the Spirit in their own part, but they also have their failings. Whoever blasphemes such a person perhaps focuses largely on their failings and becomes less aware of the good, and thus he does not necessarily blaspheme the Spirit in others; nevertheless, he still incurs a heavy guilt. Christ Jesus had the Spirit without any measure and in all purity. For this reason, blasphemies against Him are far more severe.

<summary>This page discusses the "unforgivable sin" of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, distinguishing it from insults against Jesus's human person. The commentary argues that while personal failings in Christians might excuse some criticism, rejecting the clear work of the Spirit is a much more dangerous offense.</summary>

### Chapter 13, 53-58. Unbelief in Nazareth.

53 **He departed**) It was not merely a journey, but a departure. Afterward, he did return to Capernaum, but he did not dwell there in the same way.

55) **The carpenter's son**) When one does not distinguish between what is common and civic and what is spiritual, one stumbles over that which one should use for one's benefit. Strangers do not know the former; therefore, they judge a prophet only by the spiritual.

1 **Herod**) This tetrarch was among the last in the entire land of Israel to hear of Jesus. However, there are good exceptions in this regard.

**To his servants**) In a moment of sudden terror, the great also reveal themselves to the lowly, more than they would otherwise do.

**3 John the Baptist)** Herod’s conscience was struck. John was soon and quickly perfected <note>meaning his earthly course was completed through martyrdom</note>; but those who took his life had to pay dearly for it afterward.

**4 John spoke)** Thus, marital matters do not only belong before secular judges <note>The author suggests that marriage is also a spiritual and moral matter subject to religious rebuke.</note>.

**5 An evil plan,** once it has a beginning, will eventually be put into action at the slightest opportunity.

**6 Anniversary)** There are many kinds of anniversaries: annual fairs, church consecrations, etc. Generally, worldly pleasures lead to many sorrowful affairs; and yet the world refuses to settle for anything better.

**8 On a platter)** Gallant speech, but a cruel deed!

**10 Beheaded)** This mode of death was also proof that John was not the Christ. For from Christ’s body, no bone—let alone his head—was to be removed. <note>This refers to the biblical requirement that the Passover lamb, and by extension the Messiah, have no broken bones.</note>

**12 Came)** Thus, the orphaned disciples of John sought refuge with the Lord Jesus.

...[forgetful]ness, which arose from unbelief alongside a lack of understanding, is later held against them. verse 9.

6 *Beware*) Something of the demand of the Pharisees and Sadducees might have stuck to the disciples.

*of the leaven*) This parable was applied at the right time. The disciples had previously been present at the two glorious miracles of the loaves and were themselves occupied with them; and now, in their own lack, they felt the necessity of bread. They could then think all the more deeply about the bread of the soul—how necessary sound teaching is. The Pharisees and Sadducees were two very different sects, and yet they shared a single leaven. Indeed, all false teaching of all sects is a single old leaven, which the "old man" <note>This refers to the "old self" or unregenerate human nature in biblical theology.</note> harbors.

7 *No bread*) What a person often counts as a great mistake for himself—for example, a lack of attention to worldly things—is nothing compared to other faults with which he is actually afflicted. Faith or unbelief is what truly matters.

8 *Why do you think*) With restless thoughts, people spend much of the time of their lives, both day and night.

10 *Small baskets* :: *Baskets*) This expresses the difference between the Greek words <term>kophinos <note>original: "κόφινος"</note></term> and <term>spyris <note>original: "σπυρίς"</note></term>. In ancient times, even respectable people carried *kophinos*, or small baskets, with them. *Spyrides* <note>original: "σπυρίδες"</note> were larger. Acts 9:25.

11 *Not of bread*) Jesus says nothing here about which leaven he is speaking of. The disciples had to guess something for themselves here too, just as in Chapter 17, verse 13, regarding Elijah. Such exercises exist for earnest souls; through them, the tendency to interpret the words of Jesus in a purely physical sense is wiped away.

# Matthew. 79 XVI.

[Jesus] spoke to him: Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my Father in the heavens. <margin>18</margin> | But I also say to you: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my community, and the gates of hell shall not overcome it. <margin>19</margin> | And I will give to you the keys of the heav—

---

**17 Blessed)** Peter likely did not think himself so well off. One is blessed not by declaring themselves so by their own authority, but by being praised as blessed by the Lord.

**Flesh and blood not)** This means: no human being <note>In biblical language, "flesh and blood" refers to human nature or human sources of knowledge as opposed to divine revelation.</note>.

**My Father)** It was revealed to Peter by the heavenly Father, not through a miraculous apparition, but through the Word of Christ.

**18 To you)** Here, something special is explicitly promised to Peter: just as he, with his insight and confession, surpassed the other disciples, it appears that no one else would have been so ready with the answer at that time.

**I will build)** This is fulfilled in the Acts of the Apostles, particularly in Chapters 2, 10, and 15. There, the community of Christ was built first from the Jews and then from the Gentiles, more so through Peter’s service than through the other apostles. In Hebrew or Syriac, there is a single word, *Kepha* <note>original: "Kepha"</note>, which serves as Peter's name and means a rock; in Greek and Latin, the word for rock (*Petra*) simply takes on a masculine ending common for men's names, becoming *Petrus* <note>The author is explaining that in the original language Jesus spoke, the pun between Peter's name and the word "rock" is identical: "You are Rock, and on this Rock..."</note>. None of this concerns any supposed successor to Peter. Whether Peter was ever in Rome, and specifically whether he was there for a time at liberty, is very uncertain. If he was there, he was there as an apostle; yet the community there still had its own regular overseers. It was not Peter, but these local overseers, who had the bishops of later times as their successors, until those bishops degenerated and became "Lords" and "Popes."

Everything promised to Peter here was fulfilled in Peter himself after the exaltation of Christ.

**Gates of hell)** Though they seem much more solid and firm than the community of Christ.

**19 The Keys)** Keys are not used for binding and loosing, but for opening and closing; and the very same key that opens also closes. Therefore, the text is not necessarily speaking of two separate keys. Peter likely received several. Through them, he powerfully opened the entrance into the kingdom of heaven for both Jews and Gentiles. One should compare the opposite in Chapter 23, verses 4 and 13, and Luke 11:52 <note>These verses describe religious leaders who "shut up the kingdom of heaven against men."</note>. However, with the keys, the authority to bind and to loose—

### Chap. 16, 21-28. Announcement of the suffering, death, and resurrection: Peter's objection rejected. Self-denial: future glory.

**21 From that time on)** Previously, he had only hinted at it in a veiled way. The knowledge of his person <note>That is, his identity as the Son of God.</note> had to be firmly established first. This was a wise method of teaching.

**22 Peter)** Oh, how easily one commits a greater blunder shortly after a good test!

**23 Get behind me)** You should not be a counselor, but a follower.

**Satan)** This word here means one who stands in the way <note>In Hebrew, "Satan" literally means "adversary" or "accuser."</note>. Since the temptation in the wilderness, nothing more adverse had encountered the Lord Jesus.

**Stumbling block)** With an instantaneous zeal, Jesus pushes back everything offensive, like fire pushes back water—which indeed comes close to the fire, but does not mix with it in the least. To the world, the cross is a stumbling block; to Christ, that which was contrary to the cross was a stumbling block.

**23 what is of God)** A divine mind—regarding the suffering of Christ and his own, and the glory that follows—was something Peter carried in later times, as his first letter testifies most of all.

**21 Sins)** This is not to be understood as a slight offense <note>original: "Anstoß"</note> that causes a quick and indeed sinful, but self-resolving resentment, but rather as a significant insult.

**22 Seventy times seven)** Even the two most hostile tempers will not fall out with each other so grossly <note>meaning so many times</note>. Thus, a completely tireless willingness to reconcile is required.

**24 One single)** Wherever in such speeches something is said of "One," understand yourself as being meant by it, my reader. I do so as well.

**Ten thousand talents)** No larger sum could be expressed with two words in the original language <note>original: "Grundsprache"; referring here to the Greek of the New Testament</note>. A talent was likely more than 1500 Thalers <note>An early modern silver coin used throughout Europe; the author is providing a contemporary value for his readers</note>. Thus the entire debt was 15 million Thalers. If it runs so high for one single servant—whom Peter and the other apostles were to apply to themselves—how high then does that amount reach which the Lord remits to all those who come to grace: and that which even more people must pay for without remittance in the place of torment <note>Hell</note>.

**27 Had compassion)** To forgive and remit is the greatest work of mercy.

| **Let him go)** so that he did not sell him.

**And)** on top of that. The servant had not thought to ask for this. He had only asked for a delay.
