<margin>28</margin> *Out*) After he had followed his own whim. When a person allows a sense of false security to override the experience of divine grace, that is when he can truly ruin himself and fall back under the judgment of wrath.

*Found*) Directly after an experience of divine grace, you will soon encounter an opportunity to act either in accordance with it or contrary to it.

*One*) It can happen that someone stands well with all people, yet keeps a single individual as the target of his hatred.

<margin>32</margin> *You wicked servant*) Previously he was not called this: even during the initial accounting, the Lord had not yet become angry with him.

*All*) Oh, royal magnanimity!

<margin>34</margin> *All*) Oh, royal severity!

### Chapter 21, 33-44. Parable of the Vineyard and the Builders who killed the Heir.

<margin>33 a vineyard)</margin> This was the Israelite Church in the time of Moses. The fence was the separation of the same from all other nations and the divine protection against them. The winepress was the priesthood; the tower, the kingdom.

<margin>leased it out)</margin> This is how it stands with authority in church matters. The vineyard is given over to the builders: the leaders in worldly and spiritual offices can act according to their own discretion and personal benefit, as if they themselves were masters of the vineyard. They can mistreat the servants of the Lord, they can twist church laws according to their will and whim, and while they can no longer kill the heir himself <note>A reference to Christ, the "Heir," who was killed once but now lives</note>, they can still displace him. But finally, the time of visitation <note>A biblical term for a time of divine judgment or inspection</note> comes.

<margin>went into a far country)</margin> It is as if the Lord did not wish to concern Himself with the vineyard.

### Chapter 24, 32-41. Answer to the question: When?

32 **From the)** Until now, this discourse has dealt with the destruction of the Temple and the city, and the coming of Christ as far as the events themselves are concerned: now, the time is also announced. **All these things**, which concern Jerusalem, Jesus says will happen before this generation <term>generation: *Mannsalter*, referring to the span of a single human lifetime</term> passes away: (for exactly 40 years after this discourse, when the fig tree was budding as summer approached, Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans;) but of **That Day** and the hour of my coming, no one knows.

35 **My words)** and therefore this word, concerning the Temple and the city.

36 **the angels)** who otherwise possess such great wisdom.

39 **Then)** at the coming mentioned in verse 39 and Chapter 25, 1.

40 **will be taken)** in grace, like Noah and his household. **left)** Like the people in the Great Flood.

> Lord Jesus, fill my heart with true attentiveness, and set me free from the love of the world!

# Matthew XXV.

...virgins, who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom [and the bride]. | <margin>2</margin> But five of them were wise, and five were foolish. | <margin>3</margin> Those who were foolish took their lamps, but they took no oil with them. | <margin>4</margin> But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. | <margin>5</margin> But as the bridegroom delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. | <margin>6</margin> But at midnight a cry went out: Behold, the bridegroom is coming, go out to meet [him].
<sig>H 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: meet.</meta>

---

1) **to meet the bridegroom**) In Hebrew wedding customs, things were quite different; the bride was led into the bridegroom’s house, and indeed by night and with lamps, but in such a way that the bridegroom did not come out, but instead awaited her in his house. <note>The author highlights a cultural discrepancy: while the parable depicts the virgins going out to meet the groom, historical Judean custom often saw the groom waiting at home for the bridal procession.</note>

2) **five = five**) Those who personally take up the cause of the kingdom of heaven, rather than humanity in general, are represented here. Toward the end, everyone will fall asleep, and yet also be awakened just beforehand. Five and five are named: either because the number is equal, or because the inequality <note>i.e., the true ratio of saved to lost</note> will not be known.

**Foolish**) They were mindful of the good, but not for the long term. What is indicated by the foolish and wise virgins is clearly described in 2 Peter 1:5-11.

3) **Lamps**) In a burning lamp, there is fire and oil. Through the fire, the supernatural, heavenly, fiery power of the Spirit is indicated here, which is granted to the soul without its own contribution (2 Peter 1:3-4). Through the oil is meant the holy diligence on the part of the person (2 Peter 1:5); and a person should have this not only for the present time according to necessity, but also in abundance (2 Peter 1:8) for all future cases: thus he certainly, and moreover abundantly, receives entry into the wedding house (verse 11). The foolish virgins did not simply remain in their natural state alone; there was also something of grace and the Spirit with them. Nowhere is it more clearly described than here, how far a soul can progress in goodness and yet still fail (verse 7).

**No oil**) no supply beyond what was actually in the lamps. They did not give the Holy Spirit full room.

5) **All**) The wise also fell asleep, not without danger: but upon waking, they still had enough oil. During sleep, the oil runs out for those who previously had little of it.

6) **Cry**) which surpasses all <term>cannons: *Carthaunen*, a term for heavy, large-caliber siege guns used in early modern warfare</term>. 1 Thessalonians 4:16.

<summary>This page contains the opening verses of the Parable of the Ten Virgins and a detailed commentary interpreting the lamps, fire, and oil as symbols of divine grace and human diligence. The commentator notes historical Hebrew wedding customs and warns that even those who have received the Spirit can fail if they lack a "supply" of spiritual preparedness.</summary>

### Chapter 26, 6-16. Anointing at Bethany: the traitor’s promise.

**6 at Bethany)** This anointing happened several days prior, but is inserted here because Judas was incensed by it and has now reported himself to the chief priests.

**7 Poured)** This kind of anointing can be more easily imagined if one considers that the ancients reclined while eating rather than sat. They had benches covered with cushions and stretched their feet outward.

**9 The poor)** Thus it was something the disciples were accustomed to, that the remaining provisions were given to the poor.

**10 A good work)** even though the woman did not know it herself. Many a work is better or worse than the doer knows. <note>See Chapter 26, 38. 44. and Hebrews 13, 2.</note>

**12 To prepare for the grave)** This had just been accomplished through the anointing. Thus was Jacob prepared for the grave in Egypt, and afterwards buried in the land of Canaan.

**13 This)** namely Christ’s <note>referring to "this Gospel"</note>. He speaks humbly.

**Speak)** Even now this is still happening, and Matthew, who was present there, helps in this. Hereby the word of Jesus is fulfilled. It is within the power of no monarch to bring even the greatest deed into certain and constant remembrance among posterity:
<meta>catchword: Here</meta>

**24 If)** if his mother’s womb had been his grave. This "woe" is even greater than if one were drowned in the deep sea. <note>Refers to Chapter 18, verse 6.</note>
**25 Is it I)** What honest souls say out of love, the false ones mimic.
> Lord Jesus, you know all honest and all false hearts. 
> Grant that it may always be the truth when I say: I stand with you. If Judas played you into the hands of your enemies, I would rather deliver all people into your hands, for their own good.

->Chap. 26, 26-29. The Lord’s Supper.<-

**26 This is)** truly and present.
**My body)** Since the body is mentioned without the blood, and the blood without the body, it is precisely a description of Christ's death, the memory of which shall remain until he comes. <note>Refers to verse 29.</note>
**27 All of you)** It did not say, "Eat, all of you": but after they had all eaten, it now says, "Drink, all of you." Eating is left to one's will; but after eating, drinking is not left to one's will. <note>The commentator notes that while the command to eat was implied for the group, the command to drink was explicitly addressed to everyone present, emphasizing the importance of the cup.</note>
**28 Of the New Testament)** not of the old covenant. <note>Refers to 2 Moses 24:8, known in English as Exodus 24:8.</note>
**For many)** not only for Israel.
**for the forgiveness of sins)** This is the actual blessing of the New Testament. <note>Refers to Ephesians 1:7.</note>

51 **The High Priest’s servant)** This man undoubtedly had a special order and was the most courageous among those who held Jesus.

### Ch. 27, 51-54. Great Miracles: Fear of the Guard.

**51 And behold)** This great movement in nature links the <term>Gospel history <note>original: "Evangelische Historie"; the historical account of the life of Christ as recorded in the Gospels.</note></term> partly with the death, and partly with the resurrection of the Lord: as a sign that with the killing of Christ according to the flesh, the becoming alive according to the spirit was immediately connected. ### Chapter 2, 18-22. Question and answer regarding fasting.

18 **fasted**) It was indeed a real fast: but such a one that was not commanded in the Law, but was of old tradition. Therefore, the disciples of John also kept it.
19 **the bridegroom**) That is you, O you faithful lover of our souls. Without you, those who know you can have no happy day, and with you, no sad day.

### Chap. 3, 1-6. Sabbath cure of a withered hand; the Pharisees' evil plot.

1 **In the school**) Oh, how much evil is brought into the assembly and committed within it.
**withered hand**) Matthew tells this and several preceding stories according to the chronological order much further down. Mark places the events against which the enemies raised no objections in one group (Chapter 1), and then also those against which the enemies did object (Chapter 2), until their hatred moved them to plot against the Lord. Luke also follows this method.

**43 strictly commanded)** The people, to whom the death of the maiden was known, could nonetheless know of the miracle and spread it to the glory of God. <note>The commentator notes the tension between Jesus's command for secrecy and the public nature of the girl's previous death.</note>

**something to eat)** She was now alive and, moreover, healthy, and required no medicine. <note>The command to eat serves as proof of her physical restoration.</note>

**Chap. 6, 1-6. Jesus the great Prophet is not respected in his fatherland.**

**3 the carpenter)** Thus Jesus himself performed such labor. **6 Since you, Lord Jesus, have also come to the strangers, to the Gentiles:** grant that we may all the more highly esteem you in faith. <note>This is a short prayer reflecting on how those far away (Gentiles) often value Jesus more than those who were close to him.</note>

<meta>This page continues the narrative from the previous page, where a man runs up and kneels before Jesus. The text begins mid-word ("ter") completing the address "Guter Meister" (Good Master).</meta>

<header>Mark.</header>

<margin>Ch. 10</margin>
<margin>18</margin> [Goo]d Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life? But Jesus said to him: why do you call me good? No one is good except One, namely
->God<-

---

18 **Spoke**) Jesus answers 1) the unusual title given to him; 2) the question.

**Why do you call me good?**) In Jesus’s outward appearance, there was much that might have given the ignorant a poor impression of him (John 1:47; Matthew 11:6, 19; Isaiah 53:2 ff.). Jesus did not rely on himself, but referred himself entirely to his Father. He was himself, in a certain sense, a pilgrim on earth; and considering the state in which he is described in the Psalms as wretched and poor, he strove for the eternal goodness and joy about which this man was asking (Psalm 26:2, 5 and following; <note>original: "Mein Gut ist nicht ausser dir"; My good is not apart from you</note> John 14:28; Chapter 7:5; Hebrews 5:8, 9; 9:12). Thus, he did not know himself according to the flesh, <term>compare Augustine, Book 1 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 34</term>. For within that which is "good," salvation is also understood. The man who presented himself here was seeking temporal happiness from Jesus. Therefore, he is given the answer that he will not find such a calculation with Jesus (compare Luke 9:57 f.). Yet he does not say, "I am not good," but rather: "Why do you call me good?" Just as in Matthew 22:43 he does not deny that He, David's son, is also David's Lord. God is good; goodness does not exist without the Godhead. In the Lord Jesus, this man recognized goodness to some extent—otherwise he would not have approached him—but not fully, otherwise he would not have gone away. Still less, however, did he recognize the Divinity in Him. Therefore, Jesus does not accept the title of goodness from him without the title of Divinity (compare here what is said in Luke 6:46) and at the same time preserves the honor of his Father, with whom He is one (See John 5:19). He casts a ray of his omniscience into this man's heart and shows him that he did not yet possess the knowledge appropriate to such a high title regarding Him, Jesus Christ, even though such a title was otherwise His due. This is why he does not say: "no one is good except my Father alone," but rather, "no one is good except One, namely God." The Lord often directed his speech according to the understanding of those who questioned him (John 4:22). Similarly, an officer of high birth might answer a common man who does not know him: "Why do you call me a gracious Lord?" He made his goodness well known to his disciples (Luke 10:23; Romans 14:16).

<vocab>Mark, Gospel, Good Master, eternal life, Divinity, goodness, Jesus Christ, Augustine</vocab>

<summary>This page provides a theological commentary on Jesus's response to the rich young ruler, explaining why Jesus deflected the title "Good Master." The author argues that Jesus was directing the man's focus toward the true source of goodness—God—and testing the man's limited understanding of His divine nature.</summary>
<keywords>Gospel of Mark, Christology, attributes of God, humility of Christ, Augustine, biblical exegesis, rich young ruler</keywords>

10 *Our father David*) They call David their father because he, as king, was a father of the people. There may well have been descendants of David among them as well. The throne of David is rightfully assigned to the Messiah. <note>original: "Luc. I, 32"; Luke 1:32</note>.

->*Praised be the King, Jesus Christ! Blessed be his kingdom!*<-

11 *Looked around at everything*) He signaled his disapproval of the disorder in the temple with his expression. For this reason, Matthew and Luke link the driving out of the buyers to this very day. Mark places it on the following day.

### Chapter XI, 12-26. The fig tree with leaves but no fruit is cursed. The house of prayer cleansed! Faith praised.

13 *for*) It was still too early in the year for there to have been ripe figs. Therefore, the fig tree was blamed for having only leaves, and not for its lack of ripe figs. <note>In this region, certain fig trees produce "early figs" even before the main harvest; to have leaves but no such fruit was a sign of barrenness.</note>

14 *No one*) It was not fitting that anyone should have been able to say: The Son of God found no fruit on this tree, yet I have eaten fruit from it. Thus, the tree was banished <note>or "cursed"</note> for the honor of the Son of God. Whoever refuses service to the **LORD** Jesus is not worthy of serving anyone else.

26 | And the inscription of his accusation was written above him: **The King of the Jews**.
27 | And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right, and one on his left.

30 | **save yourself**, and come down from the cross.
31 | Likewise the high priests also mocked him among themselves with the scribes, and said: He helped others; **he cannot help himself**.
32 | Let the Christ, the King of Israel, now come down from the cross, so that we may see and believe. Even those who were crucified with him insulted him.
33 | And when the **sixth hour** <note>noon</note> came, a darkness fell over the whole land until the **ninth hour** <note>3:00 PM</note>:
34 | and at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and said: **My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?** <note>original: "Elohai, Elohai, lama sabachthani?"</note>

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

***

24. 25 **Crucified**) Mark notes this twice: to indicate both the beginning and the completion of the crucifixion. There were many circumstances involved in the crucifixion. The cross was erected: in the middle of it, a piece of wood projected. Upon this, the condemned man had to sit; then he was bound, and finally nailed. This required time, and by the time the third hour arrived, the crucifixion of Jesus was accomplished.

28 **You Righteous Servant of the Lord!**) You have allowed yourself to be counted among the transgressors: for your sake, let me be recorded among the righteous.

29 **Ha!** <note>original: "Ey"</note>) In the Greek there is a small word <note>the interjection 'Oua'</note> that signifies wonder: here, however, it is a **mocking wonder**.

Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of those things which are fully accomplished among us, | just as they were delivered to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word: | it seemed good to me also, having accurately traced everything from the very start, to write it down for you in orderly fashion, most excellent Theophilus, | so that you may know the certainty of the things in which you have been instructed.

->Annotations.<-

Luke 1, 1-4. Luke dedicates his book to Theophilus, with an assurance of the truth.
1 **Everything is full)** <note>original: "Alles voll ist"</note> It was a matter that was more than well-known throughout the land.
2 **delivered)** orally.
**Eyewitnesses = ministers)** Mary, the twelve Apostles, the 70 disciples, Paul, Mary Magdalene, etc.
3 **Traced)** <note>original: "Erreichet"</note> Luke followed the first tracks and evidence in every part of the story.
**from the beginning)** verse 5.
**Most Excellent)** Theophilus was a prominent statesman in Alexandria. This same title is given to Felix and Festus <note>Roman governors mentioned in the Book of Acts</note>.
4 **the certainty)** This is found where nothing incorrect is added, nothing necessary is omitted, and everything is proven by documentary evidence.

> O God! let the testimony of Jesus Christ your Son always enliven and fill my heart.

5 **There was)** the story of Christ is, from its very first

From the beginning, this proceeded according to God’s preordained counsel: therefore, the first circumstances are presented so precisely. It is very different with deceivers, who merely happened to find an opportunity to gain a following.

<margin>5</margin>
*Abijah*) From this clue, it can be inferred that Zechariah’s week of service was from September 2nd to September 9th. *Temple Ordinances* <note>original: "Ord. Temp."</note> p. 230 f. and on September 2nd of that same year, the 1st of Tishrei <note>The first month of the Jewish civil year, beginning in autumn</note> occurred for the people of Israel. Look! In the beginning of the year, with the message of the angel to Zechariah, was the dawn of the New Testament.

<margin>8</margin>
*In the order*) In 24 weeks, the 24 priestly orders <note>The groups of priests who took turns serving in the Temple</note> completed their rotation: and so it continued until the temple was destroyed.

<margin>13</margin>
*Fear not*) Thus begins the very first message at the first dawn of the New Testament.

*your prayer*) Zechariah had made this request long ago: and he no longer expected the outcome himself.

<margin>15</margin>
*Lord Jesus!* let me regard nothing as great, except that which serves the praise of your greatness!

### Chapter I, 39-45. Mary's journey to the city of Judah: conversation with Elizabeth.

39 **In those days)** referring to the sixth month. See verses 26 and 36.

**To a city of Judah)** Here, the tribe of Judah is named rather than the specific city of Hebron. From everything here, we can infer that amidst the incomparable stirrings within Mary, Elizabeth, and John (verses 41, 42), Mary began to be the mother of Him who is the Lord of Elizabeth, David, Paul, and all of us. Consider the little word **"for"** in verse 44. The Annunciation was in Nazareth, but the conception did not necessarily happen there as well. Christ was a Nazarene not because of His conception, but because He was raised there; He is of the tribe of Judah because of His lineage, His conception at Hebron, and His birth at Bethlehem. <note>The commentator is making a historical-theological argument that while the angel appeared in Nazareth, the physical conception of Jesus may have occurred while Mary was in the territory of Judah visiting Elizabeth.</note>

41 Heavenly Father, through the Spirit who glorifies Jesus, let me also be filled with joy!

29 **Different)** The speech of men is not sufficient to express heavenly things. What is their nature? Simply different from that which we are accustomed to; also different from the then-usual appearance of Jesus Christ among mortals.
31 **In glory)** A greater degree of which might yet follow for Moses and Elijah upon the death and transfiguration of Christ. Moses and Elijah are two models of resurrection and transformation.
**Departure)** through the suffering of death toward glory.
32 **Full of sleep)** Through this sleep they were placed in forgetfulness of all earthly thoughts and imaginings. All this happened at night. <term>v. 37</term> <note>Verse 37 mentions "the next day," implying the transfiguration took place during the night.</note>.

### Chapter 10, 1–16. The Seventy are appointed and equipped.

**1 the Lord)** A glorious title. See also verses 2, 3, 9, and 11.
**Sent them)** It is not mentioned here that the power to heal the sick and cast out unclean spirits was given to them as it was to the Twelve. <note>The author distinguishes between the specific miraculous powers granted to the primary Apostles versus this larger group of seventy.</note>

**2 Pray)** Through this command, Jesus immediately prompted a prayer and a longing for laborers, and then fulfilled that very prayer.
**Send out)** This he does at once, as he says: Go your way.

**3 Lambs)** The Twelve are compared to sheep in Matthew 10:16. The seventy are compared to lambs. To both, he gave a safe passage with these words: **Behold, I send you**. He is the **Lord**.

**4 on the way)** They were required to bring their greeting into the houses (verse 5) and not delay themselves with individual acquaintances along the road. Even the omission of greetings on the way served to give people the healthy impression that the seventy had a vital and urgent task to perform.

**5 First)** Never should a servant of the Gospel begin with scolding.

> O God! let your peace in Christ Jesus be with me at all times.

<margin>38</margin> Now it happened, as they went on their way, that he entered into a village. And a woman named Martha received him into her house.
<margin>39</margin> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the feet of Jesus and listened to his speech.
<margin>40</margin> But Martha was thoroughly occupied with much serving: and she stepped forward and said: **Lord**, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then that she should lend me a hand.
<margin>41</margin> But Jesus answered and said to her: Martha, Martha, you have care and unrest regarding many things:
<margin>42</margin> but only one thing is necessary. But Mary has

---

->Chapter 10, 38-42. Martha does not gain as much with her busyness as the modest Mary.<-

<margin>38</margin> **Into her house)** Thus Martha was the mistress of the house, and Mary stayed with her.

<margin>40</margin> **Has left me)** Thus Mary had been busy previously, and had afterward seated herself at Jesus's feet.
**Tell her)** Mary was under Jesus's protection: Martha could not speak to her directly. <note>Martha appeals to Jesus's authority as a guest and teacher to direct her sister's behavior.</note>

<margin>41</margin> **Care)** from within.
**Unrest)** from without. <note>The author distinguishes between internal anxiety (Sorge) and the external commotion of being "troubled" (Unruhe).</note>

**Only one)** Some have understood this to refer to a single dish of food, with which Jesus would have been satisfied in this lodging: and by this, nothing is taken away from spiritual diligence. For the one necessary thing in spiritual matters is precisely that good part which Mary had chosen: and this therefore retains the prize. Thus, in Chapter 17, 21, nothing is taken away from the kingdom of God, which the believers have in their innermost being, even if the speech to the Pharisees is understood as: the kingdom of God and the Messiah himself is actually present in your midst. In Philippians 1, 21, Christ remains Paul's life, even if Paul says: My life, since I have to remain longer in the world, is entirely directed toward Christ. We must not presume to make the sense and understanding of the holy words, which are always spirited, even richer. The denial of human self-conceit is better than such presumed devotion. However, in this passage, the choice is left to the reader between the interpretation of a single dish of food and that of the kingdom of God.

**In their generation)** This speech is qualified. A small spark of "enlightened shrewdness" <note>original: "Lichtsklugheit"</note> is otherwise more noble than "worldly shrewdness" <note>original: "Weltklugheit"</note> in all its power. For the latter always has a transitory purpose—among statesmen, soldiers, and merchants, among scholars and artists, etc. The former aims solely at the ultimate, all-important goal, which the latter usually forgets and misses. O God! hold me to that shrewdness which has the right purpose and strives quite earnestly after it.

**9 Make friends for yourselves)** This does not happen with mere pennies and cents <note>original: "Hellern und Pfennigen"; common small coins of the era</note>.

**Comes to an end)** In death. See Ecclesiastes 9:10.

**They)** The friends. These are not only those to whom one shows kindness, but all those who are already in the eternal dwellings before such a dying person, or who have their proper place within them. They have a common cause. Acts of kindness are best invested in the children and servants of God.

**Dwellings)** They are called this because of their security.

**11 Entrust)** In this world.

**12 What is your own)** That which actually belongs to you.

**Give)** In the world to come.

->Chap. 22, 39-46. Going to the Mount of Olives: Prayer: Struggle: Strengthening. Encouragement of the disciples.<-

**40 That)** <note>original: "Daß"</note> by this, prayer is not commanded generally as a means against temptation, but rather the content of the prayer should be this: that they might not fall into temptation.

**42 Father, your will be done.**

**43 Appeared)** This is a sign of the prayer being heard. Hebrews 5:7. <note>Hebrews 5:7 describes Jesus offering prayers with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death</note>
**Strengthened)** not perhaps through a powerful exhortation, but by a heavenly power being imparted to the holy humanity of Jesus.

**44 Deathly agony)** In the face of an impending hard struggle, fear sets in even when one already knows a good outcome. So it was with Jesus.
**more earnestly)** in the second and third rounds of prayer. Thus the angel appeared at the first prayer and undoubtedly strengthened Jesus after each prayer.
**His sweat)** Because of the cold weather at that time (John 18:18) and the nighttime, this sweat was all the more miraculous. This was caused by the power received through the angel, the wrestling, the earnest prayer, and the desire to drink the cup. <note>The author highlights the "cold weather" mentioned in other Gospels to prove the sweat was caused by spiritual intensity rather than temperature</note>

**45 Rose up)** surrendered to the Father’s will.

8 **Because**) Lord Jesus, I hear and read much of you: I long to see you. Oh, what a joy that will be!

9 Lord Jesus! Your cause is no nourishment for natural curiosity <note>original: "Fürwitz," an archaic term for meddlesome or impertinent curiosity.</note>. Guide those who must testify of you, so that they do neither too little nor too much for the cause.

28 But Jesus turned to them and said: "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; but weep for yourselves and for your children.

30 Then they will begin to say to the mountains: 'Fall on us!' and to the hills: 'Cover us!'
31 For if they do these things to the green wood, what will become of the dry?"
32 There were also two other <term>criminals<note>original: "Uebelthäter," literally evildoers or those who have done wrong.</note></term> led out to be put to death with him.
33 And when they reached the place called the Skull, they crucified him there, and the criminals, one on his right and the other on his left.

---

28 *Do not weep for me)* Jesus was already on the way to his glory. He does not forbid mourning over him in the way that Zechariah 12:10 is understood. <note>Zechariah 12:10 refers to a prophecy of mourning for "the one they have pierced."</note>

*For your children)* those who are already born and those yet to be born. The misery arrived forty years later. <note>A reference to the Roman Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which occurred roughly forty years after the crucifixion.</note>

How many, how many people today feel secure who actually have great reason to weep.

->Lord Jesus! You see all that is to come, including my future and that of my family. To You all is committed!<-

30 *They)* The barren: who compare themselves in the following words to dry wood, and the fruitful to green wood. When Jerusalem was overtaken, the elderly and unfit were treated even more cruelly by the Romans than the strong and the young.

*Begin)* during an anxiety of a kind that never existed before. To be covered by a mountain is otherwise something terrible, and yet here it is something desired.

32 *Two others)* Luke carefully connects the word "two" <note>original: "zween," an archaic German form of "two."</note>, but not the word "others," with the word <term>criminals<note>original: "Maleficanten," a term derived from Latin referring to those who commit evil or capital crimes.</note></term>. Jesus was no criminal (see v. 33, 41), but the world held him to be more abominable than those two.

Luke 23:33-38. The crucifixion of Jesus between two criminals. His intercession; the dividing of his clothes; the speeches of mockery; the inscription.

33 *Skull)* <note>original: "Hirnschale" (Skull-shell) and "Calvaria" (Latin for Skull).</note> This place received its name from its shape. It was, therefore, a hill.

34 **Forgive them)** Without this intercession, divine wrath might have consumed the people instantly.

**What)** That they were crucifying him, they knew; but *whom* they were crucifying, they did not know. This ignorance was something terrifying: for otherwise they would not have crucified the **Lord** of Glory. But nevertheless, the guilt that is committed knowingly is even heavier.

35 **the people)** The word in the original text <note>The Greek word *laos*.</note> means not just the crowd in general, as in verse 48, but specifically the Jewish people.

**Watched)** securely.

**Along with them)** along with the people. Respectable people do not usually do such things publicly; but here, for the sake of malice and revenge, even reputation was set aside. No human has ever been mocked as much as Jesus. Thank him, and learn to bear mockery, primarily for his sake.

> Thanks be to you, **Lord** Jesus! that you allowed yourself to be crucified, treated like <term>criminals<note>original: "Maleficanten," an older term for condemned felons or evildoers.</note></term>, and mocked beyond all measure. Let the blessing for this rest upon me eternally.

**The Anointed)** The Jews mocked him as the Christ <note>original: "Christum"</note>; the pagan soldiers as a King of the Jews.

**The Chosen of God)** for whom it is not fitting, they mean to say, that he should die on the cross.

37 **If you are the King of the Jews, help yourself)** The soldiers caught and pieced together this mockery from the inscription on the cross and from the speeches of the rulers.

<margin>42</margin> And he said to Jesus: "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom."

->Chapter 23, 39-43. One criminal blasphemes. The other rebukes him: confesses Christ: receives a grace-filled promise.<-

<margin>39 Help)</margin> This criminal also picked up the scandalous mockery of the rulers. But because he speaks of Christ in this way, one can see that he was a Jew. See how the spirit of mockery has such a stubborn life: it proves itself even in a man being hanged.

<margin>40 Rebuked)</margin> Repentance, faith, confession, prayer, rebuke, and the whole of Christianity were gathered here together. The misuse of this truly extraordinary example is dangerous; its right use is precious <note>This refers to the "deathbed conversion," which the author suggests should not be relied upon as a reason to delay repentance, though it shows God's mercy.</note>.

**Do you not even fear)** Fear is the very first beginning of a good state of the soul. Even this was absent in that miserable man.

<margin>42 Lord!</margin> remember me in your kingdom.

<margin>43 Today)</margin> One must not read it as: "I say to you today," as if the thief had to wait an unknown length of time before he could enter Paradise. It was significant in itself that it was said to him on that very day. Jesus often said, "I say"; and never, "I say today." Rather, one must read: "Today you will be with me in Paradise." Through this, the power and grace of the Lord Jesus, as well as his own swift entry into Paradise, are praised; and the fulfillment of this promise given to the thief was served by the Jews' request regarding the breaking of legs and the breaking of the legs itself <note>The breaking of the legs (crurifragium) was intended to hasten death so the bodies could be removed before the Sabbath, thereby ensuring the criminal died "today" as promised.</note>.

->Chapter 23, 44-46. Three-hour darkness: The torn curtain. Jesus places his spirit into the Father's hands.<-

# The
## Gospel, as John
## described it.

---

<margin>I. 1 2 3</margin>
In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and God was the Word. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through the same, and without the same was not a single thing made, that has been made.

<margin>4</margin>
In the same was life, and the life was the light of men:

### Annotations.
#### Chapter I, 5. The Word, the Light. <note>While the heading mentions verse 5, the following notes primarily address the theology of the "Logos" or "Word" in verses 1 through 4.</note>

**1 In the beginning)** In the beginning of all that which has a beginning: that is, when God created heaven and earth.

**Was)** the Word was already there, and did not first come into being; it did not just then arise. Thus it was also before the beginning, eternally.

**The Word)** The very Word of which it is said hereafter: It became flesh <note>original: "Es ward Fleisch"</note>. This is the Son of God, who was already the Word before he became flesh.

**Was with God)** before anything existed outside of God.

**God was the Word)** Here the discourse reaches the highest point. Concerning the Word, John says: It was God. A brief but priceless testimony of the divinity of our Lord. O Word, O God, O life, O light! possess me! <note>The author shifts here from academic commentary into a short, prayerful exclamation.</note>

**3 All things)** Everything that has come to be.

**And without)** If all creatures could speak, each one would have to say: whatever I have become, I have not become without the Word. A similar phrasing appears in 1 Corinthians 15:10: "what I am, I am through the grace of God."

**4 And the life)** the Word, in which was life.

**The light)** Life and light are often reported together, as in Chapter 8:12, just as death and darkness are also paired.

**Of men)** from all other creatures, John moves his focus to mankind.

**5 In the darkness)** Hereby is expressed the condition of the human race from Adam's transgression until the appearance of the true light.
**Not reached)** even though it was so close.

**Chapter I, 6-14. John a witness of the light. The light was not received by many: salvation of those who did receive it. The Word became flesh.**

**6 There was)** Between the narrative of John the Baptist in verses 15 and 19, the Apostle John frequently mentions something of the glory of Christ that broke out afterward.
**7 Through him)** through John, but not *in* him <note>The author distinguishes between John as the medium/instrument of belief and Christ as the object of belief.</note>.
**9 Which)** Which, at his coming into the world, enlightens all people as much as is within him.
**All people)** In the original text <note>original: "Grundtext," referring to the Greek "panta anthrōpon"</note> it is expressed very emphatically as "every individual person" in the singular.
**10 In the world it was)** in the previous ages of the world.
**11 Into his own)** That was Israel.
**Not received)** although they already had such a right to him, ahead of the Gentiles.
**12 Received him)** as the true light: even if they were Gentiles. **The word "taking" <note>original: "nehmen"</note>** here has a broader scope than the word **"accepting" <note>original: "annehmen"</note>** in verse 11.
**Power)** so that they were so by right and justice.
**In)** not only through him, as through John in verse 7.
**His name)** as the Son of God.
**13 Who)** The actual description of the children of God.

**13 Of the flesh)** Where two are one flesh.
**A man’s)** Luke 1:34.
**Of God)** from God’s will. James 1:18.
**14 And)** Here it does not say: "There was another man sent from God, whose name was Jesus" (compare verse 6), but rather, "the Word became flesh." John was nothing before he was born of Elizabeth; but the Word was before Mary became his mother, before Abraham was, before the world was: and in his time the Word became flesh.
**Became flesh)** By this it is indicated that the Word assumed human nature, but in such a way that there were not two Messiahs, but one; not two Sons of God, but one.
**The Word)** here John restores the first designation, and so it is as much as to say: the one who was previously the Word, the Life, the Light, he became flesh. What he was before, he did not cease to be; and what he was not before, he became.
**Took up a dwelling-place)** <note>German: Hüttenwohnung</note> This implies a true but brief dwelling in the world, as if in a foreign land.
**We beheld)** especially on the mountain <note>Referring to the Transfiguration</note>, 2 Peter 1:16; indeed, even already at his baptism in the Jordan.
**Full)** The speech is connected thus: "He dwelt among us full of grace and truth." And this is the most essential thing to be pointed out in this verse. For that other part—"it became flesh"—is repeated from the preceding.
**Grace and truth)** Through which we also became children of God. This is repeated in verses 16 and 17; without grace, we could not have endured the glory.
**Grace and truth)**
> Grace and truth, O Son of God! rule over me: let your fullness fill me.

15 *of cords*) For intimidation, not for injury. <note>The author clarifies that the whip was a symbolic tool to create a sense of authority and urgency rather than a weapon to cause physical harm.</note>
*All*) If one wanted to quickly drive away all buyers and sellers from a market, how many armed men would be required? <note>This rhetorical question emphasizes the divine authority or miraculous influence Jesus exerted to clear the area single-handedly.</note>
17 *for your house*) for the Temple.
18 *Sign*) The miraculous deed itself was a sign; yet they still demanded a sign to justify it.
20 *Forty-six*) Exactly this many years before this conversation, Herod had torn down the old temple and rebuilt it more magnificently, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide vital context for first-century Judea.</note> reports.
21 *His body*) Without doubt, he pointed to his body with his hand while saying this.
22 *the Scripture*) concerning his death and his resurrection.

<margin>III.</margin> Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. <margin>6</margin> | That which is born of the flesh is flesh: and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. <margin>7</margin> | Do not marvel that I said to you: You must be born from above. <margin>8</margin> | The Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit. <margin>9</margin> | Nicodemus answered and spoke to him: how can these things happen? <margin>10</margin> | Jesus answered and spoke to him: Are you the teacher of Israel, and do not recognize these things? <margin>11</margin> | Amen, amen, I say to you, what we know, we speak, and what we have seen, we testify: and you do not receive our testimony. <margin>12</margin> | If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe: how will you believe when I tell you heavenly things?

---

**5 Of water and Spirit)** By "water," the baptism of John is understood, which the Pharisees neglected in a most dangerous manner. <note>The author suggests that the Pharisees' rejection of John the Baptist's ritual of repentance was a spiritual failing.</note> Here, the new birth is attributed to water once, but to the Spirit often and principally.

**Enter)** To "not enter" is even less than "not seeing." For seeing what is within the kingdom of God only follows after one has entered.

**7 You)** With Jesus himself, the situation was different. <note>The author clarifies that Jesus, being divine, did not require this "new birth" himself.</note>

**8 The Spirit blows)** <note>original: "Spiritus spirat"</note> The Spirit breathes. <note>The author provides the Latin phrase to highlight the linguistic connection between "spirit," "breath," and "wind."</note>

**10 the teacher)** Thus, more depended on Nicodemus than on all the others together. Without a doubt, he later built up much of Israel with what he learned here. <note>Nicodemus appears later in the Gospel, notably at Jesus' burial, suggesting he did indeed become a follower.</note>

**11 what we know)** Under this "we," the Son of God and the Spirit of God are understood. Compare Chapters 5:30 and 16:13.

**Do not receive)** Through faith.

**12 the earthly)** What seems very high to us—for example, the doctrine of rebirth—is in itself very low. <note>The author presents a paradox: the mystery of rebirth is considered "earthly" because it happens to humans on earth, serving as only the beginning of divine revelation.</note> Where the earthly ends, the heavenly only begins.

<summary>Jesus explains to Nicodemus that spiritual rebirth is a requirement for entering God's kingdom, contrasting the physical "flesh" with the "Spirit." The commentary emphasizes that even the profound concept of rebirth is merely the foundation for even greater heavenly mysteries.</summary>
<keywords>Nicodemus, rebirth, Holy Spirit, Baptism of John, Kingdom of God, Teacher of Israel, earthly vs. heavenly</keywords>

->Chapter 4, 7-26. Conversation with a Samaritan woman, who thereby comes to faith in Jesus Christ.<-

**Comes)** The Kingdom of God progresses through the ordinary circumstances of common life.

**Says)** A wonderful conversation. Jesus's first words here—'give me a drink'—sound quite ordinary <note>original: "bürgerlich," meaning mundane, civil, or relating to everyday social interactions</note>: and the seventh <note>The commentator is counting the progression of Jesus's statements throughout this dialogue.</note>, 'I am the Messiah,' is exactly what was also the final and highest revelation for the apostles. Chapter 16, 31.

**8 His Disciples)** At that time, the Twelve had not yet been officially appointed <note>While Jesus had followers, the formal group of "the Twelve" mentioned later in the Gospels had not been inaugurated at this point in the narrative.</note>: yet they were undoubtedly on this journey. Not just two, but all of them went into the city, and they undoubtedly caused a stir, so that the people subsequently gave the woman all the more hearing.

**14 A Spring)** With such a spring, there is no thirst.

20 **Who)** They did not believe themselves capable of it <note>Referring to the crowd's denial that they were trying to kill Jesus.</note>: therefore they scold him about it. Often there is more evil hidden within a person than they realize.

21 **I have done)** [Referring] to the man by the pool of Bethesda <note>See John 5, where Jesus healed a paralyzed man on the Sabbath.</note>.

24 **By appearance)** according to the flesh, Chapter <note>original: "Cap.", an abbreviation for the Latin *Capitulum*.</note> 5, 15. This also happens when one takes the letter [of the law] without the meaning. *Christ* himself judges rightly. Isaiah 11:3-4.

27 **No one knows)** One might have thought it was a pointless question whether one would know or not know where *Christ* was from: and yet a slight misunderstanding could be a great hindrance to faith. This is often the case with all sorts of impure maxims that the world carries about.

28 **Cried out)** Likewise in verse 37 and Chapter 12:44.

**And said)** He shows that, from different perspectives, they both know and do not know where he is from. That he was from *Nazareth*, they knew; that he was from *God*, they did not know.

<margin>X. 25</margin> Jesus answered them: I have told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in

---

<margin>27. 28 For)</margin> Here are six sayings, arranged in pairs: and each pair shows how the sheep of Christ and He, the Shepherd himself, relate to one another.

**My sheep hear my voice and I know them)** They know me and I know them.

**And they follow me, and I give them eternal life)** These two short sayings are closely linked. They follow me, Jesus spoke, where I go, and thus they arrive unfailingly into eternal life.

**And they will)** They do not lose themselves from me in eternity, and I do not let them be taken from me. There is no separation.

<margin>30</margin> **I and the Father are one)** Not only in will, but also in nature <note>original: "Natur"; in this theological context, it refers to the Greek "ousia" or shared divine essence</note>, so that the Father's power is also the Son's power.

> **Lord Jesus!** strengthen me in the knowledge of you and the Father.

<margin>33</margin> **God)** Jesus does not refute this accusation; rather, he confesses and defends the fact that He is God.

<margin>31</margin> | Now is the judgment of the world: now shall the

---

**Bestow honor)** A greater honor than the greatest monarch in the world could devise or bestow upon his most deserving minister or general in life and in death.

**27 Now)** An important "Now" <note>original: "Nu."; likely referring to the Greek *νῦν* (nyn), the specific "now" of the messianic moment</note>. See verse 31. This is also found in Chapter 13, 31. Following both instances is an indication of a short time remaining: here in verse 35 and in Chapter 13, verse 33.

**Troubled)** Something is "troubled" <note>The German *trübe* refers to water being cloudy, murky, or opaque</note>—for example, water in which silt or powder has been stirred up—and so a soul is troubled when two kinds of thoughts are stirred together. Two kinds of thoughts were in the holy soul of **Jesus**: "Father, save me from this hour," that is, spare me from suffering and death; and, "Father, glorify thy name through my suffering, death, resurrection, etc." **Jesus** does not speak both thoughts at once, but one after the other, as human speech requires; however, he held both thoughts in his heart simultaneously along with the address, **Father.** This was precisely the "cloudiness": and therefore he says, "what shall I say?" which of the two thoughts shall I speak first?

**For this cause)** So that I should endure the hour.

**28 I have glorified it)** through your coming out into the world and your conduct in the world.

**And will glorify it again)** through your departure from the world.

**30 For your sakes)** so that you may believe. In truth, this was a glorious testimony, just like those at the Jordan <note>The Baptism of Jesus</note> and on the holy mountain <note>The Transfiguration</note>.

**31 The judgment of this world)** a legal process and verdict as to whom the world belongs: to me or to its previous prince <note>Satan</note>.

->**Ch. 13, 31-35. Jesus speaks of his glorification, and gives his disciples a new commandment to love one another.**<-

<margin>31</margin> **Speaks)** With this, John’s narrative begins something new. Jesus spoke this discourse early on Thursday. No earlier, v. 1. 30. No later, v. 38. In this discourse, v. 31-35, is contained the summary of everything that stands until the conclusion of the 17th chapter. <note>The commentator views these verses as a foundational summary for the famous "Farewell Discourse" that follows in the next several chapters.</note>

<margin>33</margin> **Lord Jesus!** make me complete in love. In this way, the mystery of your glory will be opened to me more and more.

<margin>34</margin> **New)** Here it is called a new commandment, because the disciples until now had been able to learn at every step of their daily following of the Lord how they should behave toward one another, and only now is such a duty described for them in a summary. <note>The "newness" is interpreted here as the transition from living example to formal instruction.</note>

<margin>35</margin> **Among one another)** Children of the world love one another: **Ch. 15, 19.** Disciples of Christ love one another much more. Children of the world bear a hatred toward the disciples of Christ: therefore, whoever loves these is himself a disciple. <note>The term "children of the world" (Weltkinder) was commonly used in historical German spirituality to distinguish secular society from the community of believers.</note>

<margin>20</margin> [had] said [this], he showed them his hands and his side. Then <margin>21</margin> the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord. Whenever you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven: whenever you retain anyone's sins, they are retained. <margin>24</margin> Thomas, however, one of the twelve, who is called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came. Then <margin>25</margin> the other disciples said to him: We have seen the Lord. But he said to them: Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. <margin>26</margin> And eight days afterward, his disciples were again inside, and Thomas with them. Jesus comes,

---

> 22. They already possessed the Holy Spirit previously; they received him hereafter in full measure. Here, the act of breathing on them is the midpoint between those distributions. <note>The author suggests this was a transitional moment of spiritual empowerment.</note>
> 23. The Apostles were able to exercise the power of forgiving and retaining sins in a special way due to their deep examination of souls and their abundant power, as well as the manifest and sensory miracles that accompanied it. Yet this also belongs to all those who possess the Holy Spirit, whether they hold a public teaching office or not. Indeed, the word of the Gospel for the forgiveness of sins can even benefit those who give space to the Holy Spirit, even if the preachers themselves do not do so. This passage is parallel to Mark 16:16 and Luke 24:47.
> Chapter 20, 24-29. Thomas does not believe: but is won over.
> 25. **Not**) Thomas was undoubtedly of a lively intellect, which he uses here against faith. He does not say: when he sees the nail marks, he will believe; but rather, that without that occurrence—which he did not consider possible—he would not believe. His speech refers to what had been granted to the other disciples in verse 20. He wants at least the same for himself: and he remained in this unbelieving demand for eight days.
> 26. **Eight**) How many periods of eight days, or even eight months or years, have you spent in unbelief?

How everything within him must have been transformed! What his ten fellow disciples could not accomplish in eight days, Jesus achieved so quickly.

<margin>28 To him) to Jesus.</margin>
**My Lord and my God)** A glorious confession. It is you, my Lord, (v. 25) and my God. This confession is validated in verse 29. My Lord and my God!

<margin>29 Blessed)</margin> By this, salvation is not denied to Thomas and the other Apostles who did not believe before they had seen; rather, a special and rare praise is attributed to faith that exists without seeing. Doubtless, the Apostles held the multitude of believers who had not seen Jesus in higher regard than they held themselves.

Chapter 20, 30. 31. John indicates the purpose of this book.

<margin>30 Before his disciples)</margin> He performed the signs before all the people: but each of the disciples saw almost all of them, and thus could testify to them.

<margin>31 So that)</margin> The great purpose of the entire Gospel.
Lord Jesus! I believe that you are Christ, the Son of God. In this faith, let me live.

Chapter 21, 1-14. The third appearance of Jesus, during which he provides a great catch of fish and a midday meal.

<margin>1 Afterward)</margin> This chapter is like an appendix to the book.

# Acts of the Apostles.

<margin>VI. 1</margin> In those days, however, as the disciples were increasing in number, a murmuring arose among the Greek-speaking Jews <note>Hellenists; Jews who lived in the Greek-speaking world and had returned to Jerusalem</note> against the Hebrews <note>local Aramaic-speaking Jews</note>, because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution <note>the daily service or providing of food and aid</note>. <margin>2</margin> Then the Twelve called the multitude of the disciples together and said: It is not right that we should neglect the word of God and serve tables. <margin>3</margin> Therefore, brothers, look out among you for seven men of good reputation, who are full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint to this duty: <margin>4</margin> but we will attend to prayer and the ministry of the word. <margin>5</margin> And the speech was pleasing to the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a convert <note>original: *Judengenossen*; a proselyte, or Gentile who had converted to Judaism</note> from Antioch. <margin>6</margin> These they presented before the apostles: and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <margin>7</margin> And the word of God grew, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem increased greatly, and a large crowd of the priests became obedient to the faith.

---

->Chapter 6; 1-7. Seven men are commissioned with the administration of<-
->temporal matters. Growth<-
->of the congregation.<-

**1 Overlooked)** without intention <note>the commentator suggests the neglect was an accidental oversight rather than a deliberate slight</note>.

**3 Full)** Even for the administration of church property, holy men are required. It is only right that spiritual goods should not be treated as plunder but should be managed spiritually, just as these seven, or the apostles themselves, did while they were still living. God will one day call for an account of this.

**7 Became obedient to the faith)** Faith here refers to the credible testimony of the Gospel: as it is expressed elsewhere, being "obedient to the Gospel" <note>original: *dem Evangelio gehorsam seyn*; see Romans 10:16 and 2 Thessalonians 1:8</note>. And thus, the "obedience of faith" <note>original: *der Gehorsam des Glaubens*; see Romans 1:5 and 16:26</note>. God sets His testimony before us: whoever accepts it as truth gives a humble hearing; he is obedient. In this and all obedience, let me, O God, always be found before You.

3 **The cargo)** <note>original: "Die Ladung"</note> In this way, the kingdom of God often aligns itself with external worldly circumstances: and in secret, God steers these worldly circumstances in a way that is favorable to the expansion of His kingdom. <note>The commentator suggests that the ship's commercial schedule at Tyre provided Paul with a necessary opportunity to encourage the local believers.</note>

4 **Through the Spirit)** <note>original: "Durch den Geist"</note> The Spirit revealed what lay ahead for Paul in Jerusalem: and the suggestion that Paul should not go up there was added by the disciples out of their own well-meaning opinion. <note>The author distinguishes between the divine revelation (danger ahead) and the human reaction (trying to prevent him from going).</note>

<note>original: "O Gott! gib mir die Weisheit..."</note> <note>Reflecting on verse 8: O God! Grant me the wisdom that I may always speak exactly what is fitting.</note>
<note>original: "Wilt du)"</note> <note>Regarding verse 9, "Are you willing": God guided Festus so that he did not simply command, "You must go up to Jerusalem," but gave Paul the choice.</note>

# Paul's Epistle to the Romans.

---

<margin>
I.
1
2
</margin>
Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, a called apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, | which He promised beforehand through His prophets in

->Annotations.<-

### Chapter I, 1 - 7. Heading of the Epistle.

1 **Paul etc.**) What according to our modern manner is a signature, heading, and opening greeting, the ancient Greeks and Romans placed at the top of their letters, and usually quite briefly, as if it were said here, *Paulus Christianis Romae salutem dicit*: <note>Latin: "Paul sends greetings to the Christians at Rome."</note> Paul sends greetings to the Christians at Rome. But he expresses this from the fullness of the Spirit with many glorious words, and in particular, he highly praises Jesus Christ and the Gospel concerning Him, along with his own—Paul’s—evangelical apostolic office.

**Servant of Jesus Christ**) A servant of this kind has a message for the whole world. <note>See Chapter 15:16.</note>

**Christ : : God**) Everywhere in Paul’s writing and elsewhere in the New Testament, one will find the reference to Christ and to God joined together. This should also become familiar to us.

**Called**) Paul had become an apostle through a swift calling, without much [prior] association with Christ: and the Gentiles were called saints, without a preceding promise. Verses 6 and 7 fit well together.
**Set apart**) <term>Acts 13:2</term> <note>original: "Apg. 13, 2." — Apostelgeschichte is the German name for the Acts of the Apostles.</note>

2 **Which**) God has promised, not only that He would show His grace in His Son, but also that He would make it known to all the world. Incline your ears, and take hold with both hands.

<header>Romans. 561</header>

<margin>I.</margin> <margin>3</margin> in the holy Scriptures, | concerning His Son, who was 
<margin>4</margin> born of David’s seed, according to the flesh, | who 
was declared as God’s Son in power, according to the Spirit 
of holiness, by virtue of the resurrection of the dead, 
<margin>5</margin> (namely) of Jesus Christ our Lord, | through 
whom we have received grace and apostleship <note>The German "Gesandtschaft" implies an embassy or the office of being sent; here it refers to the apostolic commission.</note> 
for the obedience of faith among all nations for 
<margin>6</margin> His name's sake, | among whom you also are,
<meta>catchword: (as)</meta>

---

**2 In the holy Scriptures)** By this, the writings of the Old Testament <note>Original: "A. T." — Altes Testament.</note> are confirmed through their fulfillment. The believers in Rome were partly from the Jews and partly from the Gentiles. Paul looks toward the latter for the most part. Verse 13.

**3 Concerning His Son)** JESUS Christ is God’s Son: This is the basis of all rightful address by Jesus Christ to His Father and God, and the basis of our rightful address through Him, as our Lord, to His Father and our Father, and His God and our God, who has given us to Him as His own possession. He was God’s Son even before His humiliation: but through His humiliation, that Sonship was concealed, and only after His resurrection was it fully revealed. Upon this depends His justification: 1 Timothy 3:16, 1 John 2:1, and this is the basis of our justification. Romans 4:25. Therefore, He placed all His trust in the Father during His suffering—not for the sake of His works (for even the Son gave nothing to the Father beforehand that the Father would have had to repay), but because He was the Son—and thus He paved the way for us as the author and finisher of faith. <note>Hebrews 12:2.</note> It is Jesus Christ the Son of God whose blood cleanses us from sin.

**4 Declared as God’s Son in power)** Therefore it is always said: This one, and no other. Acts 9:20, 22, etc.

**According to the Spirit of holiness)** By this is understood everything that is set in opposition to the "flesh," and which Christ therefore did not have from His Davidic ancestry. Luke 1:35. Before the resurrection of Christ, the Spirit was hidden beneath the flesh: but after the resurrection, the Spirit breaks forth prominently.

**5 Obedience of faith)** Obedience is not only a fruit of faith, but faith itself is an obedience, as the testimony of God is accepted with all submission. Lord Jesus Christ, You Son of God: make me and others more and more subject to the obedience of faith.

<margin>7 To all)</margin> There is a notable difference between the books of the Old and New Testaments <note>Original: "A. und N. T." — Altes und Neues Testament.</note> in that the latter, and indeed almost all of them, are composed as if they were letters. One does not easily send letters to slaves, but certainly to adult children, and otherwise to friends near and far. Thus, this style of writing is particularly suited for the New Testament. Take, for example, the Letter to the Romans, and receive it as if Paul had written it specifically to you on Christ’s behalf.

<margin>In Rome)</margin> There was not yet an established congregation <note>The German "Gemeine" refers to an organized local church body.</note>, but rather a number of faithful Christians who were on the way of life.

<margin>Beloved of God)</margin> This is what the believers from <term>Israel</term> <note>Refers here to Jewish converts to Christianity.</note> are specifically called. cf. Chapter 11, verse 28.

<margin>Called Saints)</margin> This is what the believers from the Gentiles <note>The "Heiden" or non-Jewish peoples.</note> are specifically called. See verse 6.

<margin>Chapter I, 8 - 15.</margin> Paul testifies to the believers in Rome his joy over their spiritual well-being, and his long-standing desire to help them further through his personal presence.

<margin>8 my God)</margin> If you can truly say: *my God!* then faith, love, and hope are in their proper order. God! You are my God!

<margin>9 Witness)</margin> In an important matter where human evidence is insufficient, one may indeed call upon God as a witness. 2 Cor. 11, 31.

<margin>11 To see you)</margin> Through the personal presence of the Apostles, a very special blessing was bestowed upon the congregations. Acts 19, 2. If Peter had already been to Rome, Paul would not have had cause to long for Rome so greatly. Peter would have supplied what the Romans lacked <note>The commentator notes that Paul's desire to visit suggests Peter had not yet established the church there, a point of historical and theological debate.</note>.

### Ch. 1, 16. 17. The essence of the Gospel and therefore of this entire epistle.

16 **I am not ashamed**) In the introduction, Paul does not yet open his mouth wide <note>A German idiom meaning he is speaking modestly or with restraint at this stage.</note>: in the conclusion, he boasts greatly. <margin>Ch. 15, 17.</margin> O God! let the power of the Gospel prove itself truly powerful in me and through me.

**A power of God**) One should certainly not be ashamed of that which is powerful, indeed divine.

**for salvation**) In these two verses, the summary and the structural division of the entire treatise, as well as the proof, are contained. For Paul deals with I. Faith. Ch. 1–4. II. Salvation and life. Ch. 5–8. III. All people, both Jews and Greeks. Ch. 9–11.

17 **God's righteousness**) The prophets and apostles use this expression often. Here it signifies the entire benefit of God in Christ Jesus for the salvation of the sinner. God Himself is righteous and makes us righteous. <margin>Rom. 3, 25. 26. 10, 3.</margin>

**Revealed**) because otherwise no human would know anything about it.

**From faith to faith**) so that it remains with faith alone. Right at the beginning, Paul hereby excludes works, but gently.

**From faith**) that is, he who is righteous from faith shall live.

### Ch. I, 18 - 32. Among those under sin are first the Gentiles. <note>original: "Heiden" — referring to the non-Jewish nations.</note>

**18 Of men, who)** here the Gentiles are described.
**Unrighteousness)** Paul names this often, v. 29, because it is essentially the opposite of righteousness <note>Specifically, the "Gerechtigkeit" or righteousness of God mentioned in v. 17.</note>.
**20 His eternal power and divinity)** He has a multitude of powers, and is strong in might. *Isaiah 40:26.*
**Without excuse)** likewise in *Chapter 2, 1.*
**24 Therefore)** Whoever falls into gross sins has previously and recklessly sinned against God Himself.
**Given up)** This word occurs three times: here, and in v. 26 and 28. Each time, a debt of man is mentioned first, followed by the divine retribution. # II. Romans.

<margin>II.</margin>
<margin>3</margin> those who do such things. | But do you think this, O man, you who judge those who do such things and yet commit them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?

<note>
3 **You)** You flatter yourself and have no other reason than that it is *You* specifically, and you think that you cannot and should not fail.
4 **Kindness)** since God holds back his wrath, verse 5.
**Patience)** since God keeps himself as if unknown until he reveals himself, verse 5.
**Long-suffering)** since God allows his righteous judgment to wait, verse 5.
5 **On that day)** Oh, what a treasure will come forth then!

<margin>28 Through faith)</margin> Luther did not distort Paul’s meaning when he added the word "alone" (faith alone). From 2 (which are faith and works) subtract 1 (namely works): what remains? 1 (that is, faith) alone. Compare Chapter 2, verse 6. There are whole books full of testimonies from those who used this little word "alone" before Luther. Yet one must understand it correctly. Faith alone justifies: yet it is not and does not remain alone. It brings forth works from within and without. <note>This refers to the famous "Sola Fide" doctrine; the author argues that while faith is the sole cause of being made right with God, it naturally produces good deeds as a result.</note>

<margin>29 Also of the Gentiles)</margin> who do not have the law.

<margin>4 To him who works)</margin> One who achieves everything through works that the law requires. Paul does not say that such people actually exist; rather, he is presenting a hypothetical case.

**12 Holy)** O God! You are holy; your law is holy. Grant that I may always deal with it, for myself and others, in a way that is lawful.
**Holy)** It promotes the glory of God.
**Righteous)** It teaches all duties toward everyone.
**Good)** It prescribes for me only healthy things, leading to life.
Paul places this word *good* and repeats it in the 13th verse, so that the contrast with evil and death might emerge all the more clearly.
**Chapter 7, 13-25. Objection:** Does the law bring death?
->**Answer:** No. But sin brings death through the law.<-
**14 For)** This little word is well worth noting. Paul explains how wretched sin worked death through the good law, and thereby betrayed itself as being far too sinful. Many interpret this passage as referring to Paul’s state before his justification, and others to his state after. The former take their evidence primarily from the earlier verses, and the latter from the later verses. Paul describes the entire process in verses 13 and 14, and for that reason, he reports in succession: (1) how sin has the upper hand; (2) how afterwards the delight in the law of God gains the upper hand. Therefore, regarding "willing" in verse 18, and afterwards regarding "evil" in verse 21, the word <term>is present <note>original Greek: παρακειται (parakeitai), meaning "to lie near" or "to be at hand"</note></term> is used, which in both instances signifies a weak presence; on the other hand, verse 16 says "I agree with the law," and verse 22 says much more emphatically, "I delight." In general, it should be noted here that Paul—as he often does—is not speaking of his own person from verse 7 onwards, but rather

->Chapter 8, 12-17. Those who follow the Spirit are God’s children and heirs.<-

12 **Debtors**) This speech is shortened. We are—rightly and willingly—debtors, but not to the flesh? It brings a deadly reward. Why then to the Spirit? Because he brings life.

But what is the condition of fleshly people? They are debtors, and they confess themselves as debtors as often as they use the "impossibility of living spiritually" as an excuse.

13 **For**) The flesh pays poorly: who would want to owe it anything?

14 **For those who let themselves be driven by the Spirit of God**) This is the sum of what preceded. He drives us, most of all, to the "Abba-cry."

**These are sons of God**) This is the sum of what follows.

15 **To fear**) Specifically, the fear of death.

**Cry**) And the Spirit itself cries thus. Galatians 4:6.

**Abba, Father**) <note>original: "Abba." An Aramaic word for "Father," used by Jesus to express intimacy with God.</note> If you have not yet experienced this in your life, then grieve and learn it; if you have experienced it, then practice it with joy.

16 **With our spirit**) This spirit is human. 1 Corinthians 2:11. And thus its witness for itself is not infallible. Malachi 2:16. <note>The author suggests the human spirit's own feelings can be mistaken, requiring the Holy Spirit's external confirmation.</note>

> O God! Let that witness always rule uncorrupted in my heart, that I may be your child.

<margin>Ch. 9, 14-29. Two objections are answered.</margin>
14 **Is**) This is the first objection: Is God unjust, that he distributes so unequally between those who were not previously distinguished? <note>The commentator is addressing the problem of why God chooses some and not others when they appear equal in status.</note>

15 **to Moses**) Moses, who was so well-favored, nevertheless had to recognize it as purest mercy, and this was then granted to him abundantly. The cause why a person receives grace is grace itself. O God! be merciful to me. It is your grace that moves me to pray so: it is your grace that I want to praise.

16 **The one who wills**) in a headstrong way.
**The one who runs**) through one's own laboring. <note>The "runner" refers to someone trying to earn salvation through their own effort or "works."</note>

17 **Raised up**) made into a king.

18 **Hardens**) like Pharaoh.

19 **Then**) Second objection, taken from the answer to the first.

20 **But**) This answer sounds somewhat harsh and forceful. Defiant people only have their mouths shut; but afterwards the sweet foundation of the whole matter is revealed to those who are called, v. 24. Whoever takes only a single piece out of this presentation remains stuck: but whoever considers the 9th, 10th, and 11th chapters as a whole, comes to a right understanding. <note>The author encourages the reader to look at the broader context of Paul's argument rather than getting lost in the difficult doctrine of "hardening."</note>

...through the mercies of God, that you present your bodies (as) a sacrifice, living, holy, well-pleasing to God, (namely) your rational service <note>original: "vernünftigen Gottesdienst" — often translated as "reasonable service" or "spiritual worship," implying a devotion that engages the mind and soul rather than just outward ritual</note>:

For I say

—this treatment is derived in the same order of points as we shall now see. We wish to frame the content of such an exhortation in the manner of an exhortation itself: whoever otherwise desires practical applications <note>original: "Nutzanwendungen" — lessons for daily life</note> has them best in the text itself.

**Through the mercies of God)** which have rescued you from the wrath mentioned in Chapter I, 18. As long as a soul is under wrath, no exhortation sticks to it. Oil is only poured onto a stone <note>A metaphor for a hardened heart that cannot absorb instruction</note>. The soul must first have come under the scepter of mercy: after that, it begins to work.

**Your bodies)** not like the heathens <note>non-believers or pagans</note>, who have horribly defiled their bodies. Ch. I, 24.

**Rational)** not in heathen blindness.

<margin>2</margin> **Not like)** How do things stand with you? Do you conform yourself to the world, or are you yourself a person of the world? The latter is wretched, the former dangerous.

**Prove)** As long as you remain stuck in the old mindset, you cannot discern the will of God, no matter how much natural wit you might have. You will always want to assert this or that, and think that God will be just like you.

**Perfect)** Those who always seek out what they believe they still have the freedom to do without sinning evade this perfect will most improperly. It is just as if a traveler, instead of staying on the safe path, purposefully wanted to walk along the very edge of the shore.

**Will)** Due to special circumstances, there are always many questions about whether this or that is right or wrong. The decision is easy for those who align themselves with the will of God. But this requires a testing, an understanding. Ephesians 5, 17.

<note>9 **Evil vs. Good**) There are four types of people: 1) those who side with evil and fight against the good; 2) those who love the good but lack any particular zeal against evil; 3) those who are zealous against evil but do not rightly cherish the good; 4) those who hate evil and cling to the good so strongly that one can truly sense it in them.</note>

<note>11 **Serve the Lord**) Specifically Christ. See Chapter 14:18 and 16:18.</note>

<note>17 **Not wise in your own conceits**) Compare with Chapter 11:25.</note>

<note>17. 18 **All**) See Philippians 4:5. Often in your life you may only deal with a person once or twice; and as your witness toward them is in that moment, so they will thereafter judge you and your entire way of life.</note>

<note>19 **Vengeance is mine: I will repay**) This thought can quickly dampen all desire for revenge. Even assuming your enemy is as evil and you are as innocent as you believe, that person will eventually either attain God's grace or they will not. If they do attain it, they will certainly recognize the wrong they committed against you, even if you do not live to see it; and in that case, you would surely not wish to hold them back from their approach to God through your own enmity—</note>

<summary>This page lists practical Christian virtues, including hospitality, empathy, and humility. It concludes with a significant theological argument against personal revenge, suggesting that leaving justice to God preserves the possibility of the enemy's future repentance.</summary>

---

### Chapter 13, 8-10. Love one another.

10 **Nothing evil)** All the commandments cited here forbid something evil.
**Now)** Love in and of itself does not burn out: if it does not suffer a setback through something evil, it continues to do good; and thus, from the abstaining from evil, the fulfillment of the law—to which doing good also belongs—is concluded.
9 **God!** May your law, the law of love, be forever in my heart!

### Chapter 13, 11-14. Exhortation from the nearness of salvation.

11 **And this)** And this, which I (Chapter 12, 1, 2, etc.) have exhorted, let us do, because we know the time.
**Salvation)** The salvation—which was discussed in Chapters 5-8. This exhortation is derived from that entire preceding discussion: and this is all the shorter because that one was very detailed.
**When we became believers)** Whoever has once made a proper beginning comes ever closer to salvation, or rather salvation, as it is stated here, comes closer to him. He only needs to wait.
12 **The night)** The night of this temporal life.
**The day)** The day of Christ, when all the hope of the believers will be fulfilled.

### Chap. 16, 21-23. Greetings from Timothy and others.

21 **Timothy**) This man had not yet been to Rome; for that reason, Paul did not place him alongside himself at the beginning <note>referring to the opening salutation of the letter where co-senders are often named</note>.

22 **In you, Lord Jesus!**) this is written. In you, may it be of benefit to me and others.

### Chap. 16, 25-27. Doxology <note>original: "Lobspruch," a formal expression of praise to God</note>.

25 **To Him**) Paul had concluded his discourse with a word of praise in Chapter 11, 33-36, and so he does now with the entire letter.
**According to my Gospel**) This conclusion corresponds exactly with the beginning of the letter.
27 **Wise**) Strength (v. 25) and wisdom are joined together. 1 Cor. 1:24.
->**O God! to Thee be glory forever.**<-
