## The First
# Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians.

---

<margin>Year 1</margin>
**P**aul, called apostle of Jesus Christ, through the will of God, and Sosthenes the brother:
<margin>2</margin>
to the congregation <note>original: "Gemeine," referring to the local church body</note> of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, along with all those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in every place, both theirs and ours:
<margin>3</margin>
Grace (be granted) to you and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>4</margin>
I thank my God always on your behalf, for the grace of God which is given to you in Christ Jesus,

->Annotations.<-

### Chapter I, 1-3. The Heading.

1 *Through the will of God)* How necessary and precious it is to have the will of God on one's side. To undertake something by one’s own will, even if it already has a good name in itself, is precarious <note>original: "mißlich," meaning risky or uncertain</note>. The world can make things difficult.
2 *To the congregation)* Paul gives the Corinthians beautiful testimonies right in the heading, and continues so in the introduction (verses 4-9), even though they were inclined toward self-exaltation. Praise that comes out of the grace of God humbles a person all the more, and encourages them at the same time.
*Along with all)* The Corinthians were not alone.
*Our Lord)* Paul mentions the name of Jesus Christ our Lord uncommonly often here, in verses 1-10, and thereby clears the path to the reminder <note>original: "Erinnerung," here likely meaning an admonition or exhortation</note> that begins in verse 10.

> Lord Jesus! let me always be found among those who are sanctified in you and call upon your name.

### Chapter I, 4-9. The Spiritual Standing of the Corinthian Christians.

baptized. <margin>16</margin> I also baptized the household of *Stephanas*; beyond that, I do not know if I have baptized anyone else.

<margin>17</margin> For *Christ* did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel; not with wisdom of speech, so that the cross of *Christ* should not be emptied of its power. <margin>18</margin> For the word of the cross is indeed foolishness to those who are perishing; but to those who are being saved—(namely) to us—it is a power of God. <margin>19</margin> For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the intelligent I will cast away. <margin>20</margin> Where is the wise man? where is the scribe? where is the debater <note>original: "Disputator," a professional arguer or rhetorician</note> of this age? 16 *The household of Stephanas*) As the first converts <note>original: "Erstling," meaning first-fruits or first results</note> of Achaia. Chapter 16, 15. The other believing Corinthians could have been baptized by *Silvanus*, *Timothy*, *Crispus*, *Gaius*, and by those of *Stephanas’* household.

*Know*) I do not remember.

Chapter I, 17-25. The presentation of the Gospel is, like its content, contemptible before the world, but wise and powerful before God.

17 *Not*) From here until the end of the fourth chapter, the discourse seems at first to be very confused, and thus the Apostle provides a pattern of "apostolic foolishness"; in reality, however, everything is very wisely arranged.

*But*) With this, the Apostle prepares the entry to the main subject.

*Not in wisdom of speech*) For the sake of which one of you holds me in higher or lower regard than others.

*The Cross*) As the content of the Gospel, as a starting point. verse 18, 23. Chapter 2, 2. Whoever rejects this, for them the rest also remains hidden; whoever accepts it, to them the power and the glory also become known.

18 *Foolishness*) and weakness.

*Power*) and wisdom.

<summary>Paul concludes the list of those he personally baptized and begins a theological defense of the Gospel, arguing that God's "foolish" message of the cross transcends human intellectualism. The commentary explains that Paul's seemingly disorganized writing style is an intentional reflection of "apostolic foolishness" that hides a deeper divine wisdom.</summary>

# I. Corinthians.

<margin>I.</margin>
<margin>22</margin> since the Jews demand signs, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: <margin>23</margin> but we preach Christ, a crucified one, a stumbling block <note>original: "Aergerniß"</note> to the Jews, and to the Gentiles <margin>24</margin> a foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ, the power of God and <margin>25</margin> the wisdom of God: because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. <margin>26</margin> For you see your calling, brothers, that there are not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble: <margin>27</margin> but God has chosen the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame; and God has chosen the weak things of the world to <margin>28</margin> put to shame what is strong: and the ignoble things of the world and the despised things God has chosen, those which are nothing, that He might bring to nothing those things which are something: <margin>29.30</margin> so that no flesh should boast before God. But from Him you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification

---

<margin>22 **Signs**)</margin> mighty deeds. One does not find that any sign was performed by Paul in Corinth. **Acts 18.** <note>While Paul performed miracles in other cities, the author observes that the record of his time in Corinth in Acts 18 focuses on his teaching rather than miracles.</note>

<margin>23 **Stumbling block**)</margin> Actually, **a snare** <note>original Latin: "scandalum"</note>, that which snaps or breaks in a trap to catch something, and is therefore quite weak. Thus, nowadays, one is accustomed to calling very contemptible things "weaknesses."

<margin>24 **The Called**)</margin> see verse 26.

<margin>**Christ**)</margin> Here it does not add "a crucified one." Whoever has overcome the offense of the cross finds the mystery of Christ open to them.

->Christ, you are divine power and divine wisdom to me.<-

<margin>**Chapter 1, 26-31.**</margin> Because of this matter, Paul appeals to the experience of the Corinthians themselves.

<margin>26 **Not many wise**)</margin> This is why so little could be gained in Athens, the seat of Greek wisdom. <note>Referring to Paul's difficult time in Athens described in Acts 17, where the philosophers mocked the resurrection.</note>

<margin>**Not many noble**)</margin> Can the **Freemasons** <note>original: "Freymäurer"</note> also say this? <note>A contemporary observation by the translator or commentator, likely noting that the Freemasons of their era tended to be drawn from the higher, "noble" social classes, unlike the early Christians.</note>

<margin>27 **Chosen**)</margin> frequently. **Acts 18, 10.**

<margin>29 **No flesh**)</margin> with its own wisdom, etc.

<margin>30 **Wisdom**)</margin> as opposed to foolishness.

<margin>**Righteousness**)</margin> as opposed to weakness. **Romans 5, 6.**

<margin>**Sanctification**)</margin> as opposed to the lack of nobility.

<summary>This page explores Paul’s teaching that God deliberately chooses what the world considers weak and foolish—the message of a crucified Christ and the lowly social status of the believers—to undermine human pride. The commentary highlights the lack of miracles in Corinth and makes a contemporary comparison to the social standing of Freemasons.</summary>

1 **Mysteries**) heavenly doctrines which are unknown to the children of men without God’s revelation.

3 **By you**) This limits what he had said in Chapter 3:21, "All things are yours."

**By a human day**) All days that precede the Day of the Lord are "human." <note>This suggests that human judgment is temporary and fallible compared to divine judgment.</note>

6 **Applied**) Just as I have spoken of myself and Apollos, so you should take it as a pattern for the thoughts you ought to have of us.

**Written**) The whole of Scripture is our rule. Romans 15:4. It gives glory to God alone, but to man not at all. Chapter 1:31. And thus human boasting goes against the Scripture and its entire meaning. Luke 16:15–18, 29; Isaiah 66:2.

<margin>5</margin> is not puffed up, ¹ it does not behave unseemly, it seeks not its own, it is not provoked, it `<margin>6</margin>` does not count the evil, ¹ it does not rejoice over injustice, but it has joy in the truth, ¹ it `<margin>7</margin>` lets all things pass <note>original: "alles lässet sie hingehen"; commonly translated as "bears all things"</note>, it believes all things, it hopes all things, `<margin>8</margin>` it endures all things. ¹ Love never fails. 4 **(Is not puffed up)** through partisan attachment to this or that person above others.
5 **(It is not impolite)** This is a <term>deficiency</term> <note>original Latin: "in Defectu"</note>, just as boasting is an <term>excess</term> <note>original Latin: "in Excessu"</note>. Love allows nothing unseemly to arise. Familiarity is not rudeness.
**(It does not count the evil)** It does not think: this or that person treats me so and so, he has done this and that and deserves it <note>i.e., deserves retaliation or a grudge</note>.
->**Chapter 13, 8-13. Love’s Unending Duration.**<-
8 **(Done away)** when it comes to the act of seeing <note>referring to the beatific vision or seeing God directly</note>.
**(Cease)** even sooner.
9 It is fragmentary that we have knowledge and prophecy. Knowledge and prophecy themselves carry something imperfect with them.
12 O God! let me reach the perfect!
13 **(Now)** in this life.
**(Abide)** as those parts which are necessary for everyone.
**(Three)** that which is necessary is soon counted.

### Chapter 15, 1 - 11. Certainty of the Resurrection of Christ.

1 *I make known*) The matter itself he had previously made known to them: but now he makes the foundation even better known to them.
*Received*) This binds one for eternity.
2 *Saved*) see verses 18, 19.
*In vain*) A lamentable word. Galatians 2:2, 3:4, 4:11.
4 *Buried*) The burial of Christ is not linked so closely with death here, but rather more closely with the resurrection. For at the moment of Christ's death, the power of infinite life stirred. 1 Peter 3:18, Matthew 27:52. To the **Lord** Christ, the grave was not a container for decay, but a chamber for the entry into life. Acts 2:26.
6 *More than 500*) These were all people who therefore possessed something of an apostolic character.
*fallen asleep*) in this faith.
7 *James*) the Less <note>James the Less: likely James the son of Alphaeus, distinguished from James the son of Zebedee</note>.
8 *Last among all*) By this, the subsequent appearances <note>referring to Christ appearing to Paul after the Ascension</note> are not excluded. Acts 23:11.

## The Second Letter
# of Paul to the Corinthians.

---

**S**ince the Corinthians had been deeply moved by Paul's previous sharp letter, he now opens up his apostolic, fatherly, and tender love with repeated exhortations. Just as he had previously dealt with the Corinthians' affairs, he now reports his own circumstances, whereby he presents the legitimate reasons for his absence and demonstrates a consistent intention for the spiritual benefit of the Corinthians. The entire letter is arranged like a travelogue, and the primary historical points are found in Chapter 1, 8. 15. 2, 1. 12. 13. 7, 5. 8, 1. 10, 1. 13, 1. The rest is contained in lovely digressions <note>The author uses the term "Ausschweifungen," which here refers to Paul’s thematic detours or elaborate spiritual explanations rather than something negative.</note>. Hence, this overview emerges: In this letter there is:

### I. The Salutation, Chapter I. 1. 2

### II. The Discourse:

1. In Asia we were very hard-pressed, but even more comforted by God. For we act with sincerity; also in the fact that I have not come to you again: for which reason you should rightly follow me. 1. 12. 23 — II. 11.

2. From Troas I hurried into Macedonia to be near you; with the good progress of the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelii"</note>, whose glorious

# The Second

## Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians.

---

<margin>I. 1</margin> Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the church of God which is at Corinth, together with
<margin>2</margin> all the saints who are in all Achaia: May grace and peace befall you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>3</margin> Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God
<margin>4</margin> of all comfort, who comforts us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any tribulation, through the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted
<margin>5</margin> by God. For just as the sufferings of Christ come abundantly <note>original: "häufig," meaning frequently or in great measure</note> upon us, so also through Christ our
<margin>6</margin> comfort is abundant. Whether it be that we are distressed, it is for the sake of your comfort and salvation; or whether we are comforted, it is for the sake of your comfort, which is effective in the enduring of the very same sufferings which we also suffer; and our hope is
<margin>7</margin> steadfast for you, knowing that just as you are partakers of the sufferings, so shall you also be partakers of the comfort.

->Notes.<-

**Chap. I, 1–11. Heading. Narrative of endured tribulation and preceding praise of God because of the benefit flowing from it.**

**3 of mercies)** Before Paul mentions the tribulations, he praises [God's] mercy and help.

**4 able)** How necessary is one’s own experience; how unfit is a teacher without the same. <note>The commentator emphasizes that a pastor cannot truly comfort others without having personally experienced suffering and God's subsequent consolation.</note>

2 **Shame that hides itself**) He who is ashamed does not say what needs to be said.

4 **The God of this world**) Satan. A very great and evil work is attributed to him here: therefore a great and evil title is also given to him here.

*Chapter* 4:7—5:10. The instruments are fragile: the divine power within them is abundant, reaching even into that world beyond. Therefore they act with confidence.

7 **Earthen**) fragile, though clean.

**Power**) Both the fragility and the power are described in verse 8, and so on further.

3 **it was**) There was a double rapture: into the third heaven, and then into Paradise. Even if the first had been in the body, the other could still have been out of the body. Therefore he writes in this way twice.

6 **higher**) How many people let others think more of them, both near and far, than is actually in them; but by how much honor before God might they deprive themselves through this? Are you a child of God? Then let this light of yours shine: but deal carefully and sparingly with special experiences.

7 **A thorn in the flesh**) What was this? Paul adds the explanation immediately thereafter.

**Exalt**) What a dangerous thing self-exaltation is, since the Apostle found such a safeguard necessary.

**A satanic angel**) The phrasing is ambiguous: the angel could either be Satan himself or one belonging to Satan. Perhaps Paul himself was not permitted to know, for the sake of his even greater humiliation.

9 **Lord Jesus!** Your grace is my comfort.

5. He exhorts them to hold fast to freedom, warns against the abuse of freedom, and reminds them that they should walk not in the flesh <term>Flesh: in a Pauline context, this refers to the 'lower nature' or human impulses that lead away from God.</term>, but in the Spirit.

<margin>v. 11. 17. 18.</margin>

->Notes.<-

->Chapter I, 1. 2. Salutation.<-

1 **The Saints**) My God, I am yours: therefore I am holy <note>The commentator emphasizes that "holy" or "saint" (Heilig) refers to being set apart for God's possession through faith, rather than personal perfection.</note>. Keep me in the faith in Christ Jesus.
**who are**) There are traces from antiquity <note>This refers to the "Encyclical Theory," where scholars suggest this letter was a circular letter intended for multiple churches.</note> that Paul sent this letter via Tychicus not only to the Ephesians, but to several congregations in Asia where he himself had not been (see v. 15 and Chapter 3:2). For this reason, he frames the closing greeting in very general terms (Chapter 6:23, 24). Consequently, those in Laodicea (Colossians 4:16) and in other cities—and thus also those in Ephesus—could receive the letter as if it had been written specifically to them.

**Chapter I, 3-14. Praise to God for all spiritual blessings, as they flow from eternal election and lead to the eternal inheritance.**

3 **Blessed**) God blesses through the work itself; we bless Him with praise and thanks. This song of praise flowed from a very full heart. It extols the blessing <term>Wohlthat: a benefit or act of kindness</term> of God (v. 3-14), and the blessing of Christ (v. 7), and the blessing of the Holy Spirit (v. 13) is woven in, in the proper order.
**Blessing**) An abundance of goods.
**In Christ**) Paul has here [described] the entire course of Christ from His— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "net" indicates the next word is likely "seinem" (His).</note>

---

**14. 15** **by abolishing the enmity in his flesh, (and the law of commandments in the decrees)**
There was an enmity between Jews and Gentiles: and this enmity Christ has abolished in his flesh, that is, through his suffering and death. It was the law, which consisted of ceremonial commandments, and this he has abolished through the evangelical decrees of freedom. These appear here, and in Acts 15:4, 15:28, under the same Greek words.
**18** **Him = Spirit = Father)** Witness of the Holy Trinity. Compare Chapter 1:3, 5.

-> O Father, through your Son I have access in your Spirit to you. Let me enjoy this access at all times! <-

**19** **Strangers)** in the house.
**Guests)** among the people.
**20** **of the prophets)** in the New Testament. Chapter 3:5, 4:11. <note>The author clarifies that "prophets" here refers to New Testament prophets rather than Old Testament ones, as they are listed alongside the Apostles.</note>

**7 Right)** Paul has a sufficient ground for his hope.

**9 Your love)** which you prove in the work itself.

**In knowledge and all senses)** Sight is the most distinguished among the external senses, yet it is not the only one. So also is knowledge, as the sight of the soul, the most distinguished among the internal senses, but there is also a spiritual hearing, etc. To this belongs the joy that prevails in this letter, etc. Those who now want to reduce everything only to clear concepts <note>A critique of Enlightenment rationalism which prioritized intellectual logic over spiritual experience</note> act just as if they wanted to hear and smell with their eyes. Oh, that the world-wise <term>Weltweisen; a term used for secular philosophers or scholars</term> of today would consider this when they apply themselves to spiritual things. Here lies their main error.

**10 the best)** Those do not do this, who are always asking how far they can stretch their freedom <term>Freyheit; liberty or license</term> without sinning.

### Ch. I, 12-24. News regarding the benefit of his bonds.

**13 My bonds)** and the cause of them.

**In the whole court)** Ch. 4, 22.

<margin>I. 1 2</margin> Paul, Apostle of Jesus Christ, by the will of God, and Timothy the brother, | to the saints (residing) at Colossae <note>Colossae was an ancient city in Phrygia, in modern-day Turkey</note> and faithful brothers in Christ: Grace (be) unto you and peace from God our Father [and the Lord Jesus Christ.]

<margin>3</margin> | We thank the God and Father of our Lord <margin>4</margin> Jesus Christ, since we pray for you at all times, | since we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, <margin>5</margin> and of the love toward all saints, | for the sake of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens, of which you have heard before in the word of the truth of the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelii"</note>, <margin>6</margin> | which is present among you, as also in all the world, and brings forth fruit and grows, as also in you, from the day on which you heard and recognized the grace of God in truth: <margin>7</margin> | as you also learned from Epaphras our beloved fellow-servant <term>fellow-servant: translated from "Mitknecht", a term denoting a colleague or partner in religious service</term>, who is a faithful servant of Christ for <margin>8</margin> you, | who also reported to us your love in the Spirit. <margin>9</margin> | Therefore we also, from the day on which we heard it, do not cease to pray for you: and to ask that you be filled with the kno-

**3 We thank)** We thank [Him] for the sake of the hope.
**4. 5 Faith: Love: Hope)** this is the whole of Christianity. compare v. 9. 10. 11.

->*Chap.* I, 15-23. Glory of the Redeemer.<-

<margin>15 who)</margin> People wanted to direct the *Colossians* toward a false
humility, suggesting they should direct their devotion toward the angels.
In opposition to this, *Paul* presents *Christ* to them, and
describes his glory in such a way that they must nonetheless hold to him
himself as the Redeemer, who is at the same time the head over all things.

**The image)** God is invisible, and consequently the image
is also invisible: (yet visible in humanity *John* 14,
9.) for the invisible as well as the visible is
created in him.

**the firstborn)** All *creatures* together are a
single work along with time, by which the duration of created things
is measured. But the Son of God is, before all
creatures, not created, but born; not in created
temporality, but in divine eternity.

16 **In heaven)** such as the sun, moon, and stars.

invisible on the seventh day. Genesis 2:1.
Exodus 31:17.

Father or the Son is being discussed.

13-15 **made alive** : : **graciously granted** : : **blotted out** : : **stripped**) Freedom from sin, from the law, and from evil spirits.

14 **Blotted out the handwriting against us with the decrees, which was contrary to us**) The law, which we had transgressed, was a "handwriting" <note>an IOU or debt certificate</note>: and this handwriting, the law, was not only against us with its demand, but also against us with its accusation. But God has blotted out the handwriting through the evangelical decrees of freedom. See Ephesians 2:15, etc.

15 **In him**) In Christ. For from the 12th verse until here, the subject is God. God raised Christ; has made you alive; has taken the handwriting out of the way; has led the principalities in a display. Exactly as in Ephesians 1:20 and 2:5.

## Paul’s First Letter to the Thessalonians.

---

<margin>I. 1</margin>
Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace be unto you and peace [from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.]

<margin>2</margin>
We give thanks to God always for you all, making mention of you in our prayers, <margin>3</margin> | and remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labor of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before our God and Father: <margin>4</margin> | for we know, brothers, beloved by God, your election <note>original: "Auswahl," referring to the divine choice or "calling" of the believers.</note>, <margin>5</margin> | that our Gospel came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much fullness, just as you know how we conducted ourselves among you for your sake. <margin>6</margin> | And you became followers of us <meta>catchword: the</meta>

---

->Notes.<-

Chapter I, 1–10. Heading. Thanksgiving for the grace of God toward the Thessalonians, as it was established among them through Paul’s service.

1 **Paul**) This is the first letter among all those we have from Paul. <note>Scholars generally agree that 1 Thessalonians is the earliest of the surviving Pauline epistles, written around 50–51 AD.</note>

3 **Faith, Love, Hope**) Chapter 5, 8. 2 Thessalonians I, 3. 4.

**Labor**) Love cannot be exercised without labor: it does not flee from labor, but rather overcomes comfort, pride, etc. You might ask: who gives me enough time? Answer: do not waste time with laziness, with long banquets <note>original: "Gastungen," referring to excessive feasting or social gatherings.</note>, with useless company. In this way, much time will be gained for the labor of love.

# I. Thessalonians. 755 V.

<margin>25. 26</margin> ²⁵ Brothers, pray for us. ²⁶ Greet all the brothers with the holy kiss. <margin>27</margin> ²⁷ I adjure you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers. <margin>28</margin> ²⁸ The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

...contain comfort. If you stand in your calling, then rejoice in the faithfulness of Him who will do it. <note>This refers to the preceding verse 24: "He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it."</note>

**25 (Pray for us)** Paul requests the same in the second letter to the Thessalonians, likewise to the Romans, Ephesians, Colossians, Philemon, and in passing in the second letter to the Corinthians and to the Philippians. In the letters to Timothy and Titus, he does not include such a request, either because he wrote to them as sons, or because he was already assured of their intercession beforehand. In the first letter to the Corinthians and to the Galatians, he also does not include it: because he had to punish <note>or "reprove"</note> them with a paternal authority.

> O God! be merciful to all your servants!

**27 (I adjure you by the Lord)** The Apostles have many a precious exhortation in their letters: but this is the only passage where Paul adjures <note>original: *beſchwöret*; to charge someone under oath or solemn command</note> his so dearly beloved Thessalonians. This must be something significant. This letter is the oldest among the books of the New Testament <note>scholars generally agree 1 Thessalonians was the first of Paul's letters to be written, around 50-51 AD</note>, and just as the Scriptures of the Old Testament were read among the people of Israel, so must the Scriptures of the New Testament be read in the Christian Church; and it was precisely here in Thessalonica that the beginning had to be made. The Lord by whom he adjures them is Christ: and it is a divine honor that he adjures them by this Name.

** (That the letter be read to all the holy brothers)** The Scripture is for everyone. If not everyone can read, then it should be read aloud to everyone. It is of great importance to them. Those who suppress <note>original: *unterſchlagen*; literally "to intercept" or "to embezzle"</note> the Bible and make the reading of the Word of God so difficult for the common crowd certainly do not handle it correctly themselves, and for that reason, they shun the light. How they will fall silent when the Judge says to them: Why did you place such self-authorized prohibitions upon my words? Why did you take it away from those who would have handled it better than you yourselves? It is to be wished (so writes a brave Wittenberg theologian) that in many places, even high-ranking ones, instead of the sermons—of which there are only too many here and there—there would be established and held among the congregation the reading of several chapters from the Bible, etc. <term>Franz *de Interpr.* p. 47 <note>Referring to Wolfgang Franz (1564–1628), a Lutheran professor at Wittenberg; the work cited is *Tractatus theologicus de interpretatione Sacrae Scripturae* (Theological Treatise on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture).</note></term>. This would be right: and now it is all the more to be lamented that nowadays people think the less one brings from the Scripture into the sermons, the more beautifully it is preached.

# first Letter of Paul to Timothy.

<margin>I. 1</margin> *Paul*, Apostle of *Jesus Christ*, by the command of *God*, our Savior, <note>original: "Seligmachers"; literally "one who makes blessed," a traditional German term for Savior.</note> and *Christ* <margin>2</margin> *Jesus*, our hope; | to *Timothy* the true child in faith: Grace, mercy, peace from *God* our Father and *Christ Jesus* our Lord.

<margin>3</margin> | Even as I urged you to remain in *Ephesus*, when I went into *Macedonia*, so that you might command certain ones not to teach other doctrines, <margin>4</margin> | nor to pay attention to fables <note>original: "Mährlein"; refers to myths or idle tales.</note> and genealogies, <note>original: "Geschlechtregister"; lists of ancestors.</note> which have no end, and which provide questions rather <margin>5</margin> than the work of God, which is in faith: | but the goal of the commandment is love out of a pure <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

## Notes.

Chapter I, 1-20. See the Heading. The commandment concerning the right use of the law, which *Paul* had orally instructed *Timothy* to carry out, he now also commands him in writing, whereby he points to his own blessed example and the miserable examples of others.

1 **Apostle**) *Paul* uses this title even when addressing *Timothy* and *Titus*, so that his presentation might go all the more to their hearts. <note>Paul emphasizes his formal authority as an Apostle even in personal letters to his students to reinforce the weight of his instructions.</note>
3 **Even as**) The speech that begins here is concluded in verse 18, and in the meantime, *Paul* refutes those who taught otherwise by using his own extraordinary example of conversion.
**Teach other doctrines**) Chapter 6, 3.
5 **The commandment**) of that which Timothy is to command certain people.

<margin>2</margin>
**In all godliness)** <note>original Greek: eusebeia; original Latin: pietas</note> godliness, or the fear of God. Paul uses this word only in his letters to Timothy and Titus, but he uses it often; likewise Luke in the Acts of the Apostles, and Peter in his second letter. It is a masterstroke against the kingdom of God and to the delight of Satan in this dregs <note>The author uses the vivid German term "Grundsuppe," referring to the foul sediment at the bottom of a liquid.</note> of the wicked world, that "piety"—which at least in name has always been held as honorable—has finally been turned into a term of abuse, "Pietist," by a wicked rogue N., of whom no good end is told. This term has spread astonishingly far, even though this suffix—which rhymes with statesman, linguist, copyist, etc.—cannot in itself signify anything evil. If one wishes to designate fickle spirits and hypocrites with a special name, and has the certainty that one is not striking an innocent person: why must "piety" be the victim? This is no joke. Experience teaches it; among fools and in the taverns, as soon as someone is a little withdrawn, before he even says a word for the sake of doctrine, he is attacked with this title, which many of the common folk cannot even pronounce. Much, much piety is stifled by the "Pietist" slur, especially in its first tender bloom. God will judge it. Jude v. 15.

<margin>5</margin>
**For)** He who does not have the one mediator does not come to God. He who does not have the one God will not be saved. Now, God desires that all people be saved through the soul-saving knowledge of God and the mediator; but this will has its measured, holy order <note>The author emphasizes that while God's grace is universal, it operates through a specific divine structure or "order of salvation."</note> in which people are meant to encounter Him. All people are like a single person before God: therefore, those who have attained salvation should pray for those who are still left behind. If this were to happen, how much better would things stand for the human race? Pray, pray, whoever can pray.

<summary>This page covers 1 Timothy 2:3-8, focusing on God's desire for universal salvation and the role of Christ as the sole mediator. The commentary includes a passionate defense of "piety" against the then-contemporary slur "Pietist," arguing that mocking devotion hinders the spread of the Gospel.</summary>

<margin>2</margin> **The husband of one wife)** This is the standard description of the married state: the husband of one wife, the wife of one husband. Between two men who are otherwise equal, one should—according to Paul's instruction—appoint the married man as <term>bishop</term> <note>In the early church, this term referred to an overseer or local church leader before it evolved into the modern hierarchical title.</note> over the single man. For he can better edify the people with a good example. Human cleverness and hypocrisy have reversed this, requiring "the husband of no wife" <note>A critique of forced clerical celibacy.</note>, and because of this, many a man has become the husband of more than one wife.

*Chapter 3:16 – 4:16. The mystery of godliness, which is firm in itself, will be abandoned by many. Timothy should remain steadfast in it and rightly oversee his office.*

*16 A pillar and foundation of the truth and something confessedly greater) What is otherwise called "certain and worthy of all acceptance" (Chapter 1, verse 15), Paul expresses here with an even more magnificent formula. The discourse begins anew here. The mystery of which he wishes to speak is certain, and so important that one should—and actually does—confess it with all willingness.*

*Godliness) see verse 7; Chapter 6, verse 3.*

*Justified in the spirit) thus, immediately after the death of Christ.*

*Preached) The foundation of such preaching was already laid before the Ascension.*

*In the world) A great wonder!*

*Taken up into glory) This stands last as the highest point. The magnificent future and the eternity of glory are included here.*

*Chapter 4:1. From the faith) The foundation of which was described immediately preceding this.*

### Notes.

Ch. I, 1-18. **Heading.** Hearty encouragement of Timothy, wherein Paul's good example, and the partly adverse, partly good examples of others are cited.

1 *Of life*) Through this letter, Paul summoned Timothy to himself shortly before his martyrdom: and he brings this desire forward more and more clearly, as he first wins Timothy's heart, and only then mentions the journey itself v. 6. 8. Ch. 2, 1. 3. 4. 5. 9. 21. It seemed that physical danger was involved: but Paul speaks right at the beginning of life <note>Paul emphasizes eternal life in Christ to strengthen Timothy against the fear of death or the danger of the journey to Rome.</note>.

3 *Ancestors*) At the end of the pilgrimage <note>A common Pietist metaphor for the end of one's earthly life and the completion of the Christian journey.</note> it is especially something lovely to have the memory of holy ancestors.

# The Letter of Paul to Philemon.

---

<margin>1</margin> Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon the beloved and our fellow laborer, <margin>2</margin> and to Appia the sister, and Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in your house. <margin>3</margin> Grace <note>original: "wiederfahre," meaning to happen to or befall</note> be unto you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>4</margin> I thank my God, as I always remember you in my prayers, <margin>5</margin> as I hear of your love and faith, which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints: <margin>6</margin> that the fellowship of your faith may become active in the knowledge of all the good that comes to us for the sake of Christ (Jesus). <margin>7</margin> For we have great joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother. <margin>8</margin> Therefore, though I have much boldness in Christ to command you what is fitting, <margin>9</margin> yet for love's sake I rather appeal to you, being such a one as Paul, an elderly man <note>original: "Betagter," referring to someone advanced in years</note>, but now also a prisoner of Jesus

### Annotations.

v. 1 - 25. **Heading.** Paul asks the kind Philemon that he would graciously receive back the escaped but converted servant <note>original: "Knecht"; in the Roman context, this refers to Onesimus's status as a bondservant or slave</note> Onesimus. He also requests lodging with him.

### Conclusion.

5 **Love)** Here Paul places love before faith because he wishes to exhort Philemon to a work of love.

# Philemon.

<margin>10</margin> Christ: I therefore exhort you, for the sake of my child, whom I have begotten in my bonds, <margin>11</margin> **Onesimus**, who in times past was useless to you, but now is very useful both to you and to me; him I have herewith sent <margin>12</margin> back. But you, receive him—that is, my own heart. <margin>13</margin> I wanted to keep him with myself, so that he might serve me on your behalf in the bonds <margin>14</margin> of the Gospel; but without your consent I wanted to do nothing, so that your good deed might not be as if <margin>15</margin> out of necessity, but of your own free will. For perhaps he was separated from you for a while for this very reason, so that <margin>16</margin> you might have him back forever; no longer as a servant <note>original: "Knecht"; in this context, it refers to a bondservant or slave</note>, but more than a servant: a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the <margin>17</margin> flesh and in the Lord. If you then count me as a <margin>18</margin> partner, receive him as you would me. But if he has done you any wrong, or owes you <margin>19</margin> anything, charge that to me. I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand, I will repay it—not to mention to you <margin>20</margin> that you owe me even your own self besides. ### The
# Epistle to the Hebrews.

In this letter, the strengthening of the brothers in the faith in Jesus Christ is urged, Chap. XIII. 2. <note>original: "Cap. XIII. 2."; likely a reference to the "word of exhortation" mentioned in Hebrews 13:22, as verse 2 concerns hospitality.</note> and this is accomplished through the proof of his glory. This very point is the main matter. Chap. VIII. 1. The letter carries with it the sharpest warnings and the most powerful encouragements, and is composed throughout in the same manner, so that the doctrine and the practical application are linked in every place by the little word *therefore*. The summary is this:

-> The glory of Jesus Christ shines forth. <-

I. **Preliminary, from the comparison with the prophets and angels.** I. 1 – 14.
**Therefore we should pay attention to his word.** II. 1 – 4

II. **Principal, from the comparison of suffering and completion. Here it is to be noted:**

1. the summary presentation, from the 8th Psalm 5 – 9
2. the treatise. We have a more perfect author <term>author: translated from "Urheber," also meaning originator or pioneer</term> of salvation <term>salvation: translated from "Seligkeit," referring to eternal blessedness</term> and glory, who suffered for us beforehand, so that he (1) [might be] merci- <note>The word "wür-" is the start of "würde" (would/might be), continuing onto the next page.</note>

# The Epistle to the Hebrews.

<margin>I.</margin>
<margin>1</margin> Since in many parts and in manifold ways long ago God had spoken to the fathers in the <margin>2</margin> prophets, he has in the last of these days spoken to us in the Son, whom he has appointed as an heir of all (things), through whom he also made the world-ages <term>world-ages: translated from 'Weltzeiten,' referring to the eons or the entirety of created time and space</term>, who, since he was a radiance from his glory and a form of his substance, and sustained all things with the word of his power, [who] after he had through himself performed the cleansing of sins, seated himself at the right hand of the Majesty in the <margin>4</margin> height, whereby he has become so much better than the angels, by as much as he [obtained] a more excellent name before <meta>them</meta> <note>original: "ihnen"; this is a catchword at the bottom of the page to ensure the reader transitions correctly to the next sheet.</note>

->Notes.<-

Chapter I, 1-4. The incomparable excellence of the Lord, who has proclaimed the salvation of the New Testament, is summarily testified.

* **In many parts)** God has revealed one point after another.
* **In manifold ways)** in dreams, visions, etc.
* **Long ago)** The last prophet of the Old Testament, Malachi, prophesied several hundred years before the birth of Christ.
* **In the Son)** This is discussed in verse 5.
* **2 Whom)** In verses 2 and 3, the glory of the Son of God is described in an excellent summary.
* **Heir)** This is discussed in verses 6-9.
* **World-ages)** This is discussed in verses 10-12.
* **3 Radiance == Power)** Two reasons for the sitting at the right hand.
* **Through himself)** as his own blood was shed.
* **Seated himself)** This is discussed in verses 13 and 14.
* **4 Better)** more glorious, more blessed.
* **Name)** That he is called the Son. See verse 1.

> Lord Jesus! Fill my heart with your glory!

7 **I am here**) I come, or more accurately, I have come. This very word was, as it were, the motto <note>original: "Symbolum," meaning a creed, sign, or identifying mark</note> of the Lord Jesus. I have come, he said, to fulfill the law: Matthew 5:17; to preach: Mark 1:38; to call sinners to repentance: Luke 5:32; to bring a sword, to set man at odds: Matthew 10:34-35. I have come down from heaven to do the will of him who sent me: John 6:38 and following. These are the very words of the 40th Psalm. I am sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel: Matthew 15:24. I have come into this world for a judgment: John 9:39. I have come that they may have life and full abundance: chapter 10:10; to save that which was lost: Matthew 18:11. To rescue the souls of men: Luke 9:56; to bring a fire upon the earth: chapter 12:49; to serve: Matthew 20:28; to seek and to save that which was lost: Luke 19:10; compare 1 Timothy 1:15. I have come into the world as a light: John 12:46; and so that I may bear witness to the truth: chapter 18:37. Let your soul, O soul, allow your Savior to achieve this purpose in you. <margin>3</margin> you fall into various temptations, | because you know that the testing of your faith works patience:

->Notes.<-

Chapter I, 1–15. Heading. Instruction on how everyone should bear temptations with joy and attribute them not to God, but to themselves.

Joy) This is not hindered by trials, but rather promoted. verse 2.

2. My God! give me wisdom, give me patience.

3 Testing) verse 12.

4 and complete) When worldly people or scholars want to rightly praise a person, they call them a complete person or a whole man. Here, however, we see what is required if one is to truly bear this <term>attribute</term> <note>Original: "Prädicat." In this context, it refers to a title or descriptive characterization.</note> in truth: testing and a perfect work. What is "complete" before the world is nothing before God without faith.

6 in faith) James also gives precedence to faith at the beginning and end of his letter. In the 2nd Chapter, he only says how faith must be constituted.

## Ch. I, 19-21. Discourse.

<margin>19</margin> This verse, together with the two following, is the summary of what is dealt with in detail hereafter: namely, the readiness to hear, v. 22-27; the slowness to speak, ch. 3, 1-12; and the slowness to anger, ch. 3, 13 to 4, 17. This third point is the most prominent, because anger or impatience is what most removes itself from the righteousness of God.
**to speak)** v. 23. 26.
<margin>21</margin> **all impurity and what is excessive and thus evil)** for example, in speaking. In thoughts, words, gestures, and works, excess and vice go together. Matth. 5.
**With meekness)** without anger.
**receive)** as ready listeners.
**implanted)** that which you have heard, not from fleshly birth, but from your ancestors, insofar as they were God's people, and from childhood, and from daily practice.
> O God! through your word work in me everything that pleases you.

**Ch. I, 22-2, 13.** With hearing there should be the deed, v. 22-27, and a service of God that is not vain, but pure, 26. 27. without respect of person, ch. 2, 1-13.
<margin>22</margin> **deceive themselves)** through a false conceit regarding [the mere act of] hearing.
> My God! make me a doer of your word through your word in love.

<margin>24</margin> **he looks at himself)** It rarely happens without effect that one etc. <note>The thought is left unfinished in the source text, likely suggesting that even a brief look in a mirror should prompt a change, yet the "hearer only" forgets what he saw.</note>

# The First Letter of Saint Peter

---

<margin>I. 1</margin> Peter, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen strangers <note>original: "Fremdlingen" — also translated as exiles or sojourners; those living temporarily in a land not their own.</note> of the dispersion <note>original: "Zerstreuung" — referring to the Diaspora, or the scattering of believers across various regions.</note> in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithyn-
<margin>2</margin> [ia], according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: May grace and peace happen to you more and more.

<margin>3</margin> Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy—

->Annotations.<-

### Chapter I, 1. 2. Heading.

<margin>1</margin> **Strangers**) in regard to the heavenly fatherland. **Pontus etc.**) Peter was in Babylon, in the East, Chapter 5, 13. And from there, Pontus was the nearest province, then Galatia, etc. <note>The author assumes a geographical progression starting from Peter's location in "Babylon," which many scholars believe was a code name for Rome, though this commentator takes it literally as the Eastern city.</note>

<margin>2</margin> **God the Father == the Spirit == Jesus Christ**) Here, the mystery of the Holy Trinity is already being considered, and thereafter the text deals with the Father (v. 3, 15, 17, 21, 23), with Christ (v. 3, 7, 11, 13, 19; 2, 3), and with the Spirit (v. 11, 12, 22).
**Obedient**) this is faith.
**Sprinkling**) The believers are sprinkled with the blood of Jesus Christ. <note>A reference to ancient sacrificial rituals, here symbolizing the application of Christ’s sacrifice to the individual believer.</note>

> O God! give me grace and peace abundantly.

### Chapter I, 3-13. God has reborn us to a living hope: therefore, hope.

<margin>3</margin> **Praised == Mercy == Reborn == Resurrection == Inheritance**) This entire passage corresponds with what Paul writes in Ephesians 2:4 etc.

<vocab>Peter, Apostle, Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia, Knowledge, Sanctification, Spirit, Obedience, Sprinkling, Blood, Jesus Christ, Mercy, Trinity, Faith, Ephesians</vocab>

<summary>This page presents the opening salutation of 1 Peter, identifying the readers as "strangers" in various Roman provinces and explaining the theological foundation of their calling through the Holy Trinity. The commentary links the geographic order of the provinces to Peter's location and connects the passage to Pauline theology.</summary>

<margin>I.</margin> [mercy] has born us again <note>original: "wiedergebohren" — refers to the spiritual rebirth or regeneration of the believer.</note> to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
<margin>4</margin> to an imperishable, and undefiled, and unfading inheritance, which is kept in the heavens,
<margin>5</margin> for you, who are kept in the power of God through faith for salvation, which is ready to be revealed in the last time:
<margin>6</margin> in which you rejoice, you who now for a little while, if it must be, are grieved in manifold temptations, <margin>7</margin> so that your faith in its testing <note>original: "Bewährung" — the process of being proved or tried, like metal in a furnace.</note> might be found much more precious than perishable gold, which is tested through fire, unto praise and honor, and glory, in the revelation <note>original: "Entdeckung" — literally "discovery" or "uncovering," used here for the Second Coming or apocalypse of Christ.</note> of Jesus Christ: <margin>8</margin> Whom you have not known and yet love, whom you now do not see, and yet believe in him, and rejoice with an unspeakable and glorious joy, <margin>9</margin> and bring away the end of your faith, (namely) the salvation of souls. <margin>10</margin> For which salvation the prophets have sought and inquired, who prophesied of the grace that (would come) upon you,
<margin>11</margin> and inquired, at what or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ, who (was) in them, gave indication, when he testified beforehand of the sufferings: which (would come) to Christ, and the glories following them: <margin>12</margin> to whom it was revealed, that not to themselves, but to us—

---

**Born again**) From here until Chapter 2, verse 10, Peter reports what God has done for us, and from the treasures of salvation he derives the most powerful exhortations: to hope (v. 3-13), to sanctification and fear in faith (v. 14-21), and to love (v. 22 to ch. 2:10), where he then introduces the teaching of Christ in the most lovely manner.

**through**) verse 21.

**4 Kept**) the inheritance is kept, and the heirs are preserved (v. 5).

**5 God’s**) He is the one who does it. 1 Thessalonians 5:24, Matthew 19:26. Where else would we end up, before the adversary? 1 Peter 5:8.

**8 Lord Jesus!**) I do not yet know you by face: But I love you. Oh, the joy, as soon as I see you for the first time!

# I. Peter.

<margin>II. 18</margin> Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the <term>harsh</term><note>original: "ungeschlachten" — referring to masters who are difficult, perverse, or unfair.</note>. <margin>19</margin> For this is grace, if someone, for the sake of conscience toward God, endures grief while suffering unjustly. <margin>20</margin> For what kind of glory is it if, when you sin and are beaten with fists, you endure it patiently? But if you do good and suffer, and yet endure it patiently, this is grace with God. <margin>21</margin> For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us and left behind for you a <term>pattern</term><note>original: "Vorschrift" — literally a "writing-copy" or "template" used by students to learn to write; here, a model for living.</note>, so that you should follow in His footsteps. <margin>22</margin> He who committed no sin, nor was any deceit found in His mouth; <margin>23</margin> who, when He was reviled, did not revile in return; when He suffered, He did not threaten, but committed it to Him who judges righteously. <margin>24</margin> Who Himself lifted up our sins in His body onto <note>catchword: onto</note>

---

### Chap. 2, 18-25. Exhortation of Servants to Follow Christ.

**18 But also)** This presupposes that kind masters are served more willingly by their servants than harsh ones, unless the servants act specifically for the sake of conscience.
**19 Grace) v. 20.**
**For the sake of conscience toward God)** whether a servant's deed would be approved by any human or not. When a righteous person is not respected by people while doing good—receiving no approval, assistance, or thanks before or after, but instead bearing the contrary—it can bring much pain. But if one only stands well with God in their conscience, there is pure <term>sweetness</term><note>original: "Süssigkeit" — a common Pietist term for the inner peace and joy found in a relationship with God.</note>.
**21 Christ)** in the <term>form of a servant</term><note>original: "Knechtsgestalt" — a reference to Philippians 2:7, emphasizing that Christ's lowly status on earth makes Him a direct example for those in service.</note>.
**Left behind)** when He entered into His glory.
**23 Did not threaten)** He did not threaten regarding the future, although He acknowledged His future coming. Matthew 26:64. Threats are often the weapons of those who cannot defend themselves. Such people were the <term>slaves</term><note>original: "Sclaven" — the commentator uses this term to clarify the social status of the "Knechte" in the biblical era.</note>, who could have threatened their masters with divine judgment.
**24 Himself)** A master lets others do burdensome things; a servant must do them himself. Thus did Christ.

->Thanks be to You, great Priest, great Physician!<-

### II. Second Awakening of the Sincere Mind,
->wherein he:<-

1. exhorts fellow believers <term>Glaubensgenossen</term> <note>Literally "companions in faith," referring to the early Christian community.</note> that, as they are so abundantly equipped by God, they should apply all diligence toward growth in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ <margin>3</margin>
2. gives weight to the matter for them by presenting:
    1. the certainty of the true teachers <margin>12</margin>
    2. the wicked nature <term>Unart</term> <note>In this context, it refers to the corrupt character and behavior of those spreading false doctrines.</note> of the false teachers. <margin>II. 1-</margin>
3. protects them against the scoffers: wherein he
    1. refutes the scoffing. <margin>III. 1-</margin>
    2. describes the Final Day <term>jüngster Tag</term> <note>Literally "the youngest day," a traditional German term for the Day of Judgment or the Last Day.</note> with appropriate exhortations <margin>10</margin>

1. testifies to his and Paul's <note>original: "Pauli"</note> agreement. <margin>15</margin>
2. repeats the summary <term>Summa</term> <note>The main point or essence of the message.</note> of the letter. <margin>17</margin>

### The
# First Letter of John

In this presentation, the Apostle aims to ensure that the
blessed and holy fellowship <note>original: "Gemeinschaft"; refers to the spiritual communion or "koinonia" between the believer and the divine</note> of the believers
with God and Jesus Christ may be strengthened, and that
the marks of this state, which is so precious to
them, may be deeply imprinted upon them.

->There are three parts:<-

**I. Introduction, concerning the message of Christ and his Apostles, and of its**
1. Heavenly content. Chapter I. 1
2. Infallible certainty. 1, 2
3. Blessed purpose. 3

**II. Treatise** <note>original: "Abhandlung"; a systematic discussion of theological points</note>
1. Concerning God, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, in particular.
I. God is a pure light, verse 5.
Therefore, whoever wishes to have fellowship with Him must
1. Walk in the light. 6
2. Confess deviations <note>original: "Abweichungen"; literally "turnings away" or straying from the path</note> from the light. 8-

<meta>This page concludes the structural outline of the First Letter of St. John. It follows the previous page's discussion of the "Boldness of believers" (Chapter 5, verses 14-15) by providing the final points of the conclusion and a summary of the letter’s overall theological method.</meta>

header: Content of the First Letter of St. John.
sig: D

3. **Sealing of faith**: we know (as it is stated three times in succession <note>Referring to the repetition of "We know" in 1 John 5:18, 19, and 20, which provides the believer with finality and assurance.</note>) where we stand, in regard to:
    1. Sin.
    2. The world.
    3. Christ.
4. **Warning against idols.**

Each part consists of two elements: 1. what we have in God, and 2. how we should respond to Him <note>original: "ihm begegnen"; literally "to meet him," referring here to our conduct and spiritual stance toward the Creator</note>. From the first element, the second is always derived in the most refined manner—concerning love for God, the following of Christ, and brotherly love. And although it might seem to us that many things are repeated without order, they are nevertheless derived in the most beautiful order, based on various grounds and from different perspectives, pointing toward the same **primary duties** <note>original: "Hauptpflichten"; the essential spiritual obligations that define the Christian life</note>.

# First Letter of St. John.
---

<margin>I.</margin>
<margin>1</margin>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of Life: <margin>2</margin> and the life was made manifest <note>The author uses physical sensory language—hearing, seeing, touching—to emphasize that Jesus was a real human being, countering early heresies that claimed he was only a spirit.</note>, and we have seen it, and bear witness, and proclaim to you the life, which is eternal, which was with the Father, and was made manifest to us: <margin>3</margin> that which we have seen and heard we proclaim to you, so that you also may have fellowship with us: and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ: <margin>4</margin> and these things we write to you, so that your joy may be fulfilled.

<margin>5</margin> And this is the message which we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is a light, and in him is no darkness at all.
<margin>6</margin> If we say that we have fellowship with him, and we walk in darkness, then we lie, and do <note>The sentence is interrupted here at the end of the page; it likely concludes on the next page with "not the truth."</note>

->Commentary.<-

->**Chapter 2, 13–27. We, according to all stages of life, have everything in Him.**<-

<margin>13 I write)</margin> Those whom he generally calls "little children," he now divides into three classes according to age, and addresses here the fathers, the young men, and the children specifically with the phrase: "I write to you." Afterward, he makes a repetition to each class in this same order with these same titles—you fathers, you young men, you children—and with the phrase "I have written to you": verse 14, and again verses 14–17, and verses 18–21, 26, 27, until after completing the special address to these three classes, he gathers the "little children" together again in verse 28. The fathers were those who had already been in the world when the Son of God walked on earth. The young men were mean- <note>The German "indes-" is the start of "indessen" (meanwhile), to be continued on the next page.</note>

### V.

necessary to write to you by way of exhortation, that you should fight for the faith which was once delivered to the

---

<margin>3</margin> **To write to you**) in general.
**By way of exhortation**) in particular. The holy Apostle considers this the most necessary form of writing at this time.
<margin>7</margin> **Lie before our eyes**) The cities were not located in, but rather along the Dead Sea.
**A pattern of eternal fire**) The fire with which the sinful cities were destroyed was soon extinguished, but the fire, of which that one was a pattern <note>original: "Muster"; meaning a physical example or type of a spiritual reality</note>, is eternal.
<margin>8</margin> **These dreamers**) Through this single word, the nature of the natural man is very powerfully expressed. To a dreamer, it is as if he sees and hears many things; he has desire, joy, anxiety, fear, and the like. However, he cannot govern himself in it; rather, as one image in a dream arises from another, so it is with such people. Therefore, with all their reason, they cannot imagine that the children of Light enjoy a true freedom, as those who have awakened in the Light.

Chapters II, III.

->Notes.<-
->Chapter I, 1 - 3. Title of the Book.<-

**Unveiling)** Regarding this precious prophecy, I published a specific explanation in the year 1740, which I cannot regret having done. Whoever wishes to make use of it is free to do so. In this place, we shall make it all the more brief.

**2 has testified)** following this very command, in this very book.

**3 Blessed)** Let no one be talked out of this blessedness, more and more as time goes on.

> Jesus Christ, make me a partaker of this blessedness.

**3 the time)** of the coming of the Lord.

->Chapter I, 4 - 6. Heading and Greeting.<-

**4. 5 from = and from = and from)** Testimony of the Holy Trinity <note>original: "H. Dreyeinigkeit"; abbreviation for "Heiligen Dreyeinigkeit." The tripartite "from" refers to the Father, the Seven Spirits (Holy Spirit), and Jesus Christ.</note>.

> Grace and peace prevail over all congregations and saints.

<margin>11</margin> *who were to be killed)* in more recent times.
> Lord *Jesus*, the number of those who are to be slaughtered for your name's sake is not yet complete. Help those who are still to come to also make it through.

->*Cap. 6, 12-17.* Sixth Seal.<-

<margin>12</margin> *Earthquake)* This is not the end of the world itself. For only afterward follows the seventh seal, and under it many great things: also, this is not a preceding different judgment over the enemies, who will only be mentioned later: rather, an instantaneous terror and an anxious waiting for the end of all things is struck into the wretched dead here, just as in the previous seal the souls under the altar were given to know through grace where they stood.
It begins with the earth, as in *Chapter 20, 11.*
<margin>15</margin> *hid themselves)* Where now is the fearlessness of those who were so greatly feared in the world?
<margin>17</margin> *Who?)* those who are saved from the coming wrath and stand in the fellowship of the Lamb.
> Lord *Jesus*, the very love that you have for righteousness is a wrath against the unrighteous. Grant that I may experience your love as love, and not as wrath.

And after this I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds, so that no wind should blow over the earth, nor over the sea, nor over any tree. <margin>1</margin>

And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, who had a seal of the living God, and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, <margin>2</margin>

and said: Harm not the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we seal the servants of our God on their foreheads. <margin>3</margin>

<meta>catchword: tribe</meta>

->Chapter 7, 1-8. The sealing of the servants of God against the impending plagues.<-

**2** from the rising of the sun) Thus the plagues proceeded from the East <note>original: "Morgen"—which can mean both "morning" and "the East" in older German</note>.

to harm) by holding back the wind <note>the lack of wind was viewed as a judgment that could lead to stagnation or the death of crops</note>.

the earth and the sea) Here the trees are understood to be included. The earth is Asia, the sea Europe, the rivers (Chapter 8, 10) and the trees Africa <note>the commentator is applying a symbolic geography to the text, mapping the biblical imagery onto the then-known continents</note>.

**3** > Great God! How well off your servants are. When everything is damaged, they are protected. Let me be commended to you!

**4** 144 thousand) There were not 145 or 143, but 144 thousand: therefore, the 12 thousand for each tribe are to be taken quite literally.

Out of all tribes) Thus Dan is not entirely excluded, but because he became so thin <note>original: "dünne"—referring to the tribe becoming small or diminished in number</note>, he is tucked under the others: whereas Levi moves back in, and Joseph receives two parts, one for himself and one for Manasseh.

The brothers on the mother's side are paired together. Only Naphtali and Manasseh were not so closely related to each other: from which it is to be inferred that Dan, the brother of Naphtali, is included under this pair.

### Chap. 20, 1-3. The Thousand-Year Imprisonment of Satan.

**1 And)** Following the defeat of the beast and the false prophet, the imprisonment of Satan thus follows.

**3 Great God!** restrain the deception of the heathens until the enemy is entirely locked away in the abyss.

**A short time)** This short time begins no later than the thousand-year reign of those of the first resurrection. One must remain within the order of the prophecy. The great things of the final times are described very briefly: but one must not, for that reason, pass over them too quickly.

## Section I,

# Mr. Dr. Heumann’s Preface to the second part of his translation of the New Testament, 1748.

Concerning my new translation of the Revelation
of John, Mr. Dr. Heumann <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764) was a prominent German Lutheran theologian whose translation of the New Testament was a major scholarly work of the era.</note> writes the fol-
lowing: “From this translation I have
“improved my own in several pas-
“sages. Otherwise, however, it is
“distinguished from mine in two respects.
“First, Mr. Bengel <note>Johann Albrecht Bengel (1687–1752), the author of the work being discussed, was a pioneer in "textual criticism"—the science of comparing ancient manuscripts to find the most accurate original wording of the Bible.</note> has, in his edition of the
“Greek New Testament, altered the text in many places according to
“several manuscripts, and has also brought these
“changes into his translation: I, on the other hand,
“follow the common Greek text <note>The "common text" refers to the Textus Receptus, which was the standard version used for most Bibles since the Reformation, despite containing some known errors from later manuscript traditions.</note> in my transla-
“tion, partly because a translation of this very text is
“requested by Bible readers, and partly because I believe,
“along with the late Mr. Wolf <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739) was a contemporary scholar who often disagreed with Bengel's methods, preferring to stick closer to traditional readings.</note>, that the majority of the...

<summary>This page introduces a scholarly dialogue regarding Johann Albrecht Bengel's 18th-century translation of the Book of Revelation. It specifically quotes Dr. Heumann, who explains the differences between his own traditional translation and Bengel’s more radical approach of correcting the Greek text using ancient manuscripts.</summary>
<keywords>Christoph August Heumann, Johann Albrecht Bengel, Johann Christoph Wolf, New Testament, Book of Revelation, translation, textual criticism, Greek manuscripts</keywords>

--- Page 1086 ---
<meta>This page continues the debate between Dr. Christoph August Heumann and Johann Albrecht Bengel regarding the translation and textual criticism of the New Testament, specifically the Book of Revelation. Bengel is defending his decision to depart from the standard Greek text of his day in favor of readings found in older, more authoritative manuscripts.</meta>

<header>Appendix, Section I,</header>

“...[whether the] changes made by the Lord Abbot <note>Johann Albrecht Bengel (1687–1752) was a Prelate and Abbot in the Lutheran church; Heumann refers to him by this title.</note> were even necessary. Secondly, I have striven for the purity of our [German] language; the Lord Abbot, on the other hand, has seen fit to stay as close as possible to the Greek words. Thus, in his version, at Chapter 1, verse 7, etc.” The examples which Mr. Dr. Heumann cites here, we will examine later; and meanwhile, I reply:

I. That I have not changed the Greek text based only on a few manuscripts. I have followed other printed editions, many Greek manuscripts, ancient translators <note>Ancient versions of the Bible such as the Latin Vulgate, Syriac, or Coptic.</note>, and the Church Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians whose writings often quoted the earliest versions of the biblical text.</note>, so that I always had before me the closest antiquity following the Apostles. In doing so, I generally had the consensus of the majority <note>original: "Majora", referring to the majority of manuscript witnesses</note>, and sometimes even the unanimous <note>original: "Unanimia", referring to when all ancient witnesses agree</note> testimony (if certain scholars would finally wake up amidst such a highly renowned brilliance of flourishing sciences and listen to my explanation, which is understandable even to a beginner). I allow their testimony to stand, not according to an arbitrary whim in individual passages, but according to consistent principles. 

See Revelation 1:11, 5:14, 6:11, 11:8, 15, 17, 12:8, 15:8, [chapter] 16, 21:24, 22:6, 11. Regarding these passages, one should weigh the evidence for and against <note>original: "pro & contra"</note> in my critical apparatus <note>original: "Apparatum"; this refers to Bengel’s scholarly list of manuscript variations.</note> on pages 791–856, and at the same time consider, on page 776 of the same work <note>original: "ibid."</note>, the small number of apocalyptic manuscripts <note>Manuscripts of the Book of Revelation were historically rarer than those of the Gospels or Paul's letters.</note> available to correctly identify the majority consensus. Such improvements are then genuine, and therefore necessary (Rev. 22:18), and also sometimes very important, as my German explanation and my *Gnomon* <note>Bengel’s *Gnomon Novi Testamenti* (1742) was a famous commentary that aimed to point out the natural sense of the words like a "pointer" or sundial needle.</note> show here and there. That I have also brought these changes, with correct punctuation <note>original: "Interpunctionibus"</note>, into my translation is dear and pleasing to many. 

Mr. Dr. Heumann insists that one should apply the abundant aids of modern times, which one has in the study of Scripture, toward a good new translation, and thereby promote the common edification. One must, then, above all else, use such a rich supply for a truly precise revision of the original text...

...to make use [of these resources] (since previously, during the preparation of the Greek text commonly in print to this day, so few aids were available), and then further to apply the same wisely toward an accurate translation. Without a pure original text <term>Grundtext: the source-language text used as the basis for a translation</term>, the entire art of interpretation—especially in the Book of Revelation—is greatly hindered in its usefulness. No Bible reader has any particular reason, and to my knowledge none considers themselves to have reason, why they should demand a translation based on the common Greek text—seeing how it departs from the first apostolic hand and simultaneously often from Luther’s translation (for example, Revelation 11:1, 13:5, and elsewhere; Luke 7:11, Hebrews 9:1, etc.); although, if someone has such a desire, it has now been fulfilled by Dr. Heumann <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764), a contemporary scholar and critic of Bengel</note> to such an extent that I can all the more remain with my translation, which is arranged according to the purity of the ancient text.

*Wolf’s Studies* <note>original: "Wolfii Curæ," referring to Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739) and his work "Curæ Philologicæ et Criticæ"</note> display a rich erudition and occasionally offer a sound decision; however, not everything within them is exhausted, and not everything is beyond improvement. In the aforementioned *Gnomon* <note>Bengel’s famous "Gnomon Novi Testamenti" (1742), a commentary intended to "point the way" to the meaning of the text</note>, those who appreciate it will find—not to boast—quite a few new exegetical <term>exegetical: related to the critical explanation or interpretation of a text</term> tools. That *Wolf* has too much of a fondness for the most common Greek readings is shown with solid examples by Mr. *Johann David Michaëlis* in his *Annotations on George Benson’s Exegesis of the Epistle of James, pp. 114, 128.* Furthermore, shortly after my Greek New Testament was published, his *Observations on the Apocalypse of St. John* <note>original: "Curæ in Apocalypsin S. Joannis"</note> were released; meanwhile, that learned man was so occupied with *Libanius, Photius, etc.* <note>Ancient Greek writers and theologians; Wolf was a prolific editor of classical and patristic texts</note> that he could not consider my *Arguments* <note>original: "Rationes"</note>. Those who now cite him against me could and should know and report that all his objections were refuted in my *Gnomon*, and some additional points were addressed in the response regarding the Greek New Testament. Yet *Wolf* still often agrees with me, and not with Dr. Heumann. Revelation 14:1, 12; 15:3; 16:5, 7; 19:17; 20:12; 22:19, etc.

# Appendix, Section I,

II. Regarding the Greek words, I have remained as close [to the original] as possible: and I have applied myself to the purity of our language <note>German</note>, so far as it could be done without detriment to the subject matter, which is of far greater importance. For the free exercise of a pure language, we otherwise have enough opportunities. Dr. Heumann <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764), a German theologian and contemporary of Bengel</note> notes quite well in the preface to the first part of his translation the difference between the pure language of the ancient Greeks and that which was spoken with "Jewish tongues" <note>A reference to the Hebraic influence on the Greek used by the New Testament writers</note>. For whoever believes with Pfochen <note>Sebastian Pfochen (1597–1650), a scholar who famously argued that the Greek of the New Testament was pure, classical Attic Greek rather than a dialect influenced by Hebrew</note> that the purest and best Greek is to be found in all places of the New Testament, and that nowhere has a Hebrew idiom been expressed with Greek words—he will (says Dr. Heumann) not only take on a vain effort to prove such a thing but also misunderstand many a passage. Just as the Greek writing style of the New Testament has a great similarity with the source language of the Old Testament <note>Hebrew</note>, so too should our German writing style be arranged according to the source language of the New Testament, so that the powerful impression the Apostles had of heavenly things and the expression in our translations might harmonize beautifully, without any overly forced purity.

Now I wish to explain the examples cited by Dr. Heumann.

Chapter I, verse 7: **Every eye shall see Him.** In the Greek, it could just as well have said, **All eyes**: and since it says, **Every eye** <note>original: "alles Auge" (singular)</note>, this may not be a matter of indifference. One also says: **Every mouth, every order, every people**, etc., and Dr. Heumann translates James 1:17: **from the Father of every light.**

**Chapter IV. 4:** **Twenty four thrones** etc. In compound numbers, the larger is sometimes spoken before the smaller. <note>In 18th-century German, "four and twenty" was the standard way to say 24; Bengel is explaining why the word order might vary.</note>

**Chapter XVIII. 2:** **Of every unclean spirit** etc. This is treated the same as **every eye**.

In these passages, the translation is nowhere unclear, and the linguistic purity, hopefully, still holds up.

Perhaps a bit less would have sufficed to satisfy Dr. Heumann <note>Christoph August Heumann, a contemporary critic who advocated for more modern, "purer" German in biblical translations.</note>: yet it will likely not displease him that I have illuminated these two points somewhat more extensively for the benefit of inexperienced readers.

Otherwise, in the aforementioned other preface, it is called a great oversight that in some new editions of the Greek New Testament, the *signum interrogationis* <note>original: "signum interrogationis" (Latin for "question mark")</note> has been omitted in Romans 9:22, 23. Such a *signum interrogationis* was introduced by Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a successor to Calvin whose Greek New Testament was highly influential.</note>, whereas other editions, both older and newer, including my own, have omitted it. The learned man whom Beza cites is Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574), a leading German classical scholar of the Reformation.</note>: but the latter places no interrogation, and when others, also in Wolf's *curis* <note>original: "Wolfii curis," referring to Johann Christoph Wolf’s "Curae Philologicae et Criticae," a standard scholarly commentary of the era.</note>...

### II.

In translating the Greek words, I have remained as close as possible to the original; I have also striven for the purity of our own language, provided it could be done without detracting from the subject matter, which is of far greater importance. We have plenty of other opportunities for the free exercise of a "pure" style. *Dr. Heumann* <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764) was a notable German theologian and contemporary of Bengel who published his own translation of the New Testament.</note> quite rightly notes in the preface to the first part of his translation the distinction between the pure language of the ancient Greeks and that which was spoken with "Jewish tongues" <note>This refers to Hellenistic or Koine Greek as used by Jewish writers, which often incorporated Hebrew idioms (Hebraisms).</note>. For whoever believes, along with *Pfochenius* <note>Sebastian Pfochen (1597–1638) was a scholar who argued that the Greek of the New Testament was as "pure" and classical as that of Homer or Demosthenes.</note>, that the purest and best Greek is to be found in all parts of the New Testament, and that no Hebrew manner of speaking was ever expressed with Greek words—such a person (says *Dr. Heumann*) will not only labor in vain to prove this, but will also misunderstand many passages. Just as the Greek style of the *New Testament* has a great similarity to the original language of the *Old Testament*, so should our German style be modeled after the original language of the *New Testament*. This ensures that the powerful impression the Apostles had of heavenly things and the expression in our translations harmonize beautifully, without any overly forced linguistic purity.

->Now I wish to explain the examples cited by *Dr. Heumann*.<-

We also say: **Every mouth, every order, all people,** <term>etc.</term> <note>original: "ꝛc." (an abbreviation for etcetera)</note> and Dr. Heumann himself translates *James I. 17*: **from the Father of every light.** <note>Bengel is defending his use of the singular "every eye" (singular) rather than "all eyes" (plural) by showing it is a common biblical idiom and that even his critic, Heumann, uses similar phrasing elsewhere.</note>
