# Clarification of Various Passages, etc.

I have become aware of what the famous jurist, Johann Schilter <note>original: "Jo. Schilterus"; a noted German jurist and historian (1632–1705)</note>, wrote regarding the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> and attached to his work *Concerning the Liberty of the German Church* <note>original Latin: "de Libert. eccl. Germ."</note>. I agree with him on many main points. I will not mention other interpreters at this time. Thus, my explanation cannot be filled with many recent opinions. Rather, on the most prominent points, I have demonstrated my agreement with older, proven interpreters, even where one might not suspect it. Regarding the specific way in which I advocate only for pure Millennialism <term>Millennialism</term> <note>original Latin: "Chiliasmo"; the belief in a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth</note> and no other, see the *Supplement* <note>original: "Nachlese"</note>: pages 1107–1116 and the *Confirmed Testimony of the Truth* page 2, etc. The rest of what the *Early-Gathered Fruits* <note>original: "Früh-aufgelesene Früchten"; a contemporary theological journal critical of Bengel</note> brought against my explanation of Revelation is answered in the *Supplement* on pages 780–782.

In the year 1745, I published nothing but the aforementioned Answer and the *Cycle* <note>likely referring to his work on biblical chronology</note>. In the following year, the *Age of the World* <note>original: "Welt-Alter"</note> was added, the preface of which dates back to 1745. I hold nothing for excessive brooding: and I also do not know what occasion I [might have given] in the three recently mentioned writings to any—

# Illumination of Several Passages, etc. 955

I have become aware of what the famous jurist, Johann Schilter <note>Johann Schilter (1632–1705) was a prominent German legal scholar whose interest in church law led him to study biblical prophecy</note>, has written concerning the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, which he appended to his work *On the Liberties of the German Church* <note>original: "de Libert. eccl. Germ."</note>. I agree with him on many fundamental points. I shall not mention other interpreters at this time. Thus, my explanation cannot be filled with many modern opinions. Rather, on the most prominent points, I have demonstrated my agreement with older, proven interpreters, even where one might not expect it. Regarding the particular manner in which I advocate only for pure <term>Millennialism</term> <note>original: "Chiliasmo"; from the Greek 'chilias' (a thousand), the belief in a future 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth. Bengel distinguished his "pure" biblical view from radical political or fanatical versions.</note>, and no other kind, one may consult the *Supplement*: pages 1107-1116, and the *Confirmed Testimony of the Truth*, page 2 and following. The rest of what the authors of the *Early-Gathered Fruits* <note>A reference to the journal "Frühaufgelesene Früchte," which published critiques of contemporary theological works</note> have brought against my *Exposition of the Revelation* is answered in the *Supplement*, pages 780-782.

->§ 3.<-

In the collection of *Old and New* <note>Referring to the "Acta Historico-Ecclesiastica," a journal often abbreviated as "A. and N." for "Alte und Neue Nachrichten" (Old and New News)</note> for the year 1746, the beginning is formed by a short summary of church history for the year 1745. There, it is said of me: **"He has sought to assist the Millennialist cause among us, and has otherwise given many people cause for excessive brooding:"** which is then labeled an **offense** in the fourth index of that year's volume. My answer: If the proportions in the short summaries of church history from previous years required devoting a few lines to my own insignificance, then something could have been mentioned that I (I speak without self-love) have received through grace, and which I have in common with neither Millennialists nor brooders. In the year 1745, I published nothing other than the aforementioned answer and the *Cycle* <note>original: "Cyclum"; likely referring to his "Cyclus sive de anno mundi," a work on biblical chronology</note>. The following year, the *Age of the World* <note>original: "Welt-Alter"</note> was added, though its preface dates back to 1745. I hold no stock in excessive brooding: and I also do not know what cause I might have given anyone in these three mentioned writings—

# Appendix, Part II. Illumination etc. 956

...should have given cause for such excess. The response concerns the original text of the New Testament, where no degree of care can ever be too exact. From the *Cycle* <note>Referring to a scholarly collection or circular publication</note>, the collection promised its readers manifold benefits. My work *The Age of the World* <note>Bengel’s *Das Welt-Alter* (1741), where he calculated the chronology of human history based on the Bible</note> had to rebuff an attack made by the collection in the postscript of the preface; but there was nothing there to brood over. In the sum total of the years of the Old Testament, it concerned five hundred and fifty years <note>original: "sechsthalb Jahrhunderte"; an archaic German expression meaning five and a half centuries</note>. 

The teaching of the thousand years, found in Revelation 20, which is not pleasing to these teachers, is now labeled by them more as "fanatical millennialism" <term>Chiliasterey</term> <note>A derogatory term used by 18th-century critics to equate millennial beliefs with radical or dangerous fanaticism</note> than as "millennialism" <term>Chiliasmus</term> <note>From the Greek 'chilias' (a thousand), the theological study of Christ’s future reign</note>. I have nothing to do with fanatical millennialism; but, as previously stated, I hold constantly to pure millennialism. It is not necessary, however, for me to be the first to try and rescue that doctrine, for others complain that almost everything is now flooded with millennialism (see *The Age of the World*, page 267). The opposition to the truth in this matter, which is heard almost exclusively from this collection, will not succeed in reviving "anti-millennialism." Why is it, then, that these teachers mention me so often regarding millennialism, yet never specifically <note>original: "in specie"</note> indicate where I am supposedly in error, despite my frank challenges <note>original: "Provocationen"</note>? They can bring forward nothing of substance; I say this to the glory of God. One should simply take heed if something regarding this should appear again in the future; but in light of the current situation, one should also examine my writings.

# The Third Section,
## Where the total of the 480 years in 1 Kings 6:1 is brought together from individual scriptural numbers.

-> § 1. <-

In the second part of the *Additions to World History*, published in the year 1748, there appeared a treatise by Mr. *Johann George Walther* <note>Johann Georg Walther (1708–1761), a German jurist and historian</note>, a counselor to the Saxon court and a professor at *Wittenberg*, regarding the period of time between the departure of the *Israelites* from *Egypt* <note>The Exodus</note> and the construction of *Solomon’s* Temple. In that work, many interpretations—including well-known recent and erroneous ones—of the primary passage in 1 Kings 6:1 <note>This verse explicitly states that Solomon began building the Temple in the 480th year after the Israelites left Egypt</note> are thoroughly refuted; at the same time, however, several points are modestly raised against my own opinion regarding the 480 years in this scriptural passage.

-> § 2. <-

We both agree on the 480 years themselves, as well as their beginning in the year 3217 of the *Julian Period* <term>Julian Period</term> <note>A chronological system proposed by Joseph Scaliger in 1583 that combines various calendar cycles to create a continuous count of years; year 3217 JP corresponds to 1497 BCE</note>. I can certainly accept a correction in the summing up of the smaller numbers—from which the total of 480 years is composed—without any detriment to the scriptural timeline, and thus with good satisfaction, whether such a correction comes from me or from others.

-> § 3. <-

The Counselor and Professor adheres to my *Order of Times* <note>original: "Ordinem temporum"; referring to Bengel's 1741 work *Ordo Temporum*</note>, but he has not seen my *The Age of the World* <note>Bengel's *Das Welt-Alter*</note>, in which I had improved several points. Now, regarding what pertains to the former and not the latter of these two writings, I do not wish to say much. It will be better if I compare *The Age of the World* and this learned man’s treatise with one another; in doing so, I shall defend the former rather than completely examine the latter.

### § 6.

When all the specific yearly figures in the text are totaled, my table results in not only 480 years, but an additional 73 years; according to Mr. Walther's calculation (p. 317), it is not just 73, but more than 120 years over the limit. Therefore, the number 480 cannot be maintained as it should be, unless one treats a portion of the years—which are reported twice—as referring to the same period of time. The Councilor calls this a *synchronism* <term>synchronism: a method in chronology where two different historical events or periods are shown to have occurred at the same time</term>: and according to him, such a synchronism occurs in the middle of the 480 years, whereas in my system, it occurs after the beginning and before the end of that period.

### § 7.

I have demonstrated my arrangement in both of the aforementioned writings, as well as in the *Confirmed Testimony of the Truth*, and I will now summarily present and briefly resolve the difficulties which the Councilor brings against it on pages 330–337.

1) “In an *era* <note>original: "Aera"</note> or sequence of years, the chronological progression of years must be of a uniform nature.” Answer: In a long era, it does not matter what the nature of its individual parts may be, as long as the end of the preceding piece and the beginning of the following piece connect. In every *Olympiad* <note>original: "Olympiade"; a four-year period used by the ancient Greeks for dating</note>, three years had no competitive games and one year did. In the *Era of Nabonassar* <term>Era of Nabonassar: a chronological era starting in 747 BCE, used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy to track celestial events across different reigns</term>, the Egyptian years are uniform (just as the natural years are uniform in my table), and yet it contains *interregnums* <note>original: "Interregna"; periods between the reign of one ruler and the next</note>, and otherwise includes Assyrian, Median, Persian, Greek, Egyptian, and Roman governments. The variation of the histories within the 480 years should surprise no one; indeed, it is quite instructive. The first year of the Exodus from Egypt stands by itself: and so do the five years during which the land was conquered. Following that is the 200-year period of rest for the land,

Since *Israel* did not know how to conduct themselves in such noble freedom, the people—after *Abimelech’s* unrest—had to be kept in check without interruption by either a judge, or by servitude, or by both at once, until God, in His anger, even gave them a king. The *era* <note>original: "Aera"</note> or sequence of years from the Creation has many more variations.

2) “How is it possible to believe that the “intention of Scripture was to intermingle the years of “servitude and the years of rest?” *Answer:* It is not servitude, but rather war and bloodshed that are the opposite of the quietness of the land <term>quietness of the land: a state of peace and rest (Hebrew: 'shahat') mentioned frequently in the Book of Judges</term>. Now, in those 200 years, there were hardly any battles—specifically when *Eglon* defeated the people of *Israel*, and *Israel* defeated the *Moabites*; when *Barak* overcame *Sisera*; and when *Gideon* put the *Midianites* to flight. The years of servitude were indeed distinguished to a certain extent from the remaining years of the quietness of the land (just as the 40 days of rain are distinguished from the other days of the 150-day Great Flood <note>original: "Sündfluth"</note> until its subsiding). However, they also create a contrast for that same period (since in most places things were good and quiet, while in a few others it was occasionally idolatrous and restless) against the preceding military operations under *Joshua* (where entire nations were annihilated and so many cities burned). In contrast, under the periods of servitude, people were neither killed in such numbers nor was a single city devastated; it only involved a tribute or the loss of crops for this or that harvest year. This also contrasts with the stricter times that followed, when one judge immediately succeeded another, not without even heavier periods of servitude.

### Appendix, Section III, 962

3) “The span of years during which the **Ark of the Covenant** was in **Kiriath-jearim** cannot be reconciled with the idea that only 20 years passed from its arrival there until the time of **David**.” *Answer:* According to the word <gloss>Hebrew: *vajehi*</gloss> “and it came to pass,” the event itself is specifically indicated by the verb that immediately follows: and thus, the arrival of the Ark at **Kiriath-jearim** was followed by many days—namely, the 20 years which are the measure of time for the Ark’s stay in **Kiriath-jearim** until it was finally taken away again. 1 Samuel 7:2. The lamenting of the children of **Israel**, which is mentioned immediately thereafter, could have occurred at the beginning of those 20 years or at the end of them, according to the grammatical accents. However, that it happened at the beginning is taught by: (1) The emphatic *He* <note>The Hebrew definite article 'H'</note> in <gloss>Hebrew: *hajjamim*</gloss> “the days,” which refers and relates back to the Ark’s stay in **Kiriath-jearim**. (2) The expression itself, since it does not say thereafter "and in the twentieth year" (compare Judges 14:17; 1 Kings 20:29; Esther 4:16; 5:1), but rather states from the outset, **And all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD.** (3) The entire course of 1 Samuel 7; indeed, the whole history of **Samuel**, **Saul**, and **David**. **Samuel** certainly did not leave the office of judge vacant for 20 whole years after **Eli's** death (verse 6), as the people, since the time of **Gideon**, were never meant to remain entirely without a bridle. **Samuel** judged **Israel** all the days of his life (verse 15)—not exactly from his infancy, but certainly from the death of **Eli** the judge until he himself died; in which sense it is also said that the hand of the **LORD** was against the **Philistines** all the days of **Samuel** (verse 13). The reason why, in the case of **Samuel** alone among all the judges, no specific number of years of rest or years of judging is expressed, is this: because the years of **Samuel** and **Saul** are entirely contained within the 20 years of the Ark at **Kiriath-jearim**. In my *Order of Times* <note>original: "Ordine temporum," referring to Bengel's work *Ordo Temporum*</note> I placed the conclusion of the 20 years at the death of **Saul**, but in the *World-Age* <note>likely referring to his chronological tables</note> I placed it at the removal of the Ark from **Kiriath-jearim**. ## Regarding the passages 1 Kings 6:1, Acts 13:20, etc.

20 years will not deviate far from the exact truth.

The sum of **b** and **c** gives 3 years (see <note>original: *Ord. temp.*</note> *Order of Times*, p. 98) and the sum of **e** and **f** gives 8 years and 10 months: for entry **a**, approximately 8 years remain, and for entry **d**, a few months remain to fill the 20 years. Thus, from the death of **Eli** and the arrival of the Ark at **Kiriath-jearim** (or from the start of **Samuel’s** office as judge) until his death, there are 11 to 12 years; and from the start of **Saul’s** reign until his death, there are roughly three and a half years <note>The German "vierthalb" literally means "the fourth half," which is a traditional way of saying three and a half.</note>. This division shall now be further proven; however, we wish to address the following **difficulty** alongside it.

4) “Samuel lived many years before Saul became king, and also afterward.” *Answer:* In the <note>original: *Ordine temporum*</note> *Order of Times*, I indeed ascribed too few years of life to **Samuel**. An improvement was necessary here, which was sufficiently achieved within the overall Age of the World <note>A reference to the *Anno Mundi* or total timeline of biblical history.</note> by placing his birth long before the beginning of **Eli's** judgeship, without extending his years in office. Before **Samuel’s** birth, in 1 Samuel 1:9, **Eli** is explicitly thought of as a priest, and not yet as a judge.

<meta>This page continues the chronological analysis of the early Israelite monarchy, specifically addressing the conflicting timelines provided by the historian Josephus and the biblical account regarding the reigns of Samuel and Saul.</meta>

<page-num>964</page-num>
<header>Appendix, Section III,</header>

[In **Josephus**, Samuel alone is credited with 12 years; then 18 years are assigned to him and Saul together; and 22 years to Saul alone. To maintain that Saul reigned for 40 years (a total that does not actually appear in **Josephus**), **Mr. Walther** <note>Likely Johann Georg Walther, a contemporary scholar of biblical chronology.</note> reads these last two figures as 38 and 2. If one wishes to seek traces of the truth in **Josephus**, the most significant point may be that he attributes 12 years to Samuel. He may have had a record from the ancient **Hebrews** regarding Samuel's 12 years and misunderstood it, as those 12 years represent the time from the start of his office as judge <note>The "Judge" was the title for Israel's leaders before the era of kings.</note> until Samuel’s death, rather than just until the appointment of a king. It is also possible that eighteen months were originally attributed to the rejected King Saul, which in **Josephus** became eighteen years for Samuel and Saul together. We shall abide by the Scripture.]

Saul reigned for 2 years (1 Samuel 13:1). Within those 2 years, all the good royal deeds occurred which are recounted in 1 Samuel 10:26–27, 11:6–15, 13:4, and 14:47–48. However, when he did not obey the voice of the **LORD** in the campaign against the **Amalekites**, he was rejected. Samuel mourned for him; yet he had to break off the royal mourning—which therefore did not last 30 days (compare Deuteronomy 34:8)—and anoint David as king without further delay. At that point, Saul was "put away" and David was "raised up" (Acts 13:22; compare 1 Samuel 13:14). Consequently, the 2 years that Saul was king and the 40 years mentioned in Acts 13:21 share the same end point. When Saul perished, David was only 30 years old: and yet David was already called a "man of war" (1 Samuel 16:18) as soon as Saul became melancholic, even before he directed his hatred toward David. Thus, the 40 years in Acts 13:21 began long before Saul’s accession to the throne; and the words stating that God gave Saul to the people who desired a king for 40 years do not align <note>The author is arguing that the 40-year period mentioned in the New Testament refers to a broader era of transition, rather than the literal length of Saul's individual reign.</note>

### § 10.

Now that which Mr. Walther explicitly raised against my *Order of Times* <note>original: "Ordinem temporum," the title of Bengel’s major chronological work published in 1741.</note> has been answered; but it will not be unhelpful if I compare our two arrangements a bit further.

1) Regarding the 300 years of Jephthah in Judges 11:26: he [Walther] allows them neither to be expanded nor restricted, and indeed they are the main foundation of his <term>synchronisms</term> <note>original: "Synchronismi"—the method of aligning different historical timelines to see which events occurred simultaneously.</note>. See pages 402, 467. He counts 300 full years from the 2nd year of Joshua until the 17th year of the Ammonite servitude, so that, with 41 preceding and 138 subsequent years, they reach into the 480th year. However, these 17 years are deducted from the sum of 300, as the King of the children of Ammon wanted to seize what he claimed from Israel already at the beginning of the 18 years [of oppression]. In this manner, Mr. Walther arrives at 283 years for the 300, and I arrive at 254. Both his figure and mine could, in a dispute where the primary question was not one of exact chronology, be expressed as the round sum of three <term>centuries</term> <note>original: "Seculorum"</note>, for there were indeed two and a half <note>original: "dritthalb"—an old German expression for "two and a half" (literally: the third [unit] is only a half).</note> full centuries. One often says "one hour," even if about 10 minutes are missing. The more accurately a result emerges, the more welcome it should be to us; but in the absence of such precision, one should nevertheless allow an investigation to proceed in those areas that more properly belong to it.

# The Fourth Section,
## Concerning the Seventy Weeks,
### Daniel 9.

-> § 1. <-

Regarding the 70 weeks <note>A significant prophecy in Daniel 9:24–27, traditionally interpreted by Christians as a timeline leading to the arrival and death of the Messiah.</note>, Mr. **Dr. Benedict Gottlob Clauswitz** has authored a rich treatise. In it, he cited my *Order of Times* <note>original: *Ordinem temporum*</note> and *World Age* <note>Referring to the author's previously published chronological works.</note>, specifically concerning this important scripture passage. He did so with a modest disagreement, but even more so with thorough approval. The treatise consists of 10 sections, of which the first five were incorporated by Mr. **Dr. Siegmund Jacob Baumgarten** into the first part of the *Additions to General World History*, and the last five into the second part. I examined the first half of this treatise in the so-called *Testimony of the Truth*, pages 127–143; the other half, however, was only released after this *Testimony*, though it was undoubtedly printed before it. It is therefore regrettable that this truth-loving teacher did not see the aforementioned *Testimony* before concluding his own treatise. ### § 5.

First, one should weigh the Books of Ezra and Nehemiah and compare them both against the text of the 70 weeks. Ezra Chapter 7:10 deals with the 7th year of <term>Artaxerxes (Arthasastha): a king of the Persian Empire; scholars often debate whether this refers to Artaxerxes I or II</term>, and there the word "building" does not occur even once, though it appears so frequently in Chapters 1–6 under Cyrus and Darius, and in the Book of Nehemiah regarding the 20th year of Artaxerxes. In the main passage, Chapter 7:27, where Ezra summarizes the decree of the 7th year of Artaxerxes, he speaks only of the Temple and only of its beautification. Thus, sacred history gives us very little reason to suspect that the beginning of the 70 weeks occurred in the 7th year of this king. The King's letter to Ezra and Ezra’s entire mission presuppose a city already built, albeit without an outer wall, which Nehemiah built later. One may interpret the two expressions, "to restore and to build" and "it shall be restored and built," <note>original Hebrew: *lehaschib velibnoth* and *thaschub venibnetha*</note> in Daniel 9:25 as referring to rebuilding alone—following a Hebrew idiom <note>original Latin: *per Hebraismum*</note>—or as a general restoration and construction (the former interpretation being more certain). Nevertheless, the actual building (which is not found in the 7th year of Artaxerxes) cannot be separated from the rest of the city's restoration, nor from the start of the 70 weeks. Before <term>Johann Funck: a 16th-century German theologian who developed a prominent chronological system for Daniel’s prophecy</term>, there is no trace of any among the many ancient interpreters who thought to start the 70 weeks in the 7th year of Artaxerxes. The only exception is <term>Cedrenus: Georgius Cedrenus, an 11th-century Byzantine historian</term>, though in his work it is not the seventh but the eighth year of Artaxerxes that is mentioned, and this may have crept in as a scribal error for the twentieth, "H" for "K" <note>The author is noting a potential mistake in the Greek manuscript tradition where the letter Eta (H, representing 8) was written instead of Kappa (K, representing 20).</note>. For a prophecy that has been fulfilled for so long, this lack of historical precedent rightly brings the suspicion of an incorrect interpretation, even to those who do not bind the truth to human authority.

### § 6.

The discussion in Daniel 9:24 concerns weeks; and while "weeks of days" <note>original German: *Tagewochen*</note> are mentioned immediately afterward in Chapter 10:2, the 70 weeks are nonetheless not explicitly called "year-weeks" <note>original German: *Jahrwochen*; the author is highlighting that the text uses the general term for 'sevens' rather than a specific compound word for years.</note>.

Now, that which <term>Dr. Clauswitz: Benedikt Gottlieb Clauswitz (1707–1749), a Lutheran theologian who wrote extensively on the prophecies of Daniel</term> (for whom I have the highest respect) puts forward against my method of calculation refers to his 4th section, and specifically the 2nd basis of determination therein, which reads as follows:

And further: "A type of year that was otherwise customary in the Scriptures and among the Jews in Daniel’s time must be adopted for the further determination of these <term>year-weeks: a prophetic period where one 'week' represents seven years</term>."

On this basis of determination, Dr. Clauswitz builds almost everything in § 199 (pp. 75, 76) and § 209 (p. 132) that he brings against the 2nd year of Darius and in favor of the 7th year of Artaxerxes. I, however, have only slightly expanded this same basis of determination in my *Testimony* (pp. 130–136) and formulated it thus:

> "The entire span of time between the beginning and the end of the 70 weeks must be able to be conveniently divided into 70 equal parts, each of which revolves around the number seven, either simply or manifoldly."

By virtue of this expansion—which is justified in that same place—and the indication of "weeks" rather than "year-weeks" in the text, caution requires that one should not accept "pure year-weeks" as a settled matter at the start of the investigation, nor in its progress. Instead, one should regard them as very uncertain. One should first determine the beginning and the goal of the 70 weeks following <term>Luther: Martin Luther, whose German translation and commentaries often sought the plainest historical fulfillment of prophecy</term> as far as possible, and then see what kind of weeks fit between them.

->§ 7.<-

<term>Cyrus: Cyrus the Great (reigned c. 550–530 BC), the Persian king who issued the decree allowing the Jews to return from the Babylonian Captivity</term> issued his command more than 560 years before the death of Christ, but <term>Darius: Darius I (the Great), who reigned c. 522–486 BC and authorized the completion of the Temple</term> ruled at a time much closer to it. One must not exclude Cyrus entirely, because it was so grandly testified through <term>Isaiah: referring to the biblical book of Isaiah</term> that he would build Jerusalem (Chapters 44:26 and 45:13). Yet it is Darius through whom the edict of Cyrus, after so many hindrances, was finally put into full effect in accordance with the Word of God. Afterward, although the building of the city was not pursued at the same pace at all times, no other Persian king’s decree—whether favorable or unfavorable—was issued that referred back to Cyrus or Darius in the same way.

->§ 8.<-

The expression <note>original Hebrew: *moza dabar*</note> "the going forth of the word" or "the outcome of the matter" in Daniel 9:25 requires careful consideration. *Dabar* means a "word" when words are being quoted, or a "matter/thing" when speaking of events. The "matter" here was the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem. *Moza* means an "exit" or "going out." In human affairs, when something reaches its proper conclusion, we are accustomed to saying the matter has "turned out" <note>German: *ausgegangen*</note>. In every instance where the building of Jerusalem previously faced a standstill, the matter had to reach an "outcome" (as the text reads <note>original Latin: *impersonaliter*</note> "impersonally"). For success to be achieved, it required a divine command and a resolution from the Persian king, as well as the execution of the work by the people and their leaders. ->§ 9.<-

Destruction and building stand directly opposite one another: therefore, where destruction ends, building begins. The end of the seventy years of wrath over Jerusalem occurred in the second year of Darius, as noted in Zechariah 1:12 <note>original: "Zach. 1, 12"</note>. Immediately upon this, the building—and consequently the <term>seventy weeks: the period of 490 years prophesied in Daniel 9</term>—began. This is the reason why such a beginning cannot be postponed for more than sixty years until the seventh year of <term>Artaxerxes: Artaxerxes I Longimanus</term>. In no other historical timeline will one find such a massive gap between the proclamation of a period and its actual commencement. Those to whom the proclamation was made must have had either a share in its fulfillment or at least a near hope based on the circumstances then unfolding. Daniel himself did not necessarily have to live to see this beginning; however, to have seen it, he would not have needed to live ninety years from the time of his youth and captivity.

->§ 10.<-

Streets and moats <note>referring to Daniel 9:25, which says the city shall be built again with "street and wall" (or moat)</note> do not belong in the first 7 weeks, but rather in the course of the following 62 weeks. In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes <note>original: "Arthasastha"</note>, Nehemiah prepared the streets and moats. However, the seventh year of Artaxerxes does not precede that twentieth year by two full weeks <note>weeks of years, i.e., 14 years</note>, let alone seven weeks of years <note>49 years</note>. Therefore, the first 7 weeks—and consequently the entire 70 weeks—must begin a significant time before not only the 20th year but also the 7th year of Artaxerxes. They can begin nowhere else but in the second year of Darius.

### § 14.

Note this well: I do not add anything to the 70 weeks themselves; that would not be right, for the text mentions no more than 70 weeks. But the period commonly called "70 year-weeks" or 490 years by most interpreters does receive an addition. And since, by virtue of that expanded basis of determination, the "number seven" must be found not only in the years but also in their addition, the division of the 555 full years into 70 equal parts yields, for each of the 70 weeks, 2898 3/4 days. This is equal to 7 years and 7 times 7 times 7 days—that is, a year-week and a <term>cubic week of days: a calculation of 7³ (343) days</term> combined. This period, just as much as a precise 7 days or 7 years, is called a <term>Septimana: a Latin term for a "week" or group of seven</term> or **week**; and the full 70 weeks amount to 555 5/7 years. Concerning the second year of <term>Darius: Darius I, also known as Darius Hystaspis</term> in the books of Zechariah and Ezra, the following two propositions have long been established by others in the most thorough manner: 1. That the Darius mentioned in Zechariah and Ezra is Darius Hystaspis. 2. That the beginning of the 70 weeks is found in the books of Zechariah and Ezra. There is hardly a reputable interpreter who has not accepted one or the other of these two immovable propositions; however, due to a very common prejudice—that the 70 weeks cannot be more than 490 ordinary years—no one has been able to accept both together according to correct chronology, as it would imply a later beginning for the 70 weeks.

From so many futile efforts, one should have concluded that the error must lie in a place where it had not yet been sought. Now, one can find the correct path with these 70 weeks, which are extended beyond 490 years and yet still retain the actual "number seven" structure. This might indeed be accepted as a hallmark of truth.

->§ 15.<-

I do not attempt to prove this length of the 70 weeks solely from my apocalyptic temporal discourse; rather, after such a length has been derived through the comparison of the text and its fulfillment, I subsequently note the equality between a <term>Danielic week: a unit of seven years from the prophecy in Daniel 9</term> and half an <term>Apocalyptic month: a unit of time derived from the Book of Revelation</term> (see *Testimony* <note>original: "Zeugniß," referring to Bengel’s work *Cyclus, oder Zeugniß der Heilsamen Wahrheit*</note> page 248) and the proportion of the 555, 666 full years, etc. I do not present this as a proof, but as a pleasing harmony among the points already proven elsewhere. The years of the number 666 <note>A significant number in apocalyptic literature (Revelation 13:18), here used by the author as a chronological marker</note> have an addition, 555/555 | 5/9; and the seventy weeks—not as they are set at 490, but at 555 years—have this same proportioned addition of 555/555 | 5/9. I consider those months found in Revelation 11:2 to be ordinary months; but those in Chapter 13:5, etc., I consider to be prophetic. I do not exaggerate the significance of the "number seven," but wherever it appears, even unexpectedly, I take hold of it. Otherwise, the chronological structure of <term>Hallini: likely referring to the Latinized name of a chronologer such as Hall or a similar contemporary</term> does not come as close to mine as others, in that he makes these 70 weeks shorter than 490 ordinary years, whereas I make them longer. This should clarify the points that <term>Dr. Clauswitz: Benedikt Gottlieb Clauswitz (1707–1749), a theologian who critiqued Bengel’s system</term> very mildly reminded me of regarding my apocalyptic temporal resolution, pages 76, 98. These and other points may be judged individually as uncertain; however, anyone who grasps everything in its proper context will view it differently. In <term>deciphering: the process of breaking a code or cipher</term>, every individual character appears doubtful on its own; but the whole proves itself.

->§ 16.<-

Seven years together with an excess of 6 months are called "7 years" in 1 Kings 6:1, 38. <note>These verses describe the time taken to build Solomon's Temple, noting it was begun in the 4th year and finished in the 11th year of his reign</note> Therefore, seven years together with certain septenary numbers of days—provided it does not reach 8 years—can much more readily be called a "week" (I do not say a "year-week," but a "week"), even if many such weeks follow one another. Similarly, an <term>ordinary cubit: an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term> and a handbreadth above it...

### § 17.

Now we must decide whether the seventy weeks are better divided—according to the events that occurred—into segments of 7, 62, and 1, using either 555 5/9 years starting from the second year of Darius, or 490 years starting from the seventh year of Artaxerxes. 

### § 18.

If no interpretation is considered valid without a significant goal at the end of the first seven weeks <note>The "first seven weeks" refers to the initial 49-year period of Daniel's prophecy, usually associated with the rebuilding of Jerusalem</note>, then the prize goes to the one that assumes 49 years from the second year of <term>Darius Nothus: Darius II, a Persian king who reigned for 19 years</term> (who reigned for 19 years) to the 32nd year of his successor, Artaxerxes Mnemon. (See Nehemiah 13:6). From the seventh year of <term>Artaxerxes Longimanus: Artaxerxes I, known as "the long-handed"</term>, adding 49 years leads us to the 15th year of Darius Nothus; however, history provides nothing of particular note regarding this latter year. From the second year of <term>Darius Hystaspes: Darius the Great, who authorized the rebuilding of the Temple</term>, I arrive at the first year of Artaxerxes Longimanus after 55 full years. In the meantime, that king and Xerxes (the husband of Esther) undoubtedly showed themselves favorable toward the city of Jerusalem. (See Ezra 6:10, 7:23). That period already comprises nearly 55 years. Afterward, a certain negligence may have set in among the Jews until Ezra visited Judah and Jerusalem. (Ezra 7:14). In general, the transition from the seven weeks to the sixty-two weeks is not described so clearly in the text that one could demand from Scripture a specific historical report concerning a transition from the actual building process to a completed structural state, or anything of that nature.

->§ 19.<-

Between the 62 weeks and the final "One Week," the boundary line vanishes in the system of Dr. Clauswitz. <note>Clauswitz refers to Benedikt Gottlieb Clauswitz (1707–1749), a German theologian and contemporary of the author.</note> He is satisfied that the "strengthening of the covenant" in that final week <note>A reference to Daniel 9:27, "And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week."</note> accounts for the events from the baptism of the Savior until His death on the cross (which were completed in 2 years and roughly 4 months). Consequently, in his system, the first half of that "One Week," and a significant portion beyond it, remains empty. In my view, the 62 weeks extend very nearly to the <term>cutting off: a biblical term from Daniel 9:26 referring to the execution or death of the Messiah</term> of Christ—that is, to His death on the cross.

->§ 20.<-

Dr. Clauswitz very neatly places the 7th year of Artaxerxes in the year 4256 of the <term>Julian Period: a system used by scholars since the late 16th century to assign a unique number to every year since the beginning of a 7,980-year cycle</term>. And the death of Christ, which he makes the actual goal of the 70 weeks, occurred in the year 4743 of the Julian Period and the year 30 of the <term>Dionysian era: the common Anno Domini (AD) calendar system we use today</term> (§ 12). Thus, for the "seventy weeks," his calculation results in three full years fewer than 490 years <note>4743 minus 4256 equals 487 years, whereas seventy weeks of years should total 490.</note>. It should also not be entirely passed over in silence that if the 70 weeks were purely "year-weeks," they would undoubtedly coincide with the <term>Shemittoth: the Hebrew plural for the Sabbatical years, where the land was left fallow every seventh year</term>. By contrast, regarding the 30th and 33rd years of the Dionysian era—the former of which I identify as the year of the crucifixion, and the latter of which Dr. Clauswitz identifies as such—the situation was that a Sabbatical year only began late in the 33rd year, while the 30th year was far removed from one.

->§ 21.<-

Regarding the "One Week" and the "strengthening of the covenant," something has already been mentioned in § 11 and 19. This strengthening of the covenant began at the death of Christ (Matthew 26:28, Hebrews 9:15) and continued for "One Week" until the <term>Gentiles: non-Jewish people</term> were accepted without circumcision, which until that point had been an indispensable seal of the covenant (Acts 10).

## The Fifth Division.
# Of the Harmony of the Old and New Testaments.

->§ 1.<-

The great and good God, according to His infinite wisdom and immeasurable goodness, has joined together His purposes and arrangements for His own glory and our salvation <note>original: "Seelig-keit"; refers to the state of eternal blessedness or salvation.</note>. In a twofold manner, the glory of this great and good God presents itself to us: it is praised through works <note>Refers to the created world and acts of providence.</note> and through words. And for this reason, Scripture very often sings of both together. Ps. 19 and 119 <note>Psalm 19 begins with the heavens declaring God's glory (works) and moves to the perfection of the Law (words). Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, focusing entirely on the beauty of God's Word.</note>. Furthermore, even the works of power and grace exist through the Word. For as He speaks, so it happens; as He commands, so it stands firm. Ps. 33, 9. Whereby the excellence of the Word of God is most abundantly proven, just as it is also shown by the fact that it is called *God’s Word*. And so our salvation, which consists in fellowship with God through Christ, is preserved in this life and the life to come through the divine Word.

->§ 2.<-

The divine Word, as it is composed in writing, is the Holy Scripture, and this has two parts: the **Old** and the **New Testament**.

->§ 3.<-

These two parts are most intimately and inseparably connected, and together they constitute a whole, which proceeds from one single origin, deals with the same content, and brings those who follow it to one single goal <note>The author is emphasizing the concept of "Biblical Theology," where the two testaments are seen as a unified narrative of redemption rather than two different religions.</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the fifth division of the text, focusing on the unity of the Bible. It argues that God's glory is revealed through both His physical works and His written Word, which comprises the harmonized Old and New Testaments.</summary>

->§ 4.<-

From Moses until Malachi, within approximately a thousand years, the Scripture of the Old Testament was completed through the prophets; their sum <note>The "sum" refers to the core essence or central message of the writings.</note> is the promise of Christ and His advent, first in the flesh, and then in glory. There occurred, indeed, a considerable standstill <note>This refers to the "intertestamental period," a span of roughly 400 years between the last prophet of the Old Testament and the beginning of the New Testament events, often called the "years of silence."</note> in between, so that the waiting and longing among the faithful would be sharpened all the more. Finally, however, Christ came: for that Jesus is the Christ, whose advent happened in the flesh and shall happen in glory, He Himself made understood, and the Apostles and remaining witnesses have preached. And this testimony was presented, during a single generation <note>original: "Manns-Alters"; literally "a man's age," implying the span of about 30 to 40 years during which the New Testament was written.</note>, by the Apostles and Evangelists in the Scripture of the New Testament, together with a closer expectation of the glorious advent.

->§ 5.<-

The holy men who, over such a long period of time, have produced the Holy Scripture, constitute a fine number and are of great variety: yet they harmonize in a wondrous manner. The books of the Old Testament agree with one another: the books of the New Testament agree with one another: the books of both Testaments agree with one another.

->§ 6.<-

The books of the Old Testament are of three types:

1. the historical:
2. the teaching-books <note>original: "Lehr-Bücher"; these include the poetic and wisdom literature such as Psalms, Proverbs, and Job.</note>:
3. the prophetic.

And the books of the New Testament are likewise

1. historical,
2. teaching-books,
3. prophetic.

### § 14.

The Scripture lifts up the Church and sustains it. The Church gives testimony to the Scripture and preserves it. When the Church is vigorous, the Scripture shines; when the Church is sickly, the Scripture lies neglected. Accordingly, the condition of the Church and the Scripture usually appears as either healthy or sickly at the same time: and the treatment of the Scripture is directed from time to time by the state of the Church. This same treatment has had various periods and forms from the earliest times of the New Testament until the present day. 

The first kind could be called the natural and genuine; the second, the ethical or moralizing; the third, the meager; the fourth, the reviving; the fifth, the polemical—argumentative and focusing on dogmas and certain general practical applications; the sixth, the critical, adorned with many languages and <term>antiquities <note>The study of ancient history, customs, and artifacts to better understand the biblical world</note></term>, the <term>homiletical <note>Related to the art of preaching or writing sermons</note></term> kind, arranged for preaching. 

Thus, there has not yet arisen in the Church that experience and knowledge of Scripture which is proposed within Scripture itself. This is proven by the extravagant diversity of opinions and the obscurities in the Prophets that still cloud our eyes. We are gradually called further toward that power and skill in the Scripture which is manly and royal, and which approaches quite closely to the perfection of the Scripture. But beforehand, people will have to be purified through the <term>cross <note>German: *Creutz* — here referring to spiritual trials and suffering as a means of purification</note></term> and tribulations.

## The Sixth Section,
# Thoughts on the Passage
### Leviticus 16:8 ff. <note>In the original German, this is cited as "3 Mos." (The Third Book of Moses), the standard European naming convention for Leviticus.</note>

->§ 1.<-

When a house was cleansed from leprosy, two birds were taken, one of which was slaughtered, and the other was allowed to fly into the open field. Leviticus 14:49 ff. And the two goats have a great similarity to these <unclear>en</unclear> <note>The OCR indicates an unclear plural suffix here</note> two birds; one goat was slaughtered on the Day of Atonement, and the other was allowed to run free into the wilderness. Thus, the free run for the goat was nothing adverse, but rather a benefit.

->§ 2.<-

The goat that was slaughtered was, without any doubt, a <term>type <note>A "type" is a person, object, or event in the Old Testament that is understood to prefigure or foreshadow a person or event in the New Testament—in this case, Jesus Christ.</note></term> of Christ in His sacrifice for all our sins: and the free goat, which likewise carried away all the sins of the people, was just as much a type of Christ.

->§ 3.<-

The former signified Christ in His death; the latter signified Christ in His life: and because a single goat could not be slaughtered and simultaneously run alive into the wilderness, Aaron had to take two goats for this single figurative action.

...the goat’s blood and life. All the sins of the people were laid upon the solitary goat: it cost him nothing further, and yet, as soon as he was out of the people's sight, their sins also vanished. He might live on thereafter for as long as he wished in the wilderness and have his free dwelling there. In the same way, when Christ returned to life and to the Father in heaven, He carried away our sins without any further harm to Himself. He stands as our security. <note>German: "Er ist uns gut dafür"—an idiomatic way of saying He is our guarantor or surety.</note> 1 John 2:1, 2; John 16:10.

->§ 5.<-

What, then, is *Azazel*? <note>Azazel is the Hebrew term used in Leviticus 16:8 for the "scapegoat." Its meaning has been debated for centuries; some see it as a place, some as a demon, and others as a description of the goat's departure.</note> I side with those who recognize this as a *proper name* <note>Latin: *Nomen proprium*</note>, and I believe that Christ Himself is indicated by it. In Hebrew, a visible object is often used in place of its name to be understood in another sense <note>Latin: *Objectum loco nominis sui alio significatu accipiendi*</note>. Jeremiah 1:11, 12: "almond staff," <note>Hebrew: שקד (*shaqed*)</note> "watchfulness" <note>Hebrew: שקד (*shoqed*). The Hebrew words for "almond" and "watching" sound nearly identical, creating a symbolic pun.</note>. Jeremiah 19:1, 7: "a flask" <note>Hebrew: בקבק (*baqbuq*). The name mimics the sound of water gurgling out of a bottle, used here to symbolize the emptying out of the people.</note>. Amos 8:2: "summer fruit," <note>Hebrew: קיץ (*qayits*)</note> "end" <note>Hebrew: קיץ (*qets*)</note>. Judges 7:13: "roasted barley bread," <note>Hebrew: צליל לחם שעורים (*tselil lechem seorim*)</note> "a horrible sound of war" <note>Latin: *tinnitus belli horribilis*. The author is connecting the Hebrew word for "cake" or "rolling" (*tselil*) with the sound of clashing weapons.</note>.

->§ 6.<-

Thus, when one saw the goat running away freely, one could express it with this phrase: *Az Azel*, "the goat goes"; but *symbolically* it meant as much as: *Az*, the Strong One <note>In Hebrew, *az* means strong or fierce, while *ez* means goat; the author is drawing a symbolic connection between the two.</note>, Christ, the rightful overcomer who rose from death; *Azel*, has gone away, to God. See 1 John 3:5: "And you know that He appeared to take away our sins, and in Him is no sin."

# The Seventh Division,
## On the Right Way to Engage with Divine Things.

->§ 1.<-

The most important, best, and greatest matter that can happen to a person in this temporal life <term>Zeitlichkeit: the state of being in time rather than eternity; one's earthly life</term> does not consist in reaching the highest peaks or longest durations of science and skill, wealth and power, the gratification of the senses and desires, or advantages over their peers. Rather, it consists in finding oneself within the holy, blessed will of God in Christ Jesus during this earthly pilgrimage <term>Wallfahrt: a journey to a sacred place, used here as a metaphor for the Christian life</term>, and thus being able to attain eternal life. Whatever else a person sets as their goal is too short-sighted. Even if one were to prepare themselves most excellently to reach such worldly goals, they would still lack true wisdom and would have to accuse themselves for all eternity of acting contrary to right prudence.

->§ 2.<-

On God’s side, it is the Word of God, and on man’s side, it is faith, through which a person is brought into communion with God and thus to eternal salvation <term>Seligkeit: a state of supreme spiritual happiness or being "saved"</term>. What God tells us, we should allow to be told to us. As He teaches us, so should we allow ourselves to be taught.

->§ 3.<-

There is no doubt that when God created man, He endowed him with the knowledge <term>Erkäntniß: a deep, experiential understanding or insight</term> of God, of man, and of all creatures, and granted man the ability to practice such knowledge in the best possible way. Yet God also, even at that time <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "mal" at the top of the page indicates the German word "damals" (at that time) continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page introduces a new section focused on the proper pursuit of spiritual life, arguing that communion with God through faith and His Word is the only goal that truly matters. It defines the human life as a "pilgrimage" where worldly success is secondary to alignment with the divine will.</summary>
<keywords>pilgrimage, eternal life, Word of God, faith, divine knowledge, salvation, wisdom, prudence</keywords>

### § 10.

One has no more excellent proof of the truth and validity of the Holy Scripture, and of all the stories, teachings, promises, and threats contained within it, than the Holy Scripture itself. Just as the sun is seen through no other heavenly body—much less through a torch—but rather through itself, even if a blind man cannot comprehend it. And indeed, the sun cannot make a blind man see; but the Word of God has such power that it makes the blind see. This book is confirmed by such a magnificent body of evidence <term>Beweisthum: an older German term for a collection of proofs or a "demonstration" of truth</term>, permeating all ages and regions of the world, and carries with it such infallible characteristics that unbelief—even where it is strongest—betrays itself in its own weakness and is put to shame. The praises of the Holy Scripture make up a large part of the Holy Scripture itself; indeed, the entire Holy Scripture commends itself to us. For an exceeding amount depends upon it.

### § 11.

We must abide by this Word. If, in the world, the word of a single man often carries such weight that he himself upholds it, whatever the cost, and many others must also uphold it: how much more will Almighty God uphold His words, each and every one, even if heaven and earth were to collapse because of them. The suffering of the Son of God was unavoidable; why? Because the Scripture had to be fulfilled.

### § 12.

The effect of the Divine Word is supernatural. Sometimes it overtakes a person quite unexpectedly—most often one to whom it is something new—so that it takes him captive and kindles faith within him,

->of the right way of dealing with divine things, etc.<-

Evangelists and Apostles read publicly. At home, very few people have the opportunity, time, or skill to read the Holy Scripture clearly for themselves and to read it to others in an understandable way. Such a lack is compensated for through public reading, which is also frequently praised in the New Testament. The more arrangements there are here and there to ensure that the entire clear text of the Holy Scripture is made known to each and every person, the more certainly they will receive a complete report and understanding of what God has allowed to reach us. Nevertheless, scriptural interpretations and practical applications in sermons and writings also produce much fruit.

### § 19.

And such fruit is only obtained purely and abundantly when the spiritual delivery <note>original: "geiſtliche Vortrag"; referring to the style of preaching</note> agrees with the spiritual content, according to the manner described by the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 1, 2, and 3. Ingenious presentations, flowery embellishments, daring conclusions, and "lofty, strong, fiery" words—as people like to call them, though in truth they are ice-cold—do nothing for the matter. Where the supposed edification consists merely in an admiration of clever inventions, in a pleasing of thoughts, or a delighting of the ears—as happens in many so-called "pulpit orations"—one gains only what Paul calls a **nullification of the cross of Christ.** This is a plague that corrupts even in the "midday" of our time, which is widely considered to be enlightened. <note>The author is critiquing the theatrical or overly intellectual preaching style popular during the Enlightenment, arguing it lacks spiritual substance.</note>

### § 20.

In addition to the foundation of salvation, the Holy Scripture presents many other precious things to us. The books of which it consists did not come down to us by mere chance instead of others, as if those we have might just as easily have perished and others been preserved in their place. One should also not view them as mere little books of proverbs and examples, but as an incomparable account of the <term>Divine Economy</term> <note>From the Greek 'oikonomia,' referring to God's "household management" or His plan for governing and redeeming the world throughout history.</note> regarding all creatures, the human race, and especially the people of Israel and—

->§ 22.<-

Where one deals correctly with divine things, the boundaries between nature and grace are especially clearly distinguished. For this reason, we have two deviations to avoid at this time, which appear to move far apart but ultimately collide, as both fail to reach true grace and the purpose of Holy Scripture: namely, **false boasting of grace**, and the **exaltation of natural powers**. 

False boasting of grace has perhaps never been driven higher than in the <term>New Moravian soul-guidance</term> <note>original: "neumährischen Seelen-Führung"; referring to the Moravian Brethren or Herrnhuters under Count Zinzendorf, whose methods were controversial among traditional Pietists</note> and its collection of heart-conceits. In other respects, however, Holy Scripture is set so far aside that many (one does not wish to offend pure souls) become strangers to the voice of God. Among the learned, this seduction first rose to the high-ranking in the world, and then descended to the common people in both military and civic life. Those who do not inquire after the Word of God at all should have been let go from the start; one ought not to have set pen to paper on their behalf. # On the right way to deal with divine things, etc.

...of the **holy Trinity**, of the **Mediator** <note>a title for Jesus Christ, acting as the bridge between God and humanity</note>, of the **Order of Salvation**, of the **Sacraments**, of the **Last Things** <note>theological study of death, judgment, heaven, and hell</note>, and of many mysteries that were not known to the wisest of the heathens.

5. Some of these things reason perceives by itself; (this would also include what a heathen might take from the Holy Scripture if he viewed it not as a divine book, but as a good human book). Other things, however, it perceives from the Holy Scripture through **faith**.

6. In the latter case, reason is only an <term>organum</term> <note>original: "Organum"; a tool or organ used to perform a task</note> or <term>instrument</term>; but in the former case, it is a <term>principium</term> <note>original: "Principium"; a foundational principle or starting point</note> or ground. That is to say: the former is recognized only *through* reason, but the latter is also recognized *out of* reason.

7. Some things reason perceives to some extent by itself, but perceives those same things much more clearly from the Holy Scripture; and in that case, it acts more as an **instrument** than as a ground. This includes what was mentioned in Section 4, letters a, b, and c <note>referring to God's attributes, spirits, and the soul from the previous page</note>. How far reason can get on its own in these matters is difficult to perceive because of the "greater light" of the Holy Scripture; just as one cannot measure how far a lantern shines when the sun is out.

8. In the investigation of natural, material things and their properties, human reason, wit, diligence, and experience can go quite far. From this, much utility arises in common life, but also, through its misuse, no small amount of harm.

9. The highest utility that one can draw from this is the knowledge of the **Creator** of all things and of His **Providence**.

10. Also, by nature, some distinction between **good and evil** lies within the heart and conscience of man.

11. In those areas where reason provides a <term>principium</term> <note>foundation or basis</note>, such as in mathematics, natural philosophy, and logic <note>original: "Vernunft-lehre"</note>, one should grant the so-called **new philosophy**—about which there is such strong dispute—all its advantages. ## The Eighth Division,
# On Praying from the Heart.

->§ 1.<-

For a considerable time now, so-called **praying from the heart** has been frequently recommended to both the old and the young. This is of great benefit, as <term>souls eager for salvation</term> <note>original: "heilsbegierige Seelen"</note> are thereby most clearly instructed on how they can converse with God according to their own condition. In contrast, many who know of nothing but the customary prayers have no concept of prayer; they consider the reciting of the **Ten Commandments**, the **absolution formula**, and so on, to be "praying." Thus, they carefully proceed for the most part without actual prayer throughout their lives and even in death.

->§ 2.<-

Meanwhile, it appears as if a misunderstanding and misuse of such "praying from the heart" is threatening to take hold, as commonly happens with all wholesome instructions.

->§ 3.<-

Praying without prescribed words is good, and whoever is also able to sing in such a manner, let them be permitted to do so just as well: But praying and singing according to a prescribed form retains its value nonetheless.

->§ 4.<-

One can read from a prayer book, or hear another person read, or repeat the words from memory: the latter is the most convenient, because the <term>application of the mind</term> <note>original: "Application des Gemüths"; this refers to the mental effort and focus required to engage with a text or a thought.</note> required for reading or listening takes away a good portion of one's <term>devotion</term> to God. On the other hand, there is sometimes a fine <term>awakening</term> <note>original: "Erweckung"; a common term in Pietist circles for a moment of spiritual stirring or revitalization.</note> when one pays attention to an anointed formula without actually praying themselves, like someone who is allowed to eavesdrop as a third party on the conversation of two friends.

->§ 5.<-

Praying with one's own words can be turned into an ostentatious display: and praying with preconceived words can be practiced to the great glory of God and in true power.

->§ 6.<-

When such words that are truly appropriate for a deeply distressed or a deeply cheered soul come to mind without reflection, and flow forth so that the soul can pour itself out before God with them, it would not be right to stifle such words and instead resort to borrowed formulas. Rather, it would be desirable that one could always capture the newly-springing words of such souls in the very moment of their occurrence.

->§ 7.<-

Otherwise, however, where no particularly narrow or wide <term>disposition of the heart</term> is present, solid prescriptions—which one has made for oneself in brighter hours, or borrowed with careful choice from others—provide an acceptable aid. Even among those who are accustomed to praying with their own words, their words imperceptibly become something customary,

->§ 12.<-

In this consideration, all who love the truth will recognize that praying and singing according to certain <term>prescribed forms</term> <note>original: "Vorschriften"; written guides, liturgies, or established prayer rules.</note> is something very healing, and does not only belong to weak beginners; likewise, they will see that the Psalms have an incomparable precedence in this regard.

->§ 13.<-

Therefore, among the hymns, those are to be held as especially worthy which are derived from the Psalms or which carry with them a New Testament <term>practical application</term> <note>original: "Nutzanwendung"; a common Pietist term for the personal spiritual lesson or moral "use" derived from a scripture passage.</note>.

->§ 14.<-

In this, a person praying or singing can make use of what he finds before him with all freedom and without any compulsion: standing still here and there, inserting his own good thoughts and desires in between, expanding or supplementing what does not suit him, and so forth. For in general, in prayer, according to the <term>disposition of the heart</term> <note>original: "Herzens-Fassung"; the specific emotional and spiritual state of the person at the moment of prayer.</note> at any given time, the alternation between prescribed and newly-occurring words is the best means to maintain the conversation with God, until the person in prayer has emptied his heart—or, as one might see it, filled it—and thereby receives his leave for that time.

->§ 15.<-

Everyone knows already that the choice remains open to him to use whatever is most suitable for him at any time. It also happens that one finds oneself best off with the <term>golden text</term> <note>original: "güldenen Text"; a reference to the direct, "pure" words of the Bible itself as the most precious foundation for prayer.</note> alone.

->E N D E.<-

<summary>This concluding page argues that structured prayer and psalms are valuable for all believers, offering a flexible framework that can be combined with spontaneous personal thoughts. It emphasizes the "healing" nature of liturgical forms and the ultimate authority of the scriptural text.</summary>
